paper.title: Praxis: Practical Witness Encryption for NP

nodes.label: Lemma 3.7
nodes.name: Extractability implies hiding
nodes.statement: If $\mathsf{WE}$ is extractable with error $\delta$ and any extraction time, then for every instance $S$ that has no witness, all $m_0, m_1 \in \{0,1\}^\mu$, and every adversary $\mathcal{A}$ as in Definition 3.6, the probabilities $p_b := \Pr\bigl[ \mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{O}}(ct) = 1 : ct \leftarrow \mathsf{Enc}^{\mathcal{O}}(S, m_b) \bigr]$, for $b \in \{0,1\}$, satisfy $|p_1 - p_0| \le 2\,\delta(t, Q, Q_H)$. That is, $\mathsf{WE}$ is hiding in the sense of Garg, Gentry, Sahai, and Waters \cite{STOC:GGSW13}, with error $2\delta$.
nodes.proof: Replacing every output of $\mathcal{A}$ other than $1$ by $0$ changes neither the probabilities $p_b$ nor the resources, so let $\mathcal{A}$ output a bit $b'$. As $S$ has no witness, the event of Definition 3.6 is $b' = b$, so $\frac12 + \frac12 (p_1 - p_0) = \Pr[b' = b] \le \frac12 + \delta(t, Q, Q_H)$; likewise with $p_0 - p_1$ for the adversary that outputs $1 - b'$.
nodes.explain: If a witness encryption scheme is extractable with error δ, then on every instance without a witness the adversary accepts encryptions of m_0 and m_1 with probabilities at most 2δ apart. Proof idea: On a false instance the extractor can never output a witness, so the extractability event is simply b′ = b.

nodes.label: Lemma 4.5
nodes.name: Rank bound
nodes.proof:
(a) Let $M$ be the matrix of all rows of all $W_c$, of rank $d := \operatorname{rank} \mathbf{W}$, and fix $u$. Choose $d$ linearly independent columns of $M$, column $0$ among them unless it is zero. Given the entries of $r$ at the other indices in $[N]$, at most one value modulo $q$ of its entries at the chosen indices solves $M r = u$. Each of the independent entries $r_1, \dots, r_N$ takes a given value modulo $q$ with probability at most $1/g$, as $g + 1 < q$; so does $r_0$ given all of them. Hence $\Pr[M r = u] \le g^{-d}$, as in Odlyzko's lemma \cite[Lemma 3.1]{NW22}. If the row space is spanned by $d$ unit vectors $e_i$ with $i \in [N]$, then $(W_c r)_c$ is an injective linear function of the $d$ entries $r_i$, which take each of their $g^d$ values with probability $g^{-d}$.
(b) Write $v = \sum_c W_c^\top z_c$. Then $v^\top r = \sum_c z_c^\top W_c r$ is a function of $(W_c r)_c$, so it takes one value whenever $(W_c r)_c$ takes its likeliest value, and $\operatorname{gp}(v^\top) \ge \operatorname{gp}(\mathbf{W})$.
nodes.explain: (a) gp(W) ≤ g^(−rank W) for every stack W, with equality if the row space is spanned by unit vectors. (b) gp(v^⊤) ≥ gp(W) for every v in the row space of W. Proof idea: (a) Fix rank-many independent columns: given the other entries of r, at most one value of the chosen entries works, each with probability at most 1/g. (b) v^⊤r is a function of the products W_c·r.

nodes.label: Lemma 4.7
nodes.name: QAP criterion
nodes.proof:
By the table of Definition 4.6, (a) holds exactly when $P_W(d_j) = 0$ for every $j$ and the values of $R_W$ sum to zero over each coset. Let $R(X)$ be any polynomial in $\mathbb{F}_q^{<\nu n_{\mathsf{c}}}[X]$, as every allowed polynomial is. The identity of (b) holds with this $R$ and some $h$ exactly when $Z(X)(X - \rho)$, the vanishing polynomial of $\mathcal{P}$, divides $P_W - W_{00} L_\rho - Z_0 R$, whose values are zero at $\rho$ and $d_0$, $P_W(d_j)$ at $d_j$, and $P_W(p) - Z_0(p)\, R(p)$ at a point $p$ of a coset. So it holds exactly when $P_W(d_j) = 0$ for every $j$ and $R = R_W$, the interpolant of the $\nu\,n_{\mathsf{c}}$ values on the cosets; likewise that of (c), where $Z(X)$ divides $P_W - Z_0 R$. So (b) and (c) each hold exactly when $P_W(d_j) = 0$ for every $j$ and $R_W$ is allowed, and then only with $R = R_W$.

Finally, by the paragraph before Lemma 4.7, $R_W$ is allowed exactly when its values sum to zero over each coset. The degree bounds hold because $P_W$ has degree at most $2D - 2$, $L_\rho$ and $Z_0 R_W$ at most $D - 1$, and $Z$ exactly $D - 1$.
nodes.explain: A symmetric matrix W passes every test of the system if and only if P_W − W_(00)·L_ρ = h·Z·(X − ρ) + Z_0·R for a polynomial h and an allowed R, if and only if P_W = h′·Z + Z_0·R. Then R is the interpolant R_W, deg h < D − 1 and deg h′ < D. Proof idea: Read both sides at the evaluation points; a remainder is allowed exactly when its values sum to zero on every coset.

nodes.label: Lemma 5.4
nodes.name: Honest combination
nodes.statement:
Let $w$ be a witness of $S$ and $ct$ an output of $\mathsf{Enc}(\mathsf{pp}, m)$ (Figure [full-enc]), for any coins, with scalars $\gamma_c$ and $\kappa$ as there, with weights $\xi_c(w)$ for the forms of its matrix $M$. Then the divisions of Equation [cancel] are exact, and the combinations defined by $\mathsf{Comb}$ in Figure [full-dec] give
\[
 \Lambda = [\xi_{\mathrm{key}}(w)\, \kappa + r(w)\, \psi]_T, \qquad
 \Psi = [\psi]_T, \qquad
 \Lambda^\alpha = \alpha \cdot \Lambda, \qquad
 \Psi^\alpha = \alpha \cdot \Psi,
\]
where $\psi := y(w) \sum_{c \in C} \gamma_c\, \xi_c(w)$.
nodes.proof: As in Section 5.1, the summed factors pair to the sum of $\xi_c(w)\, w_i w_j$ times $F^{k_1}_i H^{\mathrm{leg}}_j$, whose terms $\pm \gamma_c\, y(w)\, A_w(\tau)$ cancel: the search term $r(w)\, \psi$, the QAP term $\sum_c \xi_c(w)\, \gamma_c\, A_w(\tau)\, B_w(\tau)$, and the masks' term $y(w) \sum_c \xi_c(w)\, \pi_{k_1} w^\top \vartheta_{\mathrm{leg}}$. The first identity of Equation [qap-w] serves the key copy, where $\gamma_{c_{\mathrm{key}}} L_\rho(\tau) = \kappa$, and the second the others; the powers suffice, as $h_{\mathrm{key}}, h_{\mathrm{oth}} \in \mathbb{F}_q^{<D}[X]$ with $D \le J\Delta$ and $R_w$ is allowed (Lemma 4.7), and each sum over the chunks encodes what one pairing with the whole polynomial would (Section 5.2). The tie polynomials of the honest stack, which satisfies the ties (Section 2.4), are $w$ times the numerators in Equation [cancel]; as $w_0 = 1$, the divisions are exact, and the bases of $\mathsf{B}_w$ suffice, as the factors lie in $\mathbb{F}_q^{<n}[T]$. By the mask identity, the pairing of $\mathsf{Y}_w$ with $\mathsf{B}_w$ encodes the masks' term. Finally, $\Psi$ encodes $\sum_c \xi_c(w)\, \pi_{k_1} y(w)\, s_{\mathrm{leg}} = \psi$, and $(\Lambda^\alpha, \Psi^\alpha) = \alpha \cdot (\Lambda, \Psi)$, as $\mathsf{Comb}$ is linear in $ct_2$ and $ct_2^\alpha = \alpha \cdot ct_2$.
nodes.explain: For a witness w and any coins of Enc, the combinations computed by Dec are Λ = [ξ_(key)(w)·κ + r(w)·ψ]_T and Ψ = [ψ]_T, and their α-copies are α times these. Proof idea: Expand the pairing of the summed factors; the QAP identities of w cancel the QAP term and the mask identity cancels the masks.

nodes.label: Lemma 5.5
nodes.name: Search range
nodes.statement: Let $w \in \{0,1\}^{N+1}$ with $w_0 = 1$, and let $r$ and $c_w$ be those of Figure [enc], Figure [dec], or $r \leftarrow \mathcal{D}_g$ and the center of Section 5.2. Then $|r(w) - c_w| \le B$ for every $r$ in the support, and the expectation of $(r(w) - c_w)^2$ is at most $\bigl( g \sqrt{(1 + \operatorname{wt}(w))/12} + 1/2 \bigr)^2$ in the first case and $\bigl( g \sqrt{(N+4)/48} + 3/2 \bigr)^2$ in the second.
nodes.proof:
In the first case, $r(w)$ is the sum of the $1 + \operatorname{wt}(w)$ entries $r_i$ with $w_i = 1$, which are independent, each within $(g-1)/2$ of its mean $(g+3)/2$ and of variance $(g^2 - 1)/12$. The mean $(1 + \operatorname{wt}(w))(g+3)/2$ of $r(w)$ is a multiple of $1/2$, and $c_w$ is its floor, so $|r(w) - c_w| \le (1 + \operatorname{wt}(w))(g-1)/2 + 1/2 \le B$, and the second claim follows by Minkowski's inequality in $L^2$.

In the second case, let $a := \lceil N(g+1)/2 \rceil$, $\Sigma := \sum_{i \in [N]} r_i$, and $X := r_\star + \sum_{i \in [N]} (w_i - 1/2)\, r_i$, a sum of independent terms with mean $\mu := \frac{g+3}{2} (1 + \operatorname{wt}(w) - N/2)$. Then $r(w) = a + X + \Sigma/2 - \lfloor \Sigma/2 \rfloor$ and $c_w = \lfloor a + \mu \rfloor$, so $r(w) - c_w$ is $X - \mu$ plus two rounding errors, $\Sigma/2 - \lfloor \Sigma/2 \rfloor \le 1/2$ and $a + \mu - \lfloor a + \mu \rfloor < 1$. The term $r_\star$ of $X$ is within $(g-1)/2$ of its mean and each other term within $(g-1)/4$, so $|r(w) - c_w| \le (N+2)(g-1)/4 + 3/2 \le B$. The variance of $X$ is $(1 + N/4)(g^2 - 1)/12$, so the second claim follows by Minkowski's inequality in $L^2$.
nodes.explain: |r(w) − c_w| ≤ B for every r in the support of the sampler, and E[(r(w) − c_w)²] ≤ (g·√((N+4)/48) + 3/2)² for the centered sampler. Proof idea: r(w) − c_w is a sum of independent centered terms plus two rounding errors.

nodes.label: Theorem 5.6
nodes.name: Correctness
nodes.statement: For every admissible choice of evaluation points, Praxis as specified in Appendix A is correct with error $2/q$ (Definition 3.5). For a witness $w$, decryption fails exactly when $\xi_{\mathrm{key}}(w) = 0$.
nodes.proof:
If $\xi_{\mathrm{key}}(w) = 0$, $\mathsf{Dec}$ (Figure [full-dec]) returns $\bot$. Otherwise, by Lemma 5.4, $\Lambda' = t_0 \cdot \Psi^\alpha$ for $t_0 := r(w) - c_w$, and $|t_0| \le B$ by Lemma 5.5. If $\Psi^\alpha \ne 0$, it has order $q > 2B + 1$, so line [full-search] sets $t = t_0$. If $\Psi^\alpha = 0$, line [full-search] sets $t = 0$, and $\Psi = 0$, as $\alpha \ne 0$. In both cases $K = \xi_{\mathrm{key}}(w)^{-1} \cdot ( \Lambda - r(w) \cdot \Psi ) = [\kappa]_T$, and $\mathsf{Dec}$ returns $\tilde{m} \oplus H_{\mathsf{key}}([\kappa]_T) = m$.

Finally, by Definition 5.1, as $w_0 = 1$, $z(w) - 1$ is linear, without constant term, in the coefficients of the $M_{i,j}$. So $\xi_{\mathrm{key}}(w) = U_0(w)$, a coefficient of $z(w) \cdot \sigma^{n/2-1}(z(w))$, is a polynomial of degree at most two in these coefficients, with value $1$ when all are zero. They are uniform and independent over the choice of $H_{\mathsf{seed}}$, and independent of $w$, which is fixed before $H_{\mathsf{seed}}$ (Definition 3.5), so $\xi_{\mathrm{key}}(w) = 0$ with probability at most $2/q$ by the Schwartz--Zippel lemma \cite{Sch80,Zip79}.
nodes.explain: Praxis is correct with error 2/q: decryption with a witness w returns the message unless ξ_(key)(w) = 0. Proof idea: By the honest combination the search target is (r(w) − c_w)·Ψ^α, which lies in the search range; Schwartz–Zippel bounds Pr[ξ_(key)(w) = 0].

nodes.label: Proposition 5.7
nodes.name: Efficiency
nodes.statement:
For Praxis as specified in Appendix A, with the evaluation points placed in $\mathcal{H}$ as in Section 4.4 and $n \le D$, and with $n_1 := (2K_1 + 1)(N+1) + \Delta + (\nu - 1)n_{\mathsf{c}}/J'$ and $n_2 := 6K_2 (N+1) + 3K_2 + \frac{3n}{2}(J + J') + 13n - 8$:

 
(a) \emph{Size.} A ciphertext consists of $n_1$ elements of $\mathbb{G}_1$, $2 n_2$ of $\mathbb{G}_2$, one of $\mathbb{G}_T$, the seed, and $\mu$ bits.
(b) \emph{Encryption.} $\mathsf{Enc}$ computes one scalar multiplication of a generator for each of these group elements and one more in $\mathbb{G}_T$.
(c) \emph{Decryption.} Outside line [full-search], $\mathsf{Dec}$ computes $18K_2 + 4J + 2J' + 2$ pairings; at most $(2K_1 + 1) N$ additions and MSMs (sums $\sum_{i \le s} a_i P_i$ of length $s$) of total length at most $3n + 2D + (\nu - 1)n_{\mathsf{c}}$ in $\mathbb{G}_1$; at most $12 K_2 N$ additions and MSMs of total length $3n\,(J + J') + 26n - 16$ in $\mathbb{G}_2$; and $18K_2 + 4J + 2J' + 1$ additions and four scalar multiplications in $\mathbb{G}_T$.
(d) \emph{Search.} line [full-search] can be computed with $O(\sqrt{|t|} + 1)$ operations in $\mathbb{G}_T$, where $t$ is its result. On a ciphertext of $\mathsf{Enc}$, this is $O(\sqrt{g}\, N^{1/4})$ operations in expectation over the coins of $\mathsf{Enc}$.

Each of $\mathsf{Enc}$ and $\mathsf{Dec}$ also makes $k(\ell + 1)$ queries to $H_{\mathsf{seed}}$ and at most one to $H_{\mathsf{key}}$, and performs $O(n_1 + n_2 + k(\ell + 1)\, d_R \log d_R + n \log n + D \log D + |S|)$ operations in $\mathbb{F}_q$. $\mathsf{Setup}$ performs $O(|S| + D \log D + \log q)$.
nodes.proof:
Parts (a) to (c) count Figure [full-enc], Figure [full-dec]: a sum over an index, or a single multiple in $\mathbb{G}_2$, is an MSM unless it is a sum of pairings or has the bits of $w$ as coefficients, and line [full-target], line [full-key] of $\mathsf{Dec}$ take additions and four scalar multiplications in $\mathbb{G}_T$. In $\mathbb{F}_q$, $\mathsf{Dec}$ computes the forms at $w$ as $k(\ell + 1)$ products in $R_q$, by number-theoretic transforms, and $\mathsf{Enc}$ computes $z$ at its three points by prefix sums along each $M_{i,j}$. $\mathsf{Enc}$ computes the scalar of each published element with $O(1)$ more operations, and $\mathsf{Dec}$ the weights and the cancellation polynomials with $O(1)$ products of polynomials of degree below $n$, each from four products of their halves by fast Fourier transforms over the subgroup of $\mathcal{H}$ of order $2^{\lceil \log_2 n \rceil}$, which exists as $n \le D$. In the order of Section 4.4, the vanishing polynomial of a range of $\mathcal{H}$ is a product of $O(\log D)$ binomials $X^{2^b} - c$, and the interpolant of values on a range $\mathcal{P}'$ is $f / Z'$, where $Z'$ is that of $\mathcal{H} \setminus \mathcal{P}'$ and $f$ interpolates on $\mathcal{H}$ the values times $Z'$, and zero elsewhere. $\mathsf{Setup}$ keeps each $A_i$ and $B_i$ as its nonzero values on $\mathcal{P}$, so $\mathsf{Enc}$ evaluates them at $\tau$ by the Lagrange basis, and $\mathsf{Dec}$, which interpolates only $A_w$ and $B_w$, computes its polynomials by fast Fourier transforms over $\mathcal{H}$, multiplying by halves in the same way and dividing by one binomial at a time \cite[Section 1]{Pol71}. $\mathsf{Setup}$ computes the powers of $\omega$ and of a generator of $\mathcal{H}$, the vanishing polynomials it needs at each point from their binomials, the interpolation weights from them by simultaneous inversion, and the stored values: $O(|S| + D \log D)$ operations, as $n \le D$, and $O(\log q)$ for the roots of unity.

For (d), search the intervals $|t| \le 4^j$ for $j = 0, 1, \dots$, the last cut at $B$, each with $O(2^j)$ operations by baby steps and giant steps \cite[pp. 419--420]{Sha71}, and return the solution of least absolute value in the first interval that has one: a result $t$ is found after $O(\sqrt{|t|} + 1)$, and if there is none the search ends after the interval cut at $B$, with $O(\sqrt{B})$ operations. On a ciphertext of $\mathsf{Enc}$, $t$ is $r(w) - c_w$ or $0$ (Theorem 5.6), and $\sqrt{|r(w) - c_w|}$ has expectation at most $\bigl( g \sqrt{(N+4)/48} + 3/2 \bigr)^{1/2}$ by the second case of Lemma 5.5 and Jensen's inequality; with the independent entries of Figure [enc] and the center of Figure [dec] (Section 5.1), the first case gives at most $\bigl( g \sqrt{(N+1)/12} + 1/2 \bigr)^{1/2}$, as $\operatorname{wt}(w) \le N$, of the same order.
nodes.explain: Exact counts of group elements in a ciphertext, of scalar multiplications in Enc, of pairings and multi-scalar multiplications in Dec; the final search takes O(√|t| + 1) operations in G_T, which is O(√g · N^(1/4)) in expectation. Proof idea: Count the specification line by line; search growing intervals by baby steps and giant steps.

nodes.label: Corollary 5.8
nodes.name: Asymptotic costs
nodes.statement:
With these parameters and the evaluation points placed in $\mathcal{H}$ as in Section 4.4, for systems of linear size (Section 4.1) with $N \ge \lambda^2$:

 
(a) \emph{Size.} A ciphertext has $O(\lambda N)$ field elements.
(b) \emph{Encryption.} $\mathsf{Enc}$ takes $O(\lambda^2 N / \log \lambda)$ field operations.
(c) \emph{Decryption.} $\mathsf{Dec}$ takes $O(\lambda N \log \lambda)$ field operations outside line [full-search]. In it, $\mathsf{Dec}$ takes $O(2^{\lambda/4} N^{1/4})$ field operations in expectation over the coins of $\mathsf{Enc}$.
nodes.proof: As $\nu \le 2F_{\max}$ (Section 4.4), $D \le N + 2 + 2 F_{\max}\,n_{\mathsf{c}} = O(N)$ and $\log D < \log q = O(\lambda)$. As $N \ge \lambda^2$, $n = O(N)$, and (a) follows. The work in $\mathbb{F}_q$ is $O(\lambda N \log \lambda)$, by (a) and as $k(\ell + 1)\, d_R = O(\lambda N)$. $\mathsf{Enc}$ also computes $O(\lambda N)$ multiples of each generator, in $O(\lambda N \cdot \lambda / \log(\lambda N))$ group operations, precomputed multiples included \cite[Section 3]{Pip80}. $\mathsf{Dec}$'s $O(\lambda)$ pairings, $O(\lambda N)$ additions, and MSMs and scalar multiplications, with $O(N)$ scalars at $O(\lambda)$ group operations each, take $O(\lambda N)$ field operations. The search is Proposition 5.7(d), which compares elements of $\mathbb{G}_T$, with $\sqrt{g} = \Theta(2^{\lambda/4})$.
nodes.explain: For systems of linear size with N ≥ λ²: a ciphertext has O(λN) field elements, Enc takes O(λ²N / log λ) field operations, Dec takes O(λN log λ) plus an expected O(2^(λ/4) N^(1/4)) for the search. Proof idea: Substitute the asymptotic parameter choices into Proposition 5.7.

nodes.label: Theorem 5.9
nodes.name: Extraction
nodes.statement:
Let the parameters be admissible, that is, satisfy (P1) to (P5) below. There is an extractor $\mathcal{E}$ (Appendix B.6) such that for every system $S$ of the shape, every choice of evaluation points that meets the conditions of Definition 4.6, all $m_0, m_1 \in \{0,1\}^\mu$, and every adversary $\mathcal{A}$ that on every run makes at most $Q < 2^\lambda$ calls to $\mathcal{O}_{\mathsf{GG}}$ and at most $2^\lambda$ queries to each RO:

 
(a) \emph{Extraction.} Let $s_0$ and $s_1$ be the advantages against $\mathsf{MSIS}_{k,\ell,\beta}$ (Definition 3.3) of the reductions $\mathcal{B}_0$ and $\mathcal{B}_1$ of Appendix B.5, which run $\mathcal{A}$ once and do not use its output. In the experiment of Definition 3.6,
 \[
 \Pr\bigl[\, \mathcal{A} \text{ queries } H_{\mathsf{key}} \text{ at } [\kappa]_T \;\wedge\; \mathcal{E} \text{ outputs no witness of } S \bigm| b \,\bigr] \le \frac{Q+1}{2^\lambda} + s_b .
 \]
(b) \emph{Soundness.} On every input, every output of $\mathcal{E}$ is $\bot$ or a witness of $S$.
(c) \emph{Running time.} $\mathcal{E}$ runs in time $O\bigl( (Q+1) (nN + |S|) + L \bigr)$, where $|S|$ is the length of $S$ (Section 3.5) and $L$ counts the labels given to $\mathcal{A}$ (the generators' and the ciphertext's).
nodes.proof:
From here on, $u := 2Q + 2$. A run in $\mathsf{Tgt}$ has a first mark, which is $\mathsf{init}$, $\mathsf{guess}$, charged, or good. So the rows cover $\mathsf{Tgt} \wedge \mathsf{Fail}$, and $f_i$ is at most the sum of their bounds for $b = i$. Each bound is at most what pays for it, with terms of $E(u)$ to spare, as $E$ and $\varepsilon_f$ are those of the Lean statement (Section 6.4): the row $\mathsf{guess}$ is at most $2^{\lambda}/N_{\mathsf{free}}$ (Lemma B.13), within the fifth term, and a good mark's two rows sum to $s_i + 2\varepsilon_f + 2/q \le s_i + (8u + 8)\, \varepsilon_f$. So $f_i \le E(u) + s_i$, and by (P5) and Lemma B.2, $E(u) \le (Q+1)/2^\lambda$, which gives (a).

Part (b) is Lemma B.16(a). For (c), a call makes at most three records and one difference, of $O(K_1 N + n)$ entries each, by $O(1)$ table and $O(K_1 N + n)$ field operations: a linear combination or, for a pairing, by the formula above, $K_1$ sums over the legs and a combination of the vectors $a_{k_1}$ for each $l$ and sector. A test costs $O(N)$ for the row echelon form and $O(N + |S|)$ for each of at most four candidates, and each of at most $Q$ results has at most four tests. The start samples $9n(N + 1)$ numbers and enters $L$ labels, whose records are written out when a call first uses them, within its $O(K_1 N + n)$ operations. So $\mathcal{E}$ runs in time $O\bigl( (Q+1)(K_1 N + n + |S|) + nN + L \bigr)$, which is the bound, as $K_1 \le n$ and $N \ge 1$.
nodes.explain: For admissible parameters there is one extractor E such that, for every adversary making Q < 2^λ group-oracle calls: (a) Pr[A queries H_(key) at [κ]_T and E outputs no witness | b] ≤ (Q+1)/2^λ + s_b, where s_b is the Module-SIS advantage of the reduction B_b; (b) every output of E is ⊥ or a witness; (c) E runs in time O((Q+1)(nN + |S|) + L). Proof idea: Every run that reaches the target query has a first mark. Each kind of first mark (init, guess, charged, good with a kernel vector, good without one) is paid by a term of the budget E(2Q+2) or by s_b.

nodes.label: Corollary 5.10
nodes.name: Extractability error
nodes.statement: For admissible parameters, Praxis is extractable with error $\delta$ and the extraction time of Theorem 5.9(c), where $\delta(t, Q, Q_H) = (Q+1)/2^{\lambda+1} + \mathrm{Adv}^{\mathsf{MSIS}}(t_R)$ if $Q < 2^\lambda$ and $Q_H \le 2^\lambda$, and $\delta = 1/2$ otherwise. Here $t_R = t + O(Q + d_R\, Q_H + \mu) + \mathsf{poly}(D, \log q)$ bounds the reductions' running time (Proposition B.15), and $\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathsf{MSIS}}(t_R)$ is the largest advantage against $\mathsf{MSIS}_{k,\ell,\beta}$ of an algorithm, with any advice, that runs in time at most $t_R$. Running times are as in Appendix B.5, descriptions and advice included.
nodes.proof: Within the caps, Theorem 5.9(a) and Lemma B.10 bound the probability of the event of Definition 3.6 by $1/2 + (Q+1)/2^{\lambda+1} + (s_0 + s_1)/4$, and $s_0, s_1 \le \mathrm{Adv}^{\mathsf{MSIS}}(t_R)$, as $\mathcal{B}_0$ and $\mathcal{B}_1$ carry $\mathcal{A}$'s advice, sample the oracles lazily (R1), and run in time at most $t_R$. Otherwise $1/2 + \delta = 1$; the proof of (c) uses neither cap.
nodes.explain: Praxis is extractable with error δ = (Q+1)/2^(λ+1) + Adv^(MSIS)(t_R), for Q < 2^λ group-oracle calls, where t_R = t + O(Q + d_R·Q_H + μ) + poly(D, log q) bounds the running time of the two reductions. Proof idea: Theorem 5.9(a) bounds the two target-query probabilities, Lemma B.10 turns them into a distinguishing bound, and the reductions run within t_R.

nodes.label: Lemma B.2
nodes.name: Generic bound
nodes.statement: $E$ is a polynomial of degree two in $u$ with nonnegative coefficients. If $E(2) \le 2^{-\lambda}$ and $E(2^{\lambda+1}) - E(2) \le 1 - 2^{-\lambda}$, then $E(2Q + 2) \le (Q+1)/2^\lambda$ for every integer $0 \le Q < 2^\lambda$. For $\lambda \ge 1$, the second premise requires $\theta < 2^{-(2\lambda + 1)}$.
nodes.proof: Every term of $E(u)$ is a polynomial in $u$ with nonnegative coefficients, as $L \ge 1$, of degree two for $N_{\mathrm{cmp}}(u)$ and at most two otherwise. So $Q \mapsto E(2Q+2) - (Q+1)/2^\lambda$ is convex; by the premises it is at most $0$ at $Q = 0$ and at $Q = 2^\lambda - 1$, where it is $E(2^{\lambda+1}) - 1$, hence in between. For $\lambda \ge 1$, $E(2^{\lambda+1}) - E(2) \ge \bigl(N_{\mathrm{cmp}}(2^{\lambda+1}) - N_{\mathrm{cmp}}(2)\bigr)\theta > \frac12 (2^{2\lambda+2} - 6)\,\theta$, which for $\theta \ge 2^{-(2\lambda+1)}$ is at least $1 - \frac32\, 2^{-2\lambda} > 1 - 2^{-\lambda}$.
nodes.explain: The budget E(u) is a quadratic in u with nonnegative coefficients. If E(2) ≤ 2^(−λ) and E(2^(λ+1)) − E(2) ≤ 1 − 2^(−λ), then E(2Q+2) ≤ (Q+1)/2^λ for every Q < 2^λ. Proof idea: Convexity: the difference is at most zero at both ends of the range, hence in between. Note: E has pieces that no lemma of the paper draws on, among them the “+L” of its first term, most of its fifth term, and its sixth term. The paper says its bounds fit “with terms of E(u) to spare”, because E is the bound of the Lean statement.

nodes.label: Lemma B.3
nodes.name: Degrees
nodes.statement: Let $\varpi := \Omega_{22}\, \zeta\, \zeta'\, \zeta''\, \varepsilon$ and $d_f := 3D + 2n + 2K_1 + 6$. For every expression $\mathsf{D}$ of $\mathbb{G}_T$ and every $\chi \in \mathbb{F}_q$, the function $\varpi \cdot \bigl( \operatorname{val}(\mathsf{D}; \mathbf{c}, r) - \chi\kappa \bigr)$ is a polynomial in the entries of $\mathbf{c}$ and of $r$ of total degree at most $d_f$. For expressions $\mathsf{E}, \mathsf{E}'$ of $\mathbb{G}_1$ or of $\mathbb{G}_2$, the same bound holds for $\varpi \cdot \bigl( \operatorname{val}(\mathsf{E}) - \operatorname{val}(\mathsf{E}') \bigr)$.
nodes.proof: Here $\gamma_c = \pi_{k_1} s_{\mathrm{leg}}$ has degree $k_c + 3 \le n + 2$, the entries of $z_-$, $z_\circ$, and $z_+$ have degree below $n$ in $\upsilon$, $A_i$, $B_j$, and $L_\rho$ have degree below $D$, $Z_c$ has degree $D - 1$, or $D$ for $c = c_{\mathrm{key}}$, where $k_c = 0$, $Z_0$ has degree $N + 2$, and the five factors of $\varpi$ clear every denominator. As $n \le D$, every exponent of $\mathcal{X}_1$ has degree at most $d_1 := \max\{D + 2K_1, \Delta\}$, and $\varpi$ times every exponent of $\mathcal{X}_2$, an $\alpha$-copy included, at most $d_2 := D + n + 7 + (J-1)\Delta$: the $\mathsf{B}^{\mathrm{quo}}_{c,j}$ reach $D + n + 6 + (J-1)\Delta$, and the $\mathsf{B}^{\mathrm{rem}}_{c,j}$ at most $N + n + 9 + (J'-1)\Delta' \le D + n + 7$, as $(J'-1)\Delta' \le \nu n_{\mathsf{c}} = D - N - 2$, also when $n_{\mathsf{c}} = 0$. So the first function has degree at most $d_1 + d_2$, also for its terms $\varpi\alpha\kappa$ and $\varpi\kappa$, of degrees $D + 8$ and $D + 7$, and the second at most $d_1 + 5$ or $d_2$; and $d_1 + d_2 = D + n + 7 + J\Delta + \max\{D + 2K_1 - \Delta,\, 0\} \le d_f$ by (P1), as $\Delta \ge 1$.
nodes.explain: After multiplying by five coins that clear all denominators, val(D) − χκ is a polynomial in the hidden coins of total degree at most d_f = 3D + 2n + 2K_1 + 6; the same bound holds for differences of source-group expressions. Proof idea: Add the degrees of the published exponents.

nodes.label: Lemma B.4
nodes.name: View
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathsf{D}$ be an expression of $\mathbb{G}_T$, $\chi \in \mathbb{F}_q$, and $r, r' \in \mathbb{F}_q^{N+1}$.

 
(a) \emph{Passing stacks.} If $\mathsf{D}$ is $\chi\kappa$ identically at $r$, then in each sector $\mathsf{s}$ the stack $\mathbf{W}^{\mathsf{s}}(\mathsf{D})$ passes and satisfies the ties, $W^{\mathsf{s}}_c(\mathsf{D})\, r = u^{\mathsf{s}}_c(\mathsf{D})$ for every cell $c$, and the corner $\bigl( W^{\mathrm{plain}}_{c_{\mathrm{key}}}(\mathsf{D}) \bigr)_{00}$ is $\chi$.
(b) \emph{Locus.} If $\mathsf{D}$ is $\chi\kappa$ identically at $r$ and $W^{\mathsf{s}}_c(\mathsf{D})\, r' = u^{\mathsf{s}}_c(\mathsf{D})$ for every sector and cell, then $\mathsf{D}$ is $\chi\kappa$ identically at $r'$. In particular, if $\mathsf{D}$ is $\chi\kappa$ identically at $r$ and has zero stacks, then $\mathsf{D}$ is $\chi\kappa$ formally, and $\chi = 0$.
(c) \emph{Coincidence.} If $\mathsf{D}$ is not $\chi\kappa$ identically at $r$, $\Pr[\operatorname{val}(\mathsf{D}; \mathbf{c}, r) = \chi\kappa] \le d_f/(q - D) \le \varepsilon_f$ for uniform valid $\mathbf{c}$.
(d) \emph{No formal key scalar.} If $\chi \ne 0$, then $\mathsf{D}$ is not $\chi\kappa$ formally.
(e) \emph{Source groups.} If $\mathsf{E}$ and $\mathsf{E}'$ are expressions of $\mathbb{G}_1$, or of $\mathbb{G}_2$, that are not formally equal, then for every $r$ their values at $(\mathbf{c}, r)$ are equal with probability at most $\varepsilon_f$ over $\mathbf{c}$.
nodes.proof:
The valid tuples, at which $\varpi \ne 0$, form a product of sets of at least $q - D$ elements, and $q - D > d_f$, as $\varepsilon_f = (d_f + 61)/(q - D) < 1$. So by Lemma B.3 and the Schwartz--Zippel lemma \cite{Sch80,Zip79}, $\mathsf{D}$ is $\chi\kappa$ identically at $r$ exactly if $\varpi \cdot ( \operatorname{val}(\mathsf{D}; \mathbf{c}, r) - \chi\kappa )$ is the zero polynomial in the entries of $\mathbf{c}$; otherwise it vanishes with probability at most $d_f/(q - D)$, which is (c). Such an identity, multiplied by $\varpi$, may thus be compared coefficient by coefficient and evaluated at any point, also at an invalid $\tau \in \mathcal{P}$, as $\varpi$ is free of $\tau$. For (a) and (b), let $\mathsf{D}$ be $\chi\kappa$ identically at $r$, and compare coefficients in three steps: the hidden basis leaves one coefficient matrix for each cell, the hidden scalars separate the sectors and the cells, and each cell's identity is read at the evaluation points, with the masks' terms giving the ties.

\emph{Step 1: the hidden basis.} The value $\chi\kappa - \mathsf{D}_K\, \alpha\kappa$ of the pairs of $\mathsf{D}$ is free of $\Omega$, so its terms with $\Omega_{12}^p / \Omega_{22}$, $p \ge 1$, sum to zero; this sum sets each coefficient on first coordinates against the matching one on second coordinates, and its derivative in $y_j$ at $y = B(\tau)$, where $h^2_{\mathrm{leg},j}$ vanishes, separates them. The terms come only from pairs with the $(\mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{leg}}_{j,1})^{\mathsf{s}}$ or $(\mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{leg}}_{j,2})^{\mathsf{s}}$ and sum to $-\Omega_{12}/\Omega_{22}$ times $\sum_{\mathsf{s}, a, \mathrm{leg}, j} \alpha_{\mathsf{s}}\, \delta^{\mathsf{s}}_{a,\mathrm{leg},j}\, \tilde a\, s_{\mathrm{leg}} (B_j(\tau) - y_j)$, where $a \in \mathcal{X}_1$, $\tilde a$ is the exponent of $a$ at $\Omega_{22} = 0$, and $\delta^{\mathsf{s}}_{a,\mathrm{leg},j}$ is the coefficient of $\mathsf{D}$ on $a$ and $(\mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{leg}}_{j,1})^{\mathsf{s}}$, less, for $a = \mathsf{F}^{k_1}_{i,1}$, that on $\mathsf{F}^{k_1}_{i,2}$ and $(\mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{leg}}_{j,2})^{\mathsf{s}}$. So the derivative gives $\sum_{\mathsf{s}, a, \mathrm{leg}} \delta^{\mathsf{s}}_{a,\mathrm{leg},j}\, \alpha_{\mathsf{s}}\, s_{\mathrm{leg}}\, \tilde a|_{y = B(\tau)} = 0$. These polynomials, $\alpha_{\mathsf{s}}\, s_{\mathrm{leg}}$ times $1$, $\zeta \tau^k$, $\zeta' \tau^k$, $\zeta'' B_i(\tau)$, $\pi_{k_1} B_i(\tau)$, or $\Omega_{12}\, \pi_{k_1} B_i(\tau)$, are linearly independent: the $B_i$ are, as $B(d_j) = e_j$, and the factors before $1$, $\tau^k$, and $B_i(\tau)$ have distinct monomials, as $s_{\mathrm{leg}}\, \pi_{k_1} = \gamma_c$ contains $\pi\, s_{\mathrm{X}}\, \upsilon^{k_c}$, which determines the cell $c$. So every $\delta^{\mathsf{s}}_{a,\mathrm{leg},j}$ is zero: in each sector, (i) $\mathsf{D}$ has the same coefficient on $\mathsf{F}^{k_1}_{i,2}$ and $(\mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{leg}}_{j,2})^{\mathsf{s}}$ as on $\mathsf{F}^{k_1}_{i,1}$ and $(\mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{leg}}_{j,1})^{\mathsf{s}}$, and (ii) $\mathsf{D}_{ab} = 0$ for $b = (\mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{leg}}_{j,1})^{\mathsf{s}}$ unless $a$ is some $\mathsf{F}^{k_1}_{i,1}$.

\emph{Step 2: the class of $\kappa$.} Only the exponents of $ct_2^\alpha$ and $\mathsf{K}^\alpha$ contain $\alpha$, as a factor, and the value of a pair is homogeneous of the degrees of the product of the classes of its elements. So in each sector $\mathsf{s}$ the pairs of class $\pi$, the class of $\kappa$, have total value $\alpha_{\mathsf{s}} \chi_{\mathsf{s}} \kappa$, where $\chi_{\mathrm{plain}} := \chi$ and $\chi_{\alpha} := -\mathsf{D}_K$. They are those of the $\mathsf{F}^{k_1}_{i,1}$, of class $\pi$, with the elements of class $1$, the $(\mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{leg}}_{j,1})^{\mathsf{s}}$, the $(\mathsf{S}^{\mathrm{leg}})^{\mathsf{s}}$, and, in the plain sector, $G_2$; of the $\mathsf{F}^{k_1}_{i,2}$, of class $\pi\,\Omega$, with the $(\mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{leg}}_{j,2})^{\mathsf{s}}$, of class $\Omega^{-1}$; and of the quotient and remainder powers and the $\mathsf{Y}_i$, of classes $\zeta$, $\zeta'$, and $\zeta''$, with their bases, of classes $\pi/\zeta$, $\pi/\zeta'$, and $\pi/\zeta''$. Fix $\mathsf{s}$, and let $W_c := W^{\mathsf{s}}_c(\mathsf{D})$ and $u_c := u^{\mathsf{s}}_c(\mathsf{D})$. By (i), the hidden basis cancels; by the product $F^{k_1}_i H^{\mathrm{leg}}_j$ of Section [copies] their total value is $\alpha_{\mathsf{s}} \bigl( \sum_c \gamma_c\, b_c + \Phi \bigr)$, where
\[
 b_c := y^\top ( W_c\, r - u_c ) + y^\top ( W_c - W_c^\top )\, A(\tau) + \bigl( P_{W_c} + h_c Z_c + Z_0 R_c \bigr)(\tau) .
\]
Here $h_c$ is a polynomial and $R_c$ an allowed polynomial, from the pairs of the powers with the bases of cell $c$ (Section 5.2). The rest $\Phi$, the masks' terms $\sum_c \pi_{k_1}\, y^\top W_c\, \vartheta_{\mathrm{leg}}$ of the products and the pairs with the cancellation bases and with $G_2$, is free of $s_{\mathrm{E}}$, $s_{\mathrm{O}}$, and $s_{\mathrm{V}}$. As $\kappa = \gamma_{c_{\mathrm{key}}} L_\rho(\tau)$, the coefficient of the monomial $\pi\, s_{\mathrm{X}}\, \upsilon^{k_c}$ of each $\gamma_c$ gives $b_{c_{\mathrm{key}}} = \chi_{\mathsf{s}} L_\rho(\tau)$ and $b_c = 0$ for $c \ne c_{\mathrm{key}}$, as polynomials in $y$ and $\tau$; and then $\Phi = 0$.

\emph{Step 3: cells and ties.} The part of degree one in $y$ of these identities, at $\tau = d_0$, $\rho$, and $d_j$, where $A$ is $0$, $e_0$, and $e_j - e_0$, shows that $W_c\, r = u_c$ and that $W_c$ is symmetric. The part of degree zero is condition (c) of Lemma 4.7 if $c \ne c_{\mathrm{key}}$, where $Z_c = Z$; if $c = c_{\mathrm{key}}$, where $Z_c(X) = Z(X)(X - \rho)$, its value at $\tau = \rho$ is $(W_c)_{00} = \chi_{\mathsf{s}}$, and it is then condition (b). So $W_c$ passes. By the mask identity (Equation [mask]), the terms of $\Phi$ with $\eta_a\, \varepsilon^0$ are $\pi\, \eta_a\, y^\top t_a(\upsilon)$, for the tie polynomials $t_a$ of the stack $(W_c)_c$, and multiples of $\pi\, \eta_a P(\upsilon)\, \upsilon^e y_i$ from the pairs of the $\mathsf{Y}_i$ with the tie bases $\mathsf{B}^0_{a,e}$. As $\Phi = 0$, $P(T)$ divides each $t_a(T)$: the ties hold.

\emph{Parts (b), (d), and (e).} By (ii), $r$ enters $\operatorname{val}(\mathsf{D}; \mathbf{c}, r)$ only through the pairs behind the $W^{\mathsf{s}}_c(\mathsf{D})$, so $\operatorname{val}(\mathsf{D}; \mathbf{c}, r') - \operatorname{val}(\mathsf{D}; \mathbf{c}, r) = \sum_{\mathsf{s}} \alpha_{\mathsf{s}} \sum_c \gamma_c\, y^\top W^{\mathsf{s}}_c(\mathsf{D})\, (r' - r)$. This is zero when $W^{\mathsf{s}}_c(\mathsf{D})\, r' = u^{\mathsf{s}}_c(\mathsf{D})$, which is $W^{\mathsf{s}}_c(\mathsf{D})\, r$ by (a). If both stacks are zero, then so are the $u^{\mathsf{s}}_c(\mathsf{D})$, every $r'$ qualifies, and $\chi$ is a corner of a zero matrix. For (d), if $\mathsf{D}$ is $\chi\kappa$ formally, then by (a) the product $W r$ does not depend on $r$, for $W := W^{\mathrm{plain}}_{c_{\mathrm{key}}}(\mathsf{D})$, so $W = 0$ and $\chi = W_{00} = 0$. For (e), the pairing $\mathsf{D}$ of $\mathsf{E} - \mathsf{E}'$ with $G_2$, or of $G_1$ with $\mathsf{E} - \mathsf{E}'$, has zero stacks. So by (b) it is $0$ identically at some $r$ only if $\mathsf{E}$ and $\mathsf{E}'$ are formally equal; otherwise (c) applies at every $r$.
nodes.explain: Let D be an expression in G_T. (a) If D equals χκ identically in the coins at search vector r, then in each sector its stack passes and satisfies the ties, W_c·r = u_c for every cell, and the corner of the key copy is χ. (b) The identity then holds at every r′ with the same products; with zero stacks it holds formally and χ = 0. (c) If D is not χκ identically at r, equality has probability at most ε_f. (d) For χ ≠ 0, D is never χκ formally. (e) Source-group expressions that are not formally equal agree with probability at most ε_f. Proof idea: Schwartz–Zippel turns “identically” into a polynomial identity. Comparing coefficients in three steps (the hidden basis, the class of κ, the cells and ties) reads off symmetry, the QAP criterion and the tie polynomials.

nodes.label: Lemma B.5
nodes.name: Consecutive conjugates
nodes.statement: Let $h \in \mathbb{F}_{q^n}^d$ have entries that are linearly independent over $\mathbb{F}_q$, with $d \le n$. Then for every integer $s$ the vectors $\sigma^s(h), \sigma^{s+1}(h), \dots, \sigma^{s+d-1}(h)$ form a basis of $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}^d$.
nodes.proof: The matrix with these columns has the rows $(\beta, \beta^q, \dots, \beta^{q^{d-1}})$ for the entries $\beta$ of $\sigma^s(h)$, which are linearly independent over $\mathbb{F}_q$, as those of $h$ are; so its determinant is nonzero \cite[Lemma 3.51]{LN97}.
nodes.explain: If the d ≤ n entries of h in F_(q^n)^d are linearly independent over F_q, then any d consecutive Frobenius conjugates of h form a basis of F_(q^n)^d. Proof idea: The matrix of conjugates is a Moore matrix, whose determinant is nonzero.

nodes.label: Lemma B.6
nodes.name: Classification
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathbf{W}$ be a stack of symmetric matrices that pass every Booleanity test and that satisfies the ties. Suppose that its row space $\mathcal{V}$ has dimension at most three and contains no kernel vector.

 
(a) There are a set $\mathcal{W} \subseteq \mathcal{V} \cap \{0,1\}^{N+1}$ of assignments and $\chi_w \in \mathbb{F}_q$ with $\mathbf{W} = \sum_{w \in \mathcal{W}} \chi_w\, \mathbf{H}(w)$.
(b) If $\mathbf{W}$ passes every constraint's test, every such representation has $\chi_w \ne 0$ only for witnesses $w$ of $S$.

In particular, a nonzero usable stack whose row space has dimension at most three and contains no kernel vector is a combination, with a nonzero coefficient, of honest stacks of witnesses in its row space.
nodes.proof:
\emph{Step 1: one symmetric tensor.} The symmetric matrices $W_U$ and $W_V$ over $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$ determine the stack, and with $W_s := W_U$, $W_V$, and $\sigma^{n/2+1}(W_U)$ for $s \in I := \{n/2 - 1, n/2, n/2 + 1\}$, the ties are $W_s\, z_{s'} = W_{s'}\, z_s$ for $s, s' \in I$. Let $d := \dim \mathcal{V}$, let the columns of $\mathcal{U} \in \mathbb{F}_q^{(N+1) \times d}$ be a basis of $\mathcal{V}$, with rows $u_i \in \mathbb{F}_q^d$, which span $\mathbb{F}_q^d$, and let $h_s := \mathcal{U}^\top z_s = \sigma^s(h_0)$. The entries of $h_0$, the values of $z$ on the basis, are linearly independent over $\mathbb{F}_q$, as $\mathcal{V}$ contains no kernel vector; so $d \le n$, and by Lemma B.5 the $h_s$, $s \in I$, span $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}^d$, as $d \le 3$. Each $W_s$ is symmetric with columns in the $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$-span of $\mathcal{V}$, so $W_s = \mathcal{U}\, \Xi_s\, \mathcal{U}^\top$ for a unique symmetric $\Xi_s$, and the ties read $\Xi_s\, h_{s'} = \Xi_{s'}\, h_s$. So if $\sum_{s \in I} \varrho_s h_s = 0$, then $(\sum_s \varrho_s \Xi_s)\, h_{s'} = \Xi_{s'} \sum_s \varrho_s h_s = 0$ for all $s'$, so $\sum_s \varrho_s \Xi_s = 0$, as the $h_{s'}$ span. Hence there is a linear map $\Xi$ from $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}^d$ to symmetric matrices with $\Xi(h_s) = \Xi_s$ for $s \in I$, and the trilinear form $\Xi(h; u, u') := u^\top\, \Xi(h)\, u'$ is symmetric in $u$ and $u'$ and, by the ties, in $h$ and $u'$, hence in all three. Booleanity at $j \in [N]$ is linear over $\mathbb{F}_q$, so the $W_s$ satisfy it: $\Xi(h; u_j, u_j - u_0) = 0$ for $h = h_s$, hence for all $h$. Also $\Xi_s = \sigma^s(\Xi_{n-s})$ for $s \in \{n/2-1, n/2\}$, as $\sigma^n = \mathrm{id}$ and $\sigma^{n/2}$ fixes $W_V$, a polynomial in $T^2$.

\emph{Step 2: cubes of Boolean points, for $u_0 \ne 0$.} Extend $l_0 := u_0$ by vectors $l_k := u_{j_k}$, $k \in [d-1]$, to a basis of $\mathbb{F}_q^d$. For $\delta \in \{0,1\}^{d-1}$ let $p_\delta \in \mathbb{F}_q^d$ be the point with $\langle l_0, p_\delta \rangle = 1$ and $\langle l_k, p_\delta \rangle = \delta_k$, and let $w_\delta := \mathcal{U} p_\delta$: the $w_\delta$ are the assignments in $\mathcal{V}$ that are Boolean at the $j_k$. By Booleanity at the $j_k$ and symmetry, $\Xi(l_a; l_b, l_c)$ depends only on the set $A \subseteq [d-1]$ of the nonzero indices among $a, b, c$, and the cube $\langle h, p_\delta \rangle \langle u, p_\delta \rangle \langle u', p_\delta \rangle$ of $p_\delta$ has the value $\delta^A := \prod_{k \in A} \delta_k$ there. The matrix $(\delta^A)_{A, \delta}$ is invertible, as the monomials $\delta^A$ are a basis of the functions on the Boolean cube. So there are $c_\delta \in \mathbb{F}_{q^n}$ with $\Xi(h) = \sum_{\delta} c_\delta\, \langle h, p_\delta \rangle\, p_\delta\, p_\delta^\top$; and the squares $p_\delta\, p_\delta^\top$ are linearly independent, as they have the values $\delta^A$ on the pairs $(l_a, l_b)$, whose sets $A$ are all the subsets of $[d-1]$, as $d - 1 \le 2$. Let $\bar z_\delta := z(w_\delta) = \langle h_0, p_\delta \rangle$, nonzero as $w_\delta$ is no kernel vector; then $\langle h_s, p_\delta \rangle = \sigma^s(\bar z_\delta)$, so $\Xi_s = \sum_\delta c_\delta\, \sigma^s(\bar z_\delta)\, p_\delta p_\delta^\top$. Comparing the coefficients of the squares, which are over $\mathbb{F}_q$, in $\Xi_s = \sigma^s(\Xi_{n-s})$ gives $c_\delta\, \sigma^s(\bar z_\delta) = \sigma^s(c_\delta)\, \bar z_\delta$ for $s \in \{n/2-1, n/2\}$: so $\sigma^{n/2-1}$ and $\sigma^{n/2}$, hence $\sigma$, fix $c_\delta / \bar z_\delta$, and $c_\delta = \chi_\delta\, \bar z_\delta$ with $\chi_\delta \in \mathbb{F}_q$. So $W_s = \sum_\delta \chi_\delta\, \bar z_\delta\, \sigma^s(\bar z_\delta)\, w_\delta w_\delta^\top$: $\mathbf{W} = \sum_\delta \chi_\delta\, \mathbf{H}(w_\delta)$, as $U = z\, \sigma^{n/2-1}(z)$ and $V = z\, \sigma^{n/2}(z)$.

\emph{Step 3: a test sees each point by itself.} Suppose $\mathbf{W} = \sum_\delta \chi_\delta\, \mathbf{H}(w_\delta)$ with $\chi_\delta \in \mathbb{F}_q$, and let $\varrho$ be a linear function of a matrix, with coefficients in $\mathbb{F}_q$, vanishing on every $W_c$. So $\varrho$ vanishes on $W_s = \sum_\delta \chi_\delta\, \bar z_\delta\, \sigma^s(\bar z_\delta)\, w_\delta w_\delta^\top$ for $s \in I$; that is, $h_0^\top \mathcal{Q}\, h_s = 0$ for $\mathcal{Q} := \sum_\delta \chi_\delta\, \varrho(w_\delta w_\delta^\top)\, p_\delta p_\delta^\top$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$. As the $h_s$ span, $h_0^\top \mathcal{Q} = 0$; so $\mathcal{Q} = 0$, as the entries of $h_0$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{F}_q$, and $\chi_\delta\, \varrho(w_\delta w_\delta^\top) = 0$, as the squares are linearly independent. For an assignment $w$, $w w^\top$ passes the Booleanity test of $j$ exactly if $w_j \in \{0,1\}$, and every test exactly if $w$ is a witness (Section 4.2). So the $\chi_\delta$ of Step 2 are nonzero only if $w_\delta \in \{0,1\}^{N+1}$, which is (a); and in a representation as in (a), where every $w \in \mathcal{W}$ is one of the $w_\delta$, $\chi_w \ne 0$ only for witnesses, which is (b).

\emph{Step 4: the case $u_0 = 0$.} Then $\mathcal{V}$ contains no assignment; we show $\Xi = 0$: the stack is zero, and both parts hold with $\mathcal{W} = \emptyset$. Booleanity reads $\Xi(h; u_j, u_j) = 0$, and some $u_j$ form a basis $l_1, \dots, l_d$ of $\mathbb{F}_q^d$; so by symmetry $\Xi(l_a; l_b, l_c) = 0$ unless $a$, $b$, $c$ are distinct. Hence $\Xi = 0$ if $d \le 2$. If $d = 3$, let $t := \Xi(l_1; l_2, l_3)$; then $\Xi(h; l_b, l_c)$ is $t$ times the coordinate of $h$ at $l_a$ for distinct $a$, $b$, $c$, so $\Xi_s = \sigma^s(\Xi_{n-s})$ gives $t\, h_s = \sigma^s(t)\, h_0$ for $s \in \{n/2-1, n/2\}$, as $\sigma^s(h_{n-s}) = h_0$. So $t = 0$, as $h_{n/2-1}, h_{n/2}$ are not both multiples of $h_0$ (Lemma B.5).
nodes.explain: A stack of symmetric matrices that pass every Booleanity test and satisfy the ties, whose row space has dimension at most three and contains no kernel vector, is a combination Σ χ_w·H(w) of honest stacks of Boolean assignments w in its row space. If it also passes the constraint tests, χ_w ≠ 0 only for witnesses. Proof idea: The ties make the stack one symmetric trilinear form; Booleanity writes it as a sum of cubes of Boolean points; any linear test then sees each point separately.

nodes.label: Lemma B.7
nodes.name: Inverse theorem
nodes.statement:
Let $q$ be prime. Every nonzero $v \in \mathbb{F}_q^{N+1}$ with $v_0 = 0$ and $\operatorname{gp}(v^\top) > \theta$ has a short multiple $x$, and $x_0 = 0$, if for $N$, $g$, $\theta$, and the integer $\beta$ there are an integer $b$ and positive reals $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$, $R_{\mathrm{tr}}$, $\Lambda_1, \Lambda_2, \Lambda_3$, $\Gamma_1, \Gamma_2, \Gamma_3$, $A_{\mathrm{inv}}$, $P_1$, and $P_2$ that satisfy the following conditions, in which $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}} := \theta - 100\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$, $\xi_{\mathrm{tr}} := (1 + 2/g)^{254}$, $H_3 := \xi_{\mathrm{tr}} / (g^3\mu_{\mathrm{tr}} - \xi_{\mathrm{tr}}/g)$, $H_1 := \Gamma_1/(g\mu_{\mathrm{tr}})$, $H_2 := \Gamma_2/(g^2\mu_{\mathrm{tr}})$, and $T_{\mathrm{tr}} := R_{\mathrm{tr}}\, g \sqrt{N/3}$.
(I1) $b \ge 7$ and $2^b \le g < 2^{254}$.\hskip 0.5em plus 0.2em minus 0.2em\relax
(I2) $R_{\mathrm{tr}} \ge 20$, $1000\, e^{-99 R_{\mathrm{tr}}^2/200} \le \varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}} < \mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$, and $g^3 \mu_{\mathrm{tr}} > \xi_{\mathrm{tr}}/g$.\hskip 0.5em plus 0.2em minus 0.2em\relax
(I3) $\Lambda_1 \ge 2\sqrt{3}\, R_{\mathrm{tr}} \sqrt{N}$, $\Lambda_2 \ge 27\sqrt{2}\, \pi R_{\mathrm{tr}}^2 N$, and $\Lambda_3 \ge 144\sqrt{2}\, \pi R_{\mathrm{tr}}^3 N^{3/2}$.\hskip 0.5em plus 0.2em minus 0.2em\relax
(I4) $\Gamma_3 \ge \xi_{\mathrm{tr}} (1 + H_3/g)$; $A_{\mathrm{inv}} \ge \mu_{\mathrm{tr}}/(\mu_{\mathrm{tr}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}})$; $P_2^{b-1} \ge (g^{-3} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}})/\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$ and $P_1^{b-1} \ge (g^{-2} + 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}})/\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$; $\Gamma_2^{b-1} \ge g^{-2}/\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$ and $\Gamma_1^{b-1} \ge g^{-1}/\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$; $\Gamma_2 \ge A_{\mathrm{inv}} \Lambda_1 \Gamma_3 P_2$ and $\Gamma_1 \ge A_{\mathrm{inv}} \max\{\Lambda_1 \Gamma_2, \Lambda_2 \Gamma_3\}\, P_1$.\hskip 0.5em plus 0.2em minus 0.2em\relax
(I5) $\Lambda_d \Gamma_d < \mu_{\mathrm{tr}} q$ for $d \in \{1,2,3\}$; $g^{-4} < \mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$; and $H_1 T_{\mathrm{tr}} < q$, $4 H_2 T_{\mathrm{tr}}^2 < q$, and $54 H_3 T_{\mathrm{tr}}^3 < q$.\hskip 0.5em plus 0.2em minus 0.2em\relax
(I6) $2\beta < q$, $H_1 \le \beta$, $2 H_2\, q \le \beta^2$, and $6 \lfloor H_3 \rfloor q^2 \le \beta^3$.
nodes.proof:
For $i = 1, \dots, N_0$ in turn, we find a regular saturated lattice $\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^{[i]}$ of a rank $d \in [3]$ with $v_{[i]} \in \bar\Theta$ and $m(\Theta) \ge \operatorname{gp}(v_{[i]}^\top) - 3\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$; so $m(\Theta) > \mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$ by Equation [inv-chain], and $h(\Theta) \le H_d$, for $d \le 2$ by regularity, as $H_d = \Gamma_d/(g^d \mu_{\mathrm{tr}})$, and for $d = 3$ by Lemma B.18(c). For $i = 1$, $\mathbb{Z}^{[1]}$ serves: its reduction $\mathbb{F}_q$ contains $v_{[1]}$, its fibers are points, so $m = 1/g \ge \operatorname{gp}(v_{[1]}^\top)$, and $h = 1 \le \Gamma_1$, by (I4) and $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}} < 1/g$.

\emph{Adding a coordinate.} Let $i < N_0$, and let $\Theta$ have a largest minor at $J$. Restriction to $J$ maps $\Theta$ injectively (Lemma B.17(a)) onto a lattice of determinant $h(\Theta)$ in $\mathbb{R}^J$. As the unit ball of $\|\cdot\|_1$ has volume $2^d/d!$, the successive minima $\lambda_1 \le \dots \le \lambda_d$ of that lattice for $\|\cdot\|_1$ have $\lambda_1 \cdots \lambda_d \le d!\, h(\Theta)$, by Minkowski's second theorem \cite[Chapter VIII, Theorem V]{Cas97}; and by Mahler's lemma \cite[Chapter V, Lemma 8]{Cas97}, for linearly independent vectors that attain them, the lattice has a basis of $\ell_1$ norms at most $\lambda_1$, $\lambda_2$, and $\max\{\lambda_3, (\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \lambda_3)/2\} \le \frac32 \lambda_3$. So, by the same part, $\Theta$ has a basis matrix $B$ with $\prod_j \|B e_j\|_\infty \le h(\Theta)$, $2h(\Theta)$, or $9h(\Theta)$ for $d = 1, 2, 3$.

As $v_{[i]} \in \bar\Theta$, $v_{[i]} = B c' \bmod q$ for some $c' \in \mathbb{F}_q^d$; with $c := (c', v_{i+1})$ and $\Phi(r) := (B^\top r_{[i]}, r_{i+1})$, $v_{[i+1]}^\top r = c^\top \Phi(r) \bmod q$. Let $F$ be a densest modular fiber $\{ r : v_{[i+1]}^\top r = t \bmod q \}$ of $v_{[i+1]}$, trimmed by $\Theta$, so that $\Pr[F] \ge \operatorname{gp}(v_{[i+1]}^\top) - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}} > \theta - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$ by Lemma B.19 and Equation [inv-chain]. As $v_{i+1} \ne 0$, $\Phi(F)$ lies in a coset of the subgroup $\{ y \in \mathbb{Z}^{d+1} : c^\top y = 0 \bmod q \}$ of index $q$, so $k := \dim \Phi(F) \le d$: otherwise Lemma B.20(a), regularity, and (I5) would give $\Pr[F] \le \Lambda_d \Gamma_d/q < \mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$.

Let $\Delta$ be the matrix of the differences of the points of $\Phi(F)$, of rank $k$. By the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality $(e_j^\top y)^2 \le (e_j^\top \Sigma_\Theta e_j)(y^\top \Sigma_\Theta^{-1} y)$, with $e_j^\top \Sigma_\Theta e_j \le \frac{g^2 N}{12} \|B e_j\|_\infty^2$, entries $j$ of two points of $\mathcal{T}_\Theta$ differ by at most $2 R_{\mathrm{tr}}\, g \sqrt{N/12}\, \|B e_j\|_\infty = T_{\mathrm{tr}} \|B e_j\|_\infty$, which bounds the entries of the row $j \in [d]$ of $\Delta$; those of its last row are at most $g - 1 < T_{\mathrm{tr}}$, as $R_{\mathrm{tr}} \ge 20$. As $T_{\mathrm{tr}}$ and the $\|B e_j\|_\infty$ are at least $1$, the $k \times k$ minors of $\Delta$, at most $k!$ times a product of $k$ of these bounds, are at most $d!\, T_{\mathrm{tr}}^d \prod_j \|B e_j\|_\infty$, which is at most $H_1 T_{\mathrm{tr}}$, $4 H_2 T_{\mathrm{tr}}^2$, or $54 H_3 T_{\mathrm{tr}}^3$, below $q$ by (I5). As $c^\top \Delta = 0 \bmod q$, Lemma B.17(c), for an integer vector that reduces to $c$, gives $c = u \bmod q$ for a $u \in \mathbb{Z}^{d+1}$ with $u^\top \Delta = 0$. Then $(B u_{[d]}, u_{d+1})^\top r = u^\top \Phi(r)$ is constant on $F$, so $(B u_{[d]}, u_{d+1}) \in F^\perp$, and it reduces to $(B c', v_{i+1}) = v_{[i+1]}$; so $v_{[i+1]} \in \overline{F^\perp}$ and $F^\perp \ne \{0\}$. Then $m(F^\perp) \ge \Pr[F] > \theta - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}} \ge \mu_{\mathrm{tr}} + 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$, so $F^\perp$ has rank in $[3]$, by (I5), and Lemma B.21 gives a regular saturated $\Theta^+ \supseteq F^\perp$ with $m(\Theta^+) \ge m(F^\perp) - 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}} \ge \operatorname{gp}(v_{[i+1]}^\top) - 3\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$ and $v_{[i+1]} \in \overline{\Theta^+}$: the lattice for $i + 1$.

\emph{The short multiple.} Let $\Theta$ be the lattice for $N_0$, $B$ a basis matrix of it with a largest minor at $J$, and $z_0 \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ with $B z_0 = v_{[N_0]} \bmod q$, so $z_0 \ne 0 \bmod q$. The $z \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ congruent modulo $q$ to multiples of $z_0$ form a subgroup of index $q^{d-1}$, so the $B_J z$ form a lattice of determinant $h(\Theta)\, q^{d-1}$ in $\mathbb{R}^J$, and $d!\, h(\Theta)\, q^{d-1} \le \beta^d$ by (I6): $h(\Theta) \le H_1 \le \beta$, $2 h(\Theta)\, q \le 2 H_2\, q \le \beta^2$, or $6 h(\Theta)\, q^2 \le 6 \lfloor H_3 \rfloor q^2 \le \beta^3$, as heights are integers. The closed $\ell_1$ ball of radius $\beta$ in $\mathbb{R}^J$ is convex and symmetric, and its volume $(2\beta)^d/d!$ is at least $2^d h(\Theta)\, q^{d-1}$. Thus Minkowski's theorem \cite[Section 30]{Min10}, applied after a linear map taking the lattice to $\mathbb{Z}^d$, gives a nonzero lattice point $B_J z$ in this ball. Then $x := B z$ is congruent modulo $q$ to a multiple of $v_{[N_0]}$, a nonzero one as $0 < \|x\|_\infty \le \|x_J\|_1 \le \beta < q$ (Lemma B.17(a), (I6)): $x$ is a short multiple of $v_{[N_0]}$.
nodes.explain: Under conditions (I1) to (I6) on (q, N, g, θ, β): every nonzero v in F_q^(N+1) with v_0 = 0 and gp(v^⊤) > θ has a short multiple, that is an integer vector x with ‖x‖_∞ ≤ β and x_0 = 0 whose reduction mod q is a nonzero multiple of v. Proof idea: Read the coordinates of v one at a time, keeping a saturated integer lattice of rank at most three whose reduction contains the prefix. Trimming, a lattice-point count that rules out wrap-around mod q, and a regularization step extend it; Minkowski's theorem in the last lattice gives the short multiple.

nodes.label: Lemma B.8
nodes.name: Heavy stacks
nodes.statement:
Let the parameters satisfy (P3), and let $\mathbf{W}$ be a heavy stack.

 
(a) $\operatorname{rank} \mathbf{W} \le 3$.
(b) Every kernel vector $v$ in the row space of $\mathbf{W}$ has a short multiple.
(c) If $x$ is a short multiple of a kernel vector, then $\hat x \in R^\ell$, with the $\hat x_j$ of Definition 5.1 over $\mathbb{Z}$, solves MSIS for the matrix $A$ of the columns $1, \dots, \ell$ of $M$ (Definition 3.3): $0 < \|\hat x\|_\infty \le \beta$ and $A \hat x = 0 \bmod q$.
nodes.proof:
(a) By Lemma 4.5, a stack of rank at least four has $\operatorname{gp} \le g^{-4} < \theta$.
(b) A kernel vector has $v_0 = 0$, as $\varphi_0(v) = v_0$, and $\operatorname{gp}(v^\top) \ge \operatorname{gp}(\mathbf{W}) > \theta$ by Lemma 4.5, so Lemma B.7 applies.
(c) Modulo $q$, $x$ is a nonzero multiple of a kernel vector, hence a kernel vector; so $x_0 = 0$, as $|x_0| \le \beta < q$. Then $A \hat x = 0 \bmod q$ by the remark after Definition 5.1, and $\|\hat x\|_\infty = \|x\|_\infty$, as the coefficients of $\hat x$ are $x_1, \dots, x_N$ and zeros.
nodes.explain: Let W be a heavy stack (guessing probability above θ). (a) rank W ≤ 3. (b) Every kernel vector in its row space has a short multiple. (c) A short multiple of a kernel vector packs into a Module-SIS solution for the matrix in the ciphertext. Proof idea: (a) and (b) from the rank bound and the inverse theorem; (c) from the definition of the forms.

nodes.label: Lemma B.9
nodes.name: Lifting step
nodes.statement: Let $2\beta < q$ and $24\beta^4 < q^3$. There is a deterministic algorithm that returns, on input a nonzero $v \in \mathbb{F}_q^{N+1}$ with $v_0 = 0$, a short multiple of $v$, or $\bot$ if there is none. It makes $N - 1$ extensions, each with at most $32$ integer programs and $c_{\mathrm{HNF}} = O(1)$ Hermite normal forms, both in dimension at most four, and $O(N)$ further operations, on inputs of $O(N \log q)$ bits; its running time $(N-1)\bigl(32\, T_{\mathsf{IP}} + c_{\mathrm{HNF}}\, T_{\mathsf{HNF}} + O(N)\bigr)$, for the times $T_{\mathsf{IP}}$ and $T_{\mathsf{HNF}}$ of these programs and forms, is polynomial in $N$ and $\log q$.
nodes.proof:
Drop the coordinate $0$, reorder the others, and scale $v$ so that $v_1 = 1$. For $i \in [N]$ let $\mathcal{L}_i \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^i$ be the lattice of the $x$ congruent modulo $q$ to $x_1 (v_1, \dots, v_i)$, and call a vector $x$ \emph{bounded} if $\|x\|_\infty \le \beta$. As $2\beta < q$, the short multiples of $v$ are the nonzero bounded vectors of $\mathcal{L}_N$. The bounded vectors of $\mathcal{L}_i$ span a space of dimension at most three: four of them are linearly dependent, as each of their $4 \times 4$ minors is divisible by $q^3$, because modulo $q$ they lie on a line, and is at most $4!\, \beta^4 < q^3$ in absolute value.

Starting from $\mathcal{M}_1 = \mathbb{Z}$, the algorithm computes for $i = 2, \dots, N$ a basis of a lattice $\mathcal{M}_i \subseteq \mathcal{L}_i$ of rank at most three containing the bounded vectors of $\mathcal{L}_i$, and returns a nonzero one of $\mathcal{L}_N$, or $\bot$ if there is none. The first $i$ entries of a bounded vector $y$ of $\mathcal{L}_{i+1}$ form a bounded vector of $\mathcal{L}_i$, in $\mathcal{M}_i$; so $y$ lies in the lattice $\mathcal{N}$ generated by $q\, e_{i+1}$ and the basis vectors $x$ of $\mathcal{M}_i$, each extended by an entry in $[0, q)$ congruent to $x_1 v_{i+1}$.

Written in the at most four coefficients of these generators, which lie in $\mathcal{L}_{i+1}$, these $y$ are the integer solutions of $2(i+1)$ linear inequalities, and one lies outside the span of those found exactly if one of the at most four functionals in a basis of the integer functionals vanishing on this span is at least $1$ or at most $-1$ on it. So a round of at most eight integer programs \cite[Section 1]{Len83} finds a further solution or shows that those found span all, in dimension $d \le 3$: at most four rounds, $32$ programs. Let $\mathcal{M}_{i+1}$ consist of the vectors of $\mathcal{N}$ in this span, which include all these $y$; the algorithm keeps the basis of it whose projection to $d$ coordinates, on which the bounded vectors found have a nonzero minor $h$, is in Hermite normal form \cite[Section 2, Theorem 2]{KB79}. Its entries are at most $d \cdot d!\, \beta^d \le 18\beta^3$ in absolute value, as a $d \times d$ minor of bounded vectors is at most $d!\, \beta^d$: at these coordinates they are at most the projected lattice's determinant, which divides $h$, and by Cramer's rule the others are combinations of these $d$ whose coefficients are such minors divided by $h$. By Cramer's rule, a bounded vector has coefficients at most $24\beta \max\{18\beta^3, q\}^3$; so all numbers have $O(\log q)$ bits. Hermite normal forms also give the functionals and $\mathcal{M}_{i+1}$, and the cited algorithms are polynomial.
nodes.explain: If 2β < q and 24β⁴ < q³, a deterministic algorithm LIFT returns, for a nonzero v with v_0 = 0, a short multiple of v, or ⊥ if there is none, in time polynomial in N and log q. Proof idea: Add one coordinate at a time, keeping a lattice of rank at most three that contains all bounded vectors; each extension is a few integer programs and Hermite normal forms in dimension at most four.

nodes.label: Lemma B.10
nodes.name: Factor one half
nodes.statement: In the experiment of Definition 3.6, $\Pr[\, b' = b \wedge \mathsf{Fail} \,] \le \frac12 + \frac14 (f_0 + f_1)$.
nodes.proof: By the coupling, the coins of $\mathsf{R}_\$$, which are independent of $b$, determine whether $\mathsf{Tgt}$ occurs and, if not, the output $b'$ \cite[full version, proof of Lemma 2]{EC:BelRog06}. So $\Pr[b' = b \wedge \neg\mathsf{Tgt}] \le \frac12 (1 - p)$ for $p := \Pr[\mathsf{Tgt}]$, and $f := \Pr[\mathsf{Tgt} \wedge \mathsf{Fail}] = \frac12 (f_0 + f_1) \le p$. Hence $\Pr[b' = b \wedge \mathsf{Fail}] \le \tfrac12 (1 - p) + f \le \tfrac12 + \tfrac12 f$.
nodes.explain: Pr[b′ = b and E fails] ≤ 1/2 + (f_0 + f_1)/4, where f_b is the probability, on the run with m_b, that A makes the target query and E outputs no witness. Proof idea: Until the target query the two runs have the same law, so without it the output bit is independent of b.

nodes.label: Lemma B.11
nodes.name: Initial coincidences
nodes.statement: A run's first mark is $\mathsf{init}$ with probability at most $\sum_{s \in \{1,2,T\}} \binom{L_s}{2}\, \varepsilon_f$.
nodes.proof: The mark $\mathsf{init}$ requires two received elements of one group with equal exponents and expressions that are not formally equal. For a fixed pair and every $r$ this has probability at most $\varepsilon_f$ over $\mathbf{c}$: in $\mathbb{G}_1$ or $\mathbb{G}_2$ by Lemma B.4(e), and for the pair $G_T$, $\mathsf{K}^\alpha$, with values $1$ and $\alpha\kappa$, by Lemma B.4(c); and $\mathbb{G}_s$ has $\binom{L_s}{2}$ pairs.
nodes.explain: The first mark is “init” (two received elements of one group collide although their expressions differ) with probability at most Σ_s C(L_s, 2)·ε_f. Proof idea: Each pair collides with probability at most ε_f by the View lemma; union bound.

nodes.label: Lemma B.12
nodes.name: Charged marks
nodes.statement: The first mark of a run is charged with probability at most $N_{\mathrm{cmp}}(u)\, (\theta + \varepsilon_f) + \bigl( \binom{L + 3u}{2} + L + 3u \bigr)\, \varepsilon_f$.
nodes.proof:
\emph{Step 1: the two games agree until a collision.} Sample the label injections of $\mathsf{R}_\$$, independent of $h$ and $H_{\mathsf{key}}$, lazily, given their images, deciding a label's exponent when it gets an entry \cites[proof of Theorem 1]{EC:Shoup97}{EC:BonBoy04a}. With the evaluation first, this is the symbolic game with value equality in place of formal equality, except that $\mathsf{R}_\$$ redraws a new guess variable's value if an entry already has it, which is a collision. So on the same randomness, until a collision, both games make the same calls and queries with equal answers, the monitor's table in $\mathsf{R}_\$$ is that of the symbolic game, and in each group its entries have distinct values, their labels' exponents, and no other element has a label yet. The first collision's call is the same; its answer may differ.

\vspace{0pt plus 4pt}\emph{Step 2: a charged first mark gives a bad event.} Let the first mark of $\mathsf{R}_\$$ be charged. No two received elements collide, as this sets $\mathsf{init}$, and by Step 1 the monitor sets no mark until a collision occurs at a call or $\mathcal{A}$ queries $H_{\mathsf{key}}$ at the target label. If a collision comes first, the first one is bad. Suppose that it is good, with later entry $\mathsf{X}$ and earlier entry $\mathsf{X}'$. As $\mathsf{X} - \mathsf{X}'$ lies in $\mathbb{G}_T$ and has no guess variable, $\mathsf{X}$ is not a new guess variable, which occurs in its difference with every earlier entry; so $\mathsf{X}$ is a result. In $\mathsf{R}_\$$ it has the value of $\mathsf{X}'$, hence the label of $\mathsf{X}'$, and the monitor sets $\mathsf{diff}(\mathsf{X}^\circ - \mathsf{X}'^\circ)$, a good first mark: a contradiction. If the query comes first, it sets the first mark, which is not $\mathsf{guess}$; so (M4) reads the entry of the target label, a key value by Step 1, and a bad one: the mark is $\mathsf{coll}$ if it has a guess variable, and else a $\mathsf{key}(\mathsf{D})$ that is not good.

\vspace{0pt plus 4pt}\emph{Step 3: a bad event is unlikely.} Fix a symbolic game and in it two entries, or one entry; we bound the probability over the evaluation that they form a bad event.
\emph{(i) $\mathsf{D}$ has a guess variable: at most $\varepsilon_f$.} The coefficient in $\mathsf{D}$ of some product of guess variables is not formally zero: a constant, or an expression of $\mathbb{G}_1$ or $\mathbb{G}_2$ whose value at every $r$ is then zero with probability at most $\varepsilon_f < 1$ over $\mathbf{c}$ (Lemma B.4(e)). So for every $r$, $\varpi \cdot (\operatorname{val}(\mathsf{D}) - \chi\kappa)$ is a nonzero polynomial in $\mathbf{c}$ and the guess variables, of total degree at most $d_f + 1$ by Lemma B.3, as $\varpi$ has degree five, and by Schwartz's lemma it vanishes with probability at most $(d_f + 1)/(q - D) \le \varepsilon_f$.
\emph{(ii) $\mathsf{D}$ has none: at most $\theta + \varepsilon_f$.} Over $\mathbf{c}$, the bound is $\varepsilon_f$ in $\mathbb{G}_1$ or $\mathbb{G}_2$ (Lemma B.4(e)) and in $\mathbb{G}_T$ at an $r$ at which $\mathsf{D}$ is not $\chi\kappa$ identically (Lemma B.4(c)). Every other $r$ satisfies $W_c\, r = u_c$ for the mark stack $\mathbf{W}$ of $\mathsf{D}$ and its vectors $u_c$ (Lemma B.4(a)); if there is one, $\mathbf{W}$ is nonzero, as $\mathsf{D}$ is not $\chi\kappa$ formally (Lemma B.4(b), (d)), and light, as the event is bad, so these $r$ have probability at most $\operatorname{gp}(\mathbf{W}) \le \theta$.

\vspace{0pt plus 4pt}\emph{Step 4: counts.} A call adds at most three entries, two guessed operands and a result; of the at most $L + 3Q$ entries, at most $3Q$ have a guess variable, and case (i) covers at most $\binom{L + 3Q}{2}$ pairs and $3Q \le L + 3u$ key values, as $u = 2Q + 2$. In case (ii) a collision at call $j$ pairs its result, as $\mathsf{D}$ has no guess variable (Step 2), with one of at most $L + 3j - 1$ other entries, and a key value is a result or one of the two received elements of $\mathbb{G}_T$: at most $\sum_{j=1}^{Q} (L + 3j - 1) + Q + 2 \le N_{\mathrm{cmp}}(u)$ events. A union bound gives the claim.
nodes.explain: The first mark is charged (a collision with a guessed label, or a comparison that is not a good mark) with probability at most N_(cmp)(u)(θ + ε_f) + (C(L+3u, 2) + L + 3u)·ε_f. Proof idea: Shoup's simulation argument: a symbolic game answers by formal equality and agrees with the real run until two values collide. A bad collision has probability at most ε_f over the coins, or at most θ over the search vector when its stack is light. Union bound over the comparisons.

nodes.label: Lemma B.13
nodes.name: A guessed target label
nodes.statement: If $\mathcal{A}$ makes at most $Q_H \le 2^\lambda$ queries to $H_{\mathsf{key}}$, the first mark of a run is $\mathsf{guess}$ with probability at most $Q_H / N_{\mathsf{free}} \le 2^{\lambda}/N_{\mathsf{free}}$.
nodes.proof: In $\mathsf{R}_\$$, sample $\mathsf{lab}_T$ lazily, deciding whether a string is a label, and of which element, only for the two received labels of $\mathbb{G}_T$ and, at each call, at most two operands and a result's label: at most $2 + 3Q$ strings, of which those that are labels have entries until the first mark. So $\mathsf{guess}$ is set at a query to $H_{\mathsf{key}}$ before which $[\kappa]_T$ has no label. At such a query, given the other randomness of $\mathsf{R}_\$$, which is independent of $\mathsf{lab}_T$, and the sampler's earlier decisions, which together determine the query, its label is uniform among the $U \ge 2^{\ell_{\mathsf{lab}}} - 2 - 3Q \ge N_{\mathsf{free}}$ undecided strings, so it is the query's string with probability at most $1/U$. A union bound over the at most $Q_H$ queries gives the first bound; the second holds as $Q_H \le 2^\lambda$.
nodes.explain: The first mark is “guess” (A queries H_(key) at the target label before that label was ever produced) with probability at most Q_H/N_(free). Proof idea: Sample the label map lazily: an unproduced label is uniform among at least N_(free) strings.

nodes.label: Lemma B.14
nodes.name: Reductions
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathcal{A}$ be an adversary and $b \in \{0,1\}$.

 
(a) \emph{Law.} For a uniform challenge, the run of $\mathcal{A}$ in (R1) has the law of the run with $m_b$ of the experiment, as the values that (R1) sets are uniform; the coins of (R2) are independent of it.
(b) \emph{Soundness.} Every output of $\mathcal{B}_b$ other than $\bot$ is a solution of MSIS for its challenge, the columns $1, \dots, \ell$ of $M$.
(c) \emph{Detection.} For every run whose first mark has an expression $\mathsf{D}$, an expression of (R3) is formally equal to $\mathsf{D}$, except with probability at most $\varepsilon_f$ over $\mathsf{a}_{\mathrm{p}}$.
(d) \emph{Recovery.} For every run whose first mark is good, with expression $\mathsf{D}$ and mark sector $\mathsf{s}$, the vectors $\nabla^{(l,\mathsf{s})}(\mathsf{D})$ lie in the row space of the mark stack, and span it except with probability at most $\varepsilon_f$ over the recovery points; and if $\mathsf{s}$ is the alpha sector, the vectors $\nabla^{(l,\mathrm{plain})}(\mathsf{D})$ are zero.

Consequently, in the run with $m_b$ and a uniform $M$, the probability that the first mark is good and the row space of its mark stack contains a kernel vector is at most $s_b + 2\varepsilon_f$.
nodes.proof:
(a) holds by construction, and (b) by Lemma B.8(c), as $\mathsf{LIFT}(v)$ returns only short multiples of $v$.

(c) By the invariant of Appendix B.4, at a first mark $\mathsf{key}(\mathsf{D})$ the record of the target label is formally equal to $\mathsf{D}$, as an entry without a guess variable has a record and records are never replaced. At a first mark $\mathsf{diff}(\mathsf{D})$, so is the result's record minus the label's, the first expression of (R3) unless $\operatorname{val}(\mathsf{D}; \mathsf{a}_{\mathrm{p}}) = 0$, as no earlier result in $\mathbb{G}_T$ meets a record of another value. As $\mathsf{D}$ is then not formally zero (M3), $\varpi \cdot \operatorname{val}(\mathsf{D})$ is a nonzero polynomial of total degree at most $d_f$ in $\mathbf{c}$ and $r$ (Lemma B.3), so by Schwartz's lemma it vanishes at $\mathsf{a}_{\mathrm{p}}$ with probability at most $d_f/(q - D) \le \varepsilon_f$.

(d) As $\mathsf{D}$ is $\chi\kappa$ identically at the search vector, the hidden-basis step in the proof of Lemma B.4 gives $\mathsf{D}_{ab} = 0$ for $b = (\mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{leg}}_{j,1})^{\mathsf{s}'}$ unless $a$ is some $\mathsf{F}^{k_1}_{i,1}$, whose exponent is $\pi_{k_1} y_i$. So $\nabla^{(l,\mathsf{s}')}(\mathsf{D}) = \alpha_{\mathsf{s}'} \sum_{c,i} \gamma_c\, y_i\, W_{c,i}$, with the coins of its recovery point and the rows $W_{c,i}$ of the $W^{\mathsf{s}'}_c(\mathsf{D})$: a vector of this stack's row space, zero if the stack is, as the plain one is if the mark sector is the alpha sector. Expressions formally equal to $\mathsf{D}$ have its values and stacks (Appendix B.4), so the same vectors. Let $\phi$ be a linear form nonzero on the row space $\mathcal{V}$ of the mark stack. Then $\phi(\nabla^{(l,\mathsf{s})}(\mathsf{D})) / (\alpha_{\mathsf{s}} \pi) = \sum_{c,i} \phi(W_{c,i})\, (\gamma_c / \pi)\, y_i$ is a nonzero polynomial of degree at most $n + 2$ in the coins: its monomial $s_{\mathrm{X}}\, \upsilon^{k_c} y_i$, for the kind $\mathrm{X}$ of $c$, which determines $c$ and $i$ (as in that step), has coefficient $\phi(W_{c,i})$, nonzero for some $(c, i)$ as these rows span $\mathcal{V}$. As $\alpha_{\mathsf{s}} \pi \ne 0$ at valid coins, $\phi(\nabla^{(l,\mathsf{s})}(\mathsf{D})) = 0$ with probability at most $(n+2)/(q - D)$. As $\dim \mathcal{V} \le 3$, the three vectors span $\mathcal{V}$ unless one lies in the span of the earlier ones while that span is not $\mathcal{V}$, so that such a $\phi$ vanishes on it; as the recovery points are independent, the bound holds given the earlier ones: probability at most $3(n+2)/(q - D) \le \varepsilon_f$, as $n \le D$.

For the consequence, fix such a run. Except with probability $2\varepsilon_f$, by (c) an expression of (R3) is formally equal to $\mathsf{D}$, and by (d) and its proof its vectors of (R4) are the $\nabla^{(l,\mathsf{s})}(\mathsf{D})$ and span $\mathcal{V}$ in the mark sector and, if this is the alpha sector, vanish in the plain one. So for it (R5) finds a kernel vector $v \in \mathcal{V}$ and $\mathsf{LIFT}$ a short multiple of it (Lemma B.8(b)), and $\mathcal{B}_b$ outputs a solution, for it or earlier (b): probability $s_b$ by (a).
nodes.explain: For the reduction B_b: (a) its run of A has the law of the real run with m_b; (b) every output other than ⊥ solves Module-SIS for its challenge; (c) a private monitor finds the first mark's expression except with probability ε_f; (d) three random gradients in r lie in the row space of the mark stack and span it except with probability ε_f. Hence: Pr[good first mark with a kernel vector in the row space] ≤ s_b + 2ε_f. Proof idea: Detection by evaluating at a private random point; recovery by gradients in the search vector, which are random combinations of the rows; then LIFT turns the kernel vector into a short one.

nodes.label: Proposition B.15
nodes.name: Running time of the reductions
nodes.proof:
Let $\mathcal{B}_b$ sample the coins of (R2) first and follow the calls as $\mathcal{A}$ makes them, with tables of labels, exponents, records, rejected strings, names, and answers of $H_{\mathsf{key}}$ and $H_{\mathsf{seed}}$; by Lemma B.14(a) this changes no output. Its costs beyond the running times of $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathsf{LIFT}$ are the following, by the term that pays for them.\par
{\small
\begin{itemize}[label={},leftmargin=1.5em,itemindent=-1.5em,nosep,topsep=2pt]
 \item $148\, Q$. A call to $\mathcal{O}_{\mathsf{GG}}$ has one result (of a linear operation or pairing, or the negative of a name request) and takes up to $148$ operations: $14$ for its lookups, exponent, value at $\mathsf{a}_{\mathrm{p}}$, node, label, and test of (R3); $6 \cdot 19$ for the six passes of (R4), each with three operations forwards and, for each expression, a gradient computed backwards through the calls \cite[Theorem 2]{BS83} with four operations and four for the derivatives of the received operands; $2 \cdot 8$ for two operand strings not in the tables, to decide whether each is a label and to sample its exponent; $2$ for two records of $0$; $2$ for the name.
 \item $(d_R + 5)\, Q_H$: $3$ for a query to $H_{\mathsf{key}}$ (a lookup, a sample, and an insertion); and $d_R + 2$ for a query to $H_{\mathsf{seed}}$ ($d_R$ samples, a lookup, and an insertion).
 \item $8 I$, for the exponents of all published elements at eight points, the coins of $\mathsf{Enc}$ and of (R2), $I$ operations each. With $N' := N + 1$ and $n_2$ the number of elements of $ct_2$, $I$ is the sum of $3N' + 19$ for the samples and $r_0$; $\frac72 n + \Delta + \Delta' + J + J' + 3$ for the powers of $\upsilon$, $-\omega\upsilon$, and $\tau$; $9\,k\,d_R\,N' + 3n$ for $z$ at its three points, from $M$; $5K_1 + 3K_2 + \frac32 n$ for the scalars of the legs and cells; $13K_2 N' + 17K_2$ for the masks; $(4N' + 6)(D - 1) + 2$ for $A_i$, $B_i$, $Z$, $Z_0$, and $L_\rho$ at $\tau$ by Horner's rule, from their coefficients, which depend only on $S$ and are built into $\mathcal{B}_b$; and $(2K_1 + 24K_2 + 4) N' + \Delta + (1 - 1/\nu) \Delta' + 3n (J + J') + 13n + 3K_2 + n_2 + 22$ for the published elements.
 \item $3 L$, for the label of each received element, with tables for each group: a sample $\mathsf{u}$ that is not a key, an insertion of $\mathsf{u}$ at its exponent $x$, which returns the label $\mathsf{u}'$ kept there, and one of $x$ and its record at $\mathsf{u}'$; so equal exponents get one label.
 \item $2\, C_{\mathrm{post}}$, after the run, for each expression: $3N'$ for the gradients of the alpha sector; $2(18N' + 3)$ for two row echelon forms; $2\bigl((9\,k\,d_R + 5) N' + 21\,k\,d_R + 33\bigr)$ for the intersections with the kernel of $z$ in both sectors; and $N'$ for the packing.
 \item $C_{\mathrm{set}}$: the sum of $1$ for the seed; $2k\ell + k(d_R + 2)$ for $M$, that is, $k\ell$ insertions of the challenge, then the $k(\ell + 1)$ queries of $\mathsf{Enc}$, a lookup each in columns $1$ to $\ell$ and $d_R + 2$ operations each in column $0$; $6 + \lceil \mu/\ell_{\mathsf{lab}} \rceil$ for the masked message, that is, $3$ for the label of $[\kappa]_T$ and its exponent, with no record, $3$ for the answer of $H_{\mathsf{key}}$ there, and an XOR for each block of at most $\ell_{\mathsf{lab}}$ bits of $m_b$; and $256$ for $G_T$ and $\mathsf{K}^\alpha$, counted as results.
 \item $C_{\mathrm{desc}}$, for the description of $\mathcal{B}_b$ beyond that of $\mathcal{A}$: the sum of $(2N' + 4) D + 1$ for the coefficients of $A_i$, $B_i$, $Z$, $Z_0$, and $L_\rho$ and for the evaluation points; $\lceil \mu/\ell_{\mathsf{lab}} \rceil$ for $m_b$; and the length of its code, a constant.
\end{itemize}}
 Hence $C_R = O((N + n) D + \mu)$, as $k\, d_R < n \le D$ and $J + J' \le 3D$, with $J' = 1$ if $n_{\mathsf{c}} = 0$ (Section 5.2).
nodes.explain: B_0 and B_1 run in time at most t + 148·Q + (d_R + 5)·Q_H + C_R + 2·T_(LIFT), which is t + O(Q + d_R·Q_H + μ) + poly(D, log q). Proof idea: An operation-by-operation ledger of the reduction: 148 operations per group-oracle call, d_R + 5 per oracle query, and fixed costs that do not depend on A.

nodes.label: Lemma B.16
nodes.name: Extractor
nodes.statement:
(a) Every output of $\mathcal{E}$ is $\bot$ or a witness of $S$.
(b) If the first mark of a run has an expression $\mathsf{D}$ and $\mathcal{E}$ outputs $\bot$, then the tests of the sketches of $\mathsf{D}$ in both sectors find nothing.
(c) Let $\mathbf{W}$ be a nonzero usable stack whose row space $\mathcal{V}$ has dimension at most three and contains no kernel vector, and let the $v^{(l)}_c$ be independent and uniform. Then a test of the three vectors $\sum_c W_c\, v^{(l)}_c$, $l \in [3]$, outputs a witness, except with probability at most $2/q$.

Consequently, the probability that the first mark of a run is good, the row space of its mark stack contains no kernel vector, and $\mathcal{E}$ outputs no witness is at most $2/q$.
nodes.proof:
(a) A test finds only witnesses.
(b) As $\mathcal{E}$ outputs $\bot$, its tests found nothing. At a mark $\mathsf{diff}(\mathsf{D})$, the result's label has a record and the difference that $\mathcal{E}$ tested has the sketches of $\mathsf{D}$ (Appendix B.4). At a mark $\mathsf{key}(\mathsf{D})$, $\mathsf{D}$ is $\mathsf{X}^\circ$ for an entry $\mathsf{X}$ without a guess variable: a received element, whose stacks are zero, or a result, whose sketches $\mathcal{E}$ tested. A test of zero vectors finds nothing.

(c) As the $W_c$ are symmetric, the linear map $(v_c)_c \mapsto \sum_c W_c\, v_c$ has image $\mathcal{V}$, so these vectors are independent and uniform on $\mathcal{V}$, of dimension $d \le 3$, and span it with probability $\prod_{0 \le i < d} (1 - q^{i-3}) > 1 - 2/q$ \cite[(1) and Lemma 2.3]{FG15}. Then the test finds a witness: $\mathcal{V}$ contains one (Lemma B.6), which is a candidate.

For the consequence, fix a run as stated, with expression $\mathsf{D}$. Its mark stack meets the conditions of (c) (Appendix B.4), and the probe vectors are independent of the run; so except with probability $2/q$ the test of the sketches of $\mathsf{D}$ in the mark sector finds a witness, and then $\mathcal{E}$ outputs a witness, by (b) and (a).
nodes.explain: (a) Every output of E is ⊥ or a witness. (b) If the first mark has an expression D and E outputs ⊥, the tests of the sketches of D found nothing. (c) For a nonzero usable stack of rank at most three with no kernel vector, a test of three random sketches outputs a witness except with probability 2/q. Hence: Pr[good first mark, no kernel vector, no witness from E] ≤ 2/q. Proof idea: The sketches are uniform on the row space and span it with probability above 1 − 2/q; by Classification the row space contains a witness, which the test finds among at most four candidates.

nodes.label: Lemma B.17
nodes.name: Integer lattices
nodes.statement:
Let $\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^I$ be a lattice of rank $d$ with a basis matrix $B$.

 
(a) If $\Theta$ has a largest minor at $J$, then $|y_i| \le \|y_J\|_1$ for all $y \in \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{R}}(\Theta)$ and $i \in I$.
(b) If $\Theta$ is saturated, then $B^\top \mathbb{Z}^I = \mathbb{Z}^d$.
(c) If an integer matrix $\Delta$ with rows indexed by $I$ has rank $k$ and $k \times k$ minors below $q$ in absolute value, then every $c \in \mathbb{Z}^I$ with $c^\top \Delta = 0 \bmod q$ is congruent modulo $q$ to a $u \in \mathbb{Z}^I$ with $u^\top \Delta = 0$.
nodes.proof:
(a) As $B_J$ is invertible, Cramer's rule writes each row of $B$ as a combination of the rows of $B_J$ with coefficients, ratios of $d \times d$ minors of $B$ (or zero) to $\det B_J$, of absolute value at most $1$; and $y_i$ is the same combination of the entries of $y_J$.
(b) As $\Theta$ is saturated, the columns of $B$ extend to a basis of $\mathbb{Z}^I$ \cite[Chapter I, Theorem I, Corollary 3]{Cas97}, the columns of a unimodular matrix $(B, B')$, and the first $d$ rows of its integer inverse form a left inverse of $B$, so $B^\top \mathbb{Z}^I = \mathbb{Z}^d$.
(c) As $\Delta$ has rank $k$ and a nonzero $k \times k$ minor below $q$ in absolute value, it has rank $k$ modulo $q$, so the reductions of these $c$ form a subspace of $\mathbb{F}_q^I$ of dimension $|I| - k$. It contains the reduction of the saturated lattice of the $u \in \mathbb{Z}^I$ with $u^\top \Delta = 0$, of rank $|I| - k$, whose basis matrices have integer left inverses by (b); so that reduction has dimension $|I| - k$ too, and the two are equal.
nodes.explain: (a) At a largest minor J, |y_i| ≤ ‖y_J‖_1 on the real span. (b) A saturated lattice with basis B has B^⊤Z^I = Z^d. (c) If an integer matrix Δ has rank k and k×k minors below q, every c with c^⊤Δ ≡ 0 mod q is congruent to an integer u with u^⊤Δ = 0. Proof idea: Cramer's rule and the extension of a basis of a saturated lattice to a basis of Z^I.

nodes.label: Lemma B.18
nodes.name: Prefix lattices
nodes.statement:
Let $\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^I$ be a saturated lattice of rank $d \ge 1$ with a basis matrix $B$ and a largest minor at $J$. Order $I$ as $i_1, \dots, i_{|I|}$ with $J$ first, and for $d \le k \le |I|$ let $I_k := \{ i_1, \dots, i_k \}$, and let $\Theta_k \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^{I_k}$ be the integer points of the column span of the submatrix $B_{I_k}$, with height $h_k$ and largest fiber density $m_k$.

 
(a) $\Theta_d = \mathbb{Z}^{I_d}$, so $h_d = 1$ and $m_d = g^{-d}$; $\Theta_{|I|} = \Theta$; and each $\Theta_k$ has rank $d$ and a largest minor at $J$.
(b) For $d \le k < |I|$ there is an integer $s_k \ge 1$ with $h_{k+1} = s_k h_k$ and $m_{k+1} \le m_k \lceil g/s_k \rceil/g$. If $s_k \ge g$, the entry at $i_{k+1}$ is constant on each fiber of $\Theta_{k+1}$; if $s_k < g$, then $m_{k+1}^b h_{k+1}^{b-1} \le m_k^b h_k^{b-1}$.
(c) If $d = 3$ and $m(\Theta) \ge \mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$, then $h(\Theta) \le H_3$ and $\Theta$ is regular.
nodes.proof:
For $d \le k \le |I|$, $B_{I_k}$ contains the invertible $B_J$, so $\Theta_k$ has rank $d$, and $B_{I_k} = YC$ for a basis matrix $Y$ of $\Theta_k$ and an integer matrix $C$ with $\det C \ne 0$. So the fibers of $\Theta_k$ are the level sets of $r \mapsto B_{I_k}^\top r$; the group $G_k := B_{I_k}^\top \mathbb{Z}^{I_k} = C^\top \mathbb{Z}^d$ has index $|\det C|$ in $\mathbb{Z}^d$, by Lemma B.17(b); and the minors of $B_{I_k}$ are those of $Y$ times $\det C$, the largest being $|\det B_J| = h(\Theta)$.
