Hence $h_k\, [\mathbb{Z}^d : G_k] = h(\Theta)$, and $\Theta_k$ has a largest minor at $J$. As $B_J$ is invertible, $\Theta_d = \mathbb{Z}^{I_d}$, whose fibers are points; and $\Theta_{|I|} = \Theta$, as $\Theta$ is saturated. This proves (a).

(b) Let $s_k$ be the order of $B_{i_{k+1}}^\top$ modulo $G_k$, a subgroup of finite index. Then $G_{k+1} = G_k + \mathbb{Z} B_{i_{k+1}}^\top$, so $[\mathbb{Z}^d : G_k] = s_k\, [\mathbb{Z}^d : G_{k+1}]$ and $h_{k+1} = s_k h_k$. For box points $(r', x)$ on $I_{k+1}$, with $x$ the entry at $i_{k+1}$, $B_{I_{k+1}}^\top (r', x) = t$ requires $t - x B_{i_{k+1}}^\top \in G_k$, as $B_{I_k}^\top r' \in G_k$; this holds for $x$ in at most one class modulo $s_k$, which has at most $\lceil g/s_k \rceil$ elements in $[2, g+1]$, and at most one if $s_k \ge g$. Averaging over the uniform $x$ gives $m_{k+1} \le m_k \lceil g/s_k \rceil/g \le m_k$, which proves the last claim for $s_k = 1$. For $2 \le s := s_k < g$, as $h_{k+1}^{b-1} = s^{b-1} h_k^{b-1}$, it follows from $\lceil g/s \rceil/g < 1/s + 1/g \le s^{-1+1/b}$: for $s \ge 2^b$, $1/s + 1/g < 2/s \le s^{-1+1/b}$; for $s < 2^b$, $1/s + 1/g \le 1/s + 2^{-b}$ by (I1), and $1 + s\, 2^{-b} \le s^{1/b}$, as the concave function $s^{1/b} - 1 - s\, 2^{-b}$ vanishes at $s = 2^b$ and is positive at $s = 2$, where $2^{1/b} - 1 > (\ln 2)/b > 2^{1-b}$, as $b \ge 7$.

(c) Let $h := h(\Theta)$. By (a) and (b), and as $\lceil g/s \rceil/g < 1/s + 1/g$, $m(\Theta) \le g^{-3} \prod_k (1/s_k + 1/g)$ over the $n'$ steps with $s_k \ge 2$, whose $s_k$ multiply to $h$. Expanded, the product is $1/h$ plus terms with a factor $1/g$ and other factors at most $1/2$, which sum to at most $(\frac12 + \frac1g)^{n'} - 2^{-n'} \le \frac{n'}{g} (\frac12 + \frac1g)^{n'-1} \le (1 + \frac2g)/g \le \xi_{\mathrm{tr}}/g$, by the mean value theorem and as $n' (\frac12 + \frac1g)^{n'-1}$ is largest at $n' = 2$, since $(1 + \frac1{n'})(\frac12 + \frac1g) < 1$ for $n' \ge 2$, by (I1). So $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}} \le m(\Theta) \le g^{-3} \xi_{\mathrm{tr}} (1/h + 1/g)$, whence $h \le \xi_{\mathrm{tr}}/(g^3 \mu_{\mathrm{tr}} - \xi_{\mathrm{tr}}/g) = H_3$ by (I2), and $m(\Theta)\, h \le g^{-3} \xi_{\mathrm{tr}} (1 + H_3/g) \le \Gamma_3/g^3$ by (I4).
nodes.explain: Along the prefixes of a saturated lattice: (a) the first prefix is all of Z^d and each prefix keeps the largest minor; (b) heights multiply by an integer s_k while fiber density drops by ⌈g/s_k⌉/g; (c) a rank-three lattice with a dense fiber has height at most H_3 and is regular. Proof idea: Index computations in Z^d and an elementary inequality in s_k.

nodes.label: Lemma B.19
nodes.name: Trimming
nodes.statement: Trimming a set by such a lattice $\Theta$ lowers its density by at most $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
nodes.proof: Let $B$ be a basis matrix of $\Theta$, $X := B^\top r_I - y_\Theta$, and $\Sigma := \Sigma_\Theta$. Each $r_i - \frac{g+3}{2}$ is uniform on $g$ points spaced by $1$ around $0$; adding an independent uniform variable on the real interval $[-\frac12, \frac12]$, whose moment generating function is at least $1$, makes it uniform on an interval of length $g$, so $\mathbb{E}\, e^{t (r_i - (g+3)/2)} \le \sinh(y)/y \le e^{y^2/6}$ for $y = tg/2$, as $(2k+1)! \ge 6^k k!$. By independence, $\mathbb{E}\, e^{u^\top X} \le e^{(g^2/24) \|B u\|^2} = e^{u^\top \Sigma u/2}$ for $u \in \mathbb{R}^d$. For a standard Gaussian vector $Z$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$, independent of $r$, Fubini's theorem then gives $\mathbb{E}\, e^{99 X^\top \Sigma^{-1} X/200} = \mathbb{E}\, e^{(99/100)^{1/2} Z^\top \Sigma^{-1/2} X} \le \mathbb{E}\, e^{99 \|Z\|^2/200} = 10^d$; so $X^\top \Sigma^{-1} X > R_{\mathrm{tr}}^2$ with probability at most $10^d e^{-99 R_{\mathrm{tr}}^2/200} \le \varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$, by Markov's inequality and (I2), and trimming removes only such points.
nodes.explain: Restricting a set of box points to the trimming ellipsoid of a lattice of rank at most three lowers its density by at most ε_(tr). Proof idea: A sub-Gaussian moment bound for uniform integers and Markov's inequality.

nodes.label: Lemma B.20
nodes.name: Trimmed sets are sparse
nodes.statement:
Let $\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^I$, with $|I| \le N$, be a lattice of rank $d \in [3]$ with a basis matrix $B$, $F$ a nonempty set of box points on $I \cup \{i'\}$, $i' \notin I$, trimmed by $\Theta$, and $\Phi(r) := (B^\top r_I, r_{i'})$.

 
(a) If $\dim \Phi(F) = d + 1$ and $\Phi(F)$ is in a coset of a subgroup of index $q$ of $\mathbb{Z}^{d+1}$, then $\Pr[F] \le \Lambda_d\, g^d\, h(\Theta)\, m(\Theta)/q$.
(b) If $F^\perp$ has a rank $d'$ with $1 \le d' < d$ and a largest minor at a set $J \subseteq I$, and the restriction to $I$ of each vector of $F^\perp$ lies in $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{R}}(\Theta)$, then $\Pr[F]\, h(F^\perp) \le \Lambda_{d-d'}\, g^{d-d'}\, h(\Theta)\, m(\Theta)$.
nodes.proof:
The box points $r$ with $\Phi(r) = (y, x)$ have density $\Pr[B^\top r_I = y]/g$, so $\Pr[F] \le |\Phi(F)|\, m(\Theta)/g$; we count $\Phi(F)$, which lies in $\mathcal{C} := \mathcal{T}_\Theta \times \{ x \in \mathbb{R} : 2 \le x \le g+1 \}$, after a projection to $k$ coordinates. Write $B = (B_1, B_2)$, with $B_2$ the last $k - 1$ columns of $B$, and $y = (y_1, y_2)$ accordingly.

In (a), $k := d + 1$, so $B_1$ is empty; let $J := \emptyset$, $\det (B_1)_J := 1$, $\delta := q$, and $p$ the identity. Part (b) does not depend on $B$, which we choose as follows, with $k := d + 1 - d'$. As $Y_J$, for a basis matrix $Y$ of $F^\perp$, is invertible and its columns lie in $B_J \mathbb{R}^d$ by hypothesis, $B_J$ has rank $d'$. Extending a basis of the saturated lattice of the $z \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ with $B_J z = 0$ to one of $\mathbb{Z}^d$ in which it comes last \cite[Chapter I, Theorem I, Corollary 3]{Cas97}, and changing $B$ accordingly, we may take $(B_2)_J = 0$, so that $(B_1)_J$ is invertible; $F$ stays trimmed.

\emph{Image normals.} The injective map $\Phi^*(a) := (B a_{[d]}, a_{d+1})$ has $\Phi^*(a)^\top r = a^\top \Phi(r)$, and each vector of $F^\perp$ is a $\Phi^*(a)$, as its restriction to $I$ lies in $B\, \mathbb{R}^d$; so $\Phi^*$ maps the real vectors orthogonal to the differences of $\Phi(F)$ onto those of $F$, the span of $F^\perp$, and $\Phi(F)^\perp$ has rank $d'$ and $\dim \Phi(F) = k$. A basis matrix $V$ of $\Phi(F)^\perp$, with row blocks $V_1$, $V_2$, and $V_3$ of $d'$, $k-1$, and $1$ rows, maps under $\Phi^*$ to $Y C$ for an integer matrix $C$ with $\det C \ne 0$; at the rows $J$, this reads $(B_1)_J V_1 = Y_J C$, so $|\det (B_1)_J| \cdot |\det V_1| \ge h(F^\perp)$.

\emph{Projected lattice.} Let $\delta := |\det V_1|$ and $p(y, x) := (y_2, x)$, which is injective on $\ker V^\top$, as $V_1$ is invertible; $\ker V^\top$ contains the differences of $\Phi(F)$. As $V^\top \mathbb{Z}^{d+1} = \mathbb{Z}^{d'}$ by Lemma B.17(b), $(y_2, x) \mapsto V_2^\top y_2 + x V_3^\top$ maps $\mathbb{Z}^k$ onto $\mathbb{Z}^{d'}/V_1^\top \mathbb{Z}^{d'}$, of order $\delta$, with kernel $p(\ker V^\top \cap \mathbb{Z}^{d+1})$.

\emph{Counting and volume.} In both parts, then, $p(\Phi(F))$ has $|\Phi(F)|$ points and affine dimension $k$, and lies in a coset of a subgroup of index $\delta$ of $\mathbb{Z}^k$ and in $p(\mathcal{C})$. So $|\Phi(F)| \le k!\, \operatorname{vol}(p(\mathcal{C}))/\delta + k \le (k+1)!\, \operatorname{vol}(p(\mathcal{C}))/\delta$, by Blichfeldt's inequality \cite[(1.1)]{HW08}, for the image of the convex hull of $p(\Phi(F))$ under an affine map that takes the coset to $\mathbb{Z}^k$ and divides volumes by $\delta$, and as that hull contains a simplex with vertices in the coset, of volume at least $\delta/k!$. Here $p(\mathcal{C})$ is the product of an interval of length $g - 1$ and the projection of $\mathcal{T}_\Theta = y_\Theta + R_{\mathrm{tr}} \Sigma^{1/2} \mathbb{B}^d$ to the coordinates of $y_2$, the ellipsoid $(y_\Theta)_2 + R_{\mathrm{tr}} \Sigma_{22}^{1/2} \mathbb{B}^{k-1}$ of volume $\operatorname{vol}(\mathbb{B}^{k-1}) R_{\mathrm{tr}}^{k-1} (\det \Sigma_{22})^{1/2}$, where $\Sigma := \Sigma_\Theta$, its block at $y_2$ is $\Sigma_{22} = \frac{g^2}{12} B_2^\top B_2$, and $\mathbb{B}^e$ is the unit ball of $\mathbb{R}^e$. By the Cauchy--Binet formula, $\det (B_2^\top B_2)$ is the sum of the $\det((B_2)_{J''})^2$ over the sets $J'' \subseteq I \setminus J$ of $k - 1$ indices, as $(B_2)_J = 0$; and $|\det (B_1)_J \det (B_2)_{J''}| = |\det B_{J \cup J''}| \le h(\Theta)$. Altogether, $\Pr[F]\, |\det (B_1)_J|\, \delta$ is at most $g^{k-1} h(\Theta)\, m(\Theta)$ times $(k+1)!\, \operatorname{vol}(\mathbb{B}^{k-1})\, R_{\mathrm{tr}}^{k-1} \bigl( \binom{N}{k-1} / 12^{k-1} \bigr)^{1/2}$, and as $\binom{N}{k-1} \le N^{k-1}/(k-1)!$, this factor is at most $2\sqrt{3}\, R_{\mathrm{tr}} \sqrt{N}$, $\sqrt{2}\, \pi R_{\mathrm{tr}}^2 N$, and $\frac{20\pi}{9\sqrt{2}} R_{\mathrm{tr}}^3 N^{3/2}$ for $k - 1 = 1, 2, 3$, hence at most $\Lambda_{k-1}$ by (I3). This is (a), and it gives (b), as $|\det (B_1)_J|\, \delta \ge h(F^\perp)$.
nodes.explain: For a set F trimmed by a lattice Θ of rank d: (a) if its image has full affine dimension d + 1 inside a coset of index q, then Pr[F] ≤ Λ_d·g^d·h(Θ)·m(Θ)/q; (b) a transition bound Pr[F]·h(F^⊥) ≤ Λ_(d−d′)·g^(d−d′)·h(Θ)·m(Θ). Proof idea: Count lattice points of the trimming ellipsoid with Blichfeldt's inequality after projecting to the right coordinates.

nodes.label: Lemma B.21
nodes.name: Regularization
nodes.statement: Let $\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^I$, $|I| \le N$, be a saturated lattice of a rank $d \in [3]$ with $m(\Theta) \ge \mu_{\mathrm{tr}} + (3 - d)\, \varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$. Then $\Theta$ lies in a regular saturated $\Theta' \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^I$ of rank in $[d, 3]$ with $m(\Theta') \ge m(\Theta) - (3 - d)\, \varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
nodes.proof:
We use downward induction on $d$. For $d = 3$, the lattice $\Theta' := \Theta$ is regular, by Lemma B.18(c). Let $d \le 2$, and take $B$, $J$, and the $I_k$, $\Theta_k$, $h_k$, $m_k$, and $s_k$ of Lemma B.18; by its part (b), $m_k \ge m(\Theta) \ge \mu_{\mathrm{tr}} + (3-d)\, \varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$ for all $k$.

For $k = d, \dots, |I|$, let $F_k$ be a densest fiber of $\Theta_k$, trimmed by $\tilde\Theta_{k-1}$ if $k > d$ and $F_{k-1}^\perp \ne \Theta_{k-1}$, so that $\Pr[F_k] \ge m_k - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$ (Lemma B.19). Here, if $F_k^\perp \ne \Theta_k$, then $F_k^\perp \supseteq \Theta_k$ has a rank $d_k \in [d+1, 3]$, as rank four or more would give $\Pr[F_k] \le g^{-4} < \mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$, by (I5); and $m(F_k^\perp) \ge \Pr[F_k] \ge \mu_{\mathrm{tr}} + (2-d)\, \varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}} \ge \mu_{\mathrm{tr}} + (3-d_k)\, \varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$, so the induction hypothesis gives a regular saturated $\tilde\Theta_k \supseteq F_k^\perp$ with $m(\tilde\Theta_k) \ge \Pr[F_k] - (2-d)\, \varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}} \ge m_k - (3-d)\, \varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$.

\emph{Promotion.} If $F_{|I|}^\perp \ne \Theta$, take $\Theta' := \tilde\Theta_{|I|} \supseteq \Theta$.

\emph{The last prefix with more equations.} Otherwise, let $j$ be the last $k < |I|$ with $F_k^\perp \ne \Theta_k$, or $j := d - 1$ if there is none. For $j < k < |I|$, $s_k < g$: else the entry at $i_{k+1}$ is constant on $F_{k+1}$ (Lemma B.18(b)), so $e_{i_{k+1}} \in F_{k+1}^\perp = \Theta_{k+1}$, a nonzero vector that vanishes at $J$, against Lemma B.17(a) and Lemma B.18(a). As $m(\Theta) \ge \mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$, Lemma B.18(b) then gives $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}} (m(\Theta)\, h(\Theta))^{b-1} \le m(\Theta)^b h(\Theta)^{b-1} \le m_{j+1}^b h_{j+1}^{b-1}$, so $\Theta' := \Theta$ is regular once $m_{j+1}^b h_{j+1}^{b-1} \le \mu_{\mathrm{tr}} (\Gamma_d/g^d)^{b-1}$, as $b \ge 2$.

\emph{The bound at $j + 1$.} If $j = d - 1$, this condition reads $g^{-d} \le \mu_{\mathrm{tr}} \Gamma_d^{b-1}$ (Lemma B.18(a)), which is (I4). If $j \ge d$, let $\tilde d$ be the rank of $\tilde\Theta_j$. Lemma B.20(b) applies to $\tilde\Theta_j$, $i_{j+1}$, and $F_{j+1}$: $F_{j+1}^\perp = \Theta_{j+1}$ has rank $d < \tilde d$ and a largest minor at $J \subseteq I_j$, and its vectors restricted to $I_j$ lie in $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{R}}(\Theta_j) \subseteq \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{R}}(F_j^\perp) \subseteq \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{R}}(\tilde\Theta_j)$. With the regularity of $\tilde\Theta_j$ and as $\Pr[F_{j+1}] \ge m_{j+1} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}} \ge m_{j+1}/A_{\mathrm{inv}}$ by $m_{j+1} \ge \mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$ and (I4), it gives $m_{j+1} h_{j+1} \le A_{\mathrm{inv}} \Pr[F_{j+1}]\, h_{j+1} \le A_{\mathrm{inv}} \Lambda_{\tilde d - d}\, g^{\tilde d - d}\, h(\tilde\Theta_j)\, m(\tilde\Theta_j) \le A_{\mathrm{inv}} \Lambda_{\tilde d - d} \Gamma_{\tilde d}/g^d$. And $m_{j+1} \le m_j \le \Pr[F_j] + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}} \le m(F_j^\perp) + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}} \le g^{-d-1} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}} \le \mu_{\mathrm{tr}} P_d^{b-1}$, as $F_j^\perp$ has rank above $d$, by (I4). So, by the last two conditions of (I4), as $(d, \tilde d)$ is $(2, 3)$, $(1, 2)$, or $(1, 3)$, $m_{j+1}^b h_{j+1}^{b-1} \le \mu_{\mathrm{tr}} (A_{\mathrm{inv}} \Lambda_{\tilde d - d} \Gamma_{\tilde d} P_d/g^d)^{b-1} \le \mu_{\mathrm{tr}} (\Gamma_d/g^d)^{b-1}$.
nodes.explain: A saturated lattice of rank d ≤ 3 with a dense fiber lies in a regular saturated lattice of rank between d and 3 whose densest fiber is at most (3 − d)·ε_(tr) less dense. Proof idea: Downward induction on the rank, along the prefix lattices, using the transition bound at the last prefix that satisfies more integer equations.

nodes.label: Definition 3.1
nodes.name: Bilinear groups and the generic bilinear group model
nodes.statement:
A bilinear group $(\mathbb{G}_1,\mathbb{G}_2,\mathbb{G}_T,q,G_1,G_2,e)$ consists of cyclic groups $\mathbb{G}_1$, $\mathbb{G}_2$, and $\mathbb{G}_T$ of prime order $q$, generators $G_1$ of $\mathbb{G}_1$ and $G_2$ of $\mathbb{G}_2$, and a non-degenerate bilinear map $e\colon \mathbb{G}_1 \times \mathbb{G}_2 \to \mathbb{G}_T$. We write the groups additively and let $G_T := e(G_1,G_2)$. For $s \in \{1,2,T\}$, $[x]_s := x\,G_s$ is the encoding of $x \in \mathbb{F}_q$ in $\mathbb{G}_s$, taken entrywise for vectors and matrices, so that $e([x]_1,[y]_2) = [x\,y]_T$. Our groups are of Type III: no efficiently computable homomorphism between $\mathbb{G}_1$ and $\mathbb{G}_2$ is known, in either direction.

Generic bilinear group model. Fix the order $q$ and a label length $\ell_{\mathsf{lab}}$ with $2^{\ell_{\mathsf{lab}}} \ge q$. At the start of each run of an experiment, the model samples independent, uniformly random injections $\mathsf{lab}_1,\mathsf{lab}_2,\mathsf{lab}_T\colon \mathbb{F}_q \to \{0,1\}^{\ell_{\mathsf{lab}}}$; the label of $[v]_s$ is $\mathsf{lab}_s(v)$. Every group element that an algorithm receives or outputs is a label, and every algorithm receives the labels of $G_1$, $G_2$, and $G_T$. For $s \in \{1,2,T\}$, $a, b \in \{0,1\}^{\ell_{\mathsf{lab}}}$, and $c \in \mathbb{F}_q$, the group oracle $\mathcal{O}_{\mathsf{GG}}$ answers $\mathsf{add}(s,a,b) := \mathsf{lab}_s(\mathsf{lab}_s^{-1}(a) + \mathsf{lab}_s^{-1}(b))$, $\mathsf{smul}(s,c,a) := \mathsf{lab}_s(c\,\mathsf{lab}_s^{-1}(a))$, $\mathsf{pair}(a,b) := \mathsf{lab}_T(\mathsf{lab}_1^{-1}(a)\,\mathsf{lab}_2^{-1}(b))$, and $\mathsf{name}(a) := \{\mathsf{lab}_T(v), \mathsf{lab}_T(-v)\}$ for $v := \mathsf{lab}_T^{-1}(a)$, and returns $\bot$ if an argument is not a label of its group. It also returns $\bot$ for $\mathsf{name}(a)$ unless the algorithm has received $a$ as a label of $\mathbb{G}_T$ in its input or as the answer to an $\mathsf{add}$ or $\mathsf{smul}$ call in $\mathbb{G}_T$ or to a $\mathsf{pair}$ call; a label that it has seen only in a name does not count (its name is that name). A call to $\mathcal{O}_{\mathsf{GG}}$ counts also when it returns $\bot$.

An algorithm may call $\mathcal{O}_{\mathsf{GG}}$, or query a random oracle, on a string that it has not received: a string fixed before the injections are sampled is a label with probability $q/2^{\ell_{\mathsf{lab}}}$. A guessed label is that of an element whose exponent the algorithm does not know, as in oblivious sampling, and the security proof treats it as a new variable.
nodes.explain: This is the model in which security is proved. The adversary never sees group elements, only random strings (labels) that stand for them, and it can combine them only by asking an oracle to add, scale, or pair. So all it learns is which of its combinations land on the same label. The model is Shoup's, extended to pairings, without an isomorphism oracle from $\mathbb{G}_2$ to $\mathbb{G}_1$. One addition is specific to this paper: the oracle also says which two labels are $V$ and $-V$ in the target group (the name), because the search in decryption uses it. Tiny example: from the labels of $[x]_1$ and $[y]_2$, the call $\mathsf{pair}$ returns the label of $[xy]_T$, but the strings reveal nothing about $x$, $y$ or $xy$. Usual misreading: calls that return $\bot$ are not free, they count toward the adversary's $Q$ calls, and a string the adversary makes up may happen to be a valid label.

nodes.label: Definition 3.2
nodes.name: Random oracle model; the key oracle and the seed oracle
nodes.statement:
Random oracle model. At the start of each run of an experiment, the model samples independent, uniformly random functions $H_1, \dots, H_{n_H}$ from bit strings to finite sets. Every algorithm may query them, with inputs encoded as bit strings.

Praxis uses two random oracles (ROs): a key oracle $H_{\mathsf{key}}$, which derives the key from an element of $\mathbb{G}_T$, and a seed oracle $H_{\mathsf{seed}}$, which expands a short seed into the matrix of the scheme's public forms, one entry per query. Neither outputs group elements. The reductions and the extractor of the extraction theorem (Theorem 5.9) see none of the adversary's RO queries, and only the reductions program an oracle: $H_{\mathsf{seed}}$, at one fresh seed, where they place their Module-SIS challenge. So they are non-observing, and for $H_{\mathsf{key}}$ also non-programming.
nodes.explain: A random oracle is a public function whose outputs are fresh uniform values, sampled anew in each run; everyone, the adversary included, can only query it. Praxis has two. The key oracle turns one hidden group element into the string that masks the message, so the message stays hidden until someone queries exactly that element. The seed oracle stretches a short seed into the large public matrix, so the ciphertext carries the seed in place of the matrix. The proof uses the oracles sparingly: the extractor and the reductions never look at what the adversary asked, and the only programming is that a reduction fixes the seed oracle's answers at one fresh seed to plant its Module-SIS challenge. Usual misreading: this is not a proof that reads the adversary's hash queries to learn something; the witness is read from the group-oracle calls only.

nodes.label: Definition 3.3
nodes.name: The ring $R_q$ and Module-SIS
nodes.statement:
Let $d_R$ be a power of two, $R := \mathbb{Z}[Y]/(Y^{d_R}+1)$, and $R_q := R/qR = \mathbb{F}_q[Y]/(Y^{d_R}+1)$ for the group order $q$, with $q \equiv 1 \bmod 2d_R$. For $a \in R$, $\|a\|_\infty$ is the largest absolute value of a coefficient of $a$, and for a vector over $R$ the largest over its entries. Module-SIS (MSIS) is the module version of Ajtai's short integer solution problem.

MSIS. Let $k, \ell \in \mathbb{N}$ and $0 < \beta < q/2$. A solution of MSIS for a matrix $A \in R_q^{k \times \ell}$ is a vector $\mathbf{z} \in R^\ell$ with $0 < \|\mathbf{z}\|_\infty \le \beta$ and $A \mathbf{z} = 0 \bmod q$. The advantage of an adversary $\mathcal{A}$ against $\mathsf{MSIS}_{k,\ell,\beta}$ over $R_q$ is the probability that $\mathbf{z}$ is a solution for $A$, for $A$ uniform in $R_q^{k \times \ell}$ and $\mathbf{z} \gets \mathcal{A}(A)$.
nodes.explain: Module-SIS is the lattice problem that the security bound refers to: given a uniformly random matrix over the polynomial ring $R_q$, find a nonzero vector of polynomials with small integer coefficients that the matrix sends to zero modulo $q$. Small means that every coefficient is at most $\beta$ in absolute value. In Praxis the matrix is public (it defines the scheme's forms), and the modulus $q$ is the order of the pairing groups. Tiny example: with $d_R = 2$ an element of $R$ is $a_0 + a_1 Y$ with $Y^2 = -1$, and its norm is $\max(|a_0|, |a_1|)$. The extraction theorem does not assume the problem hard: it says that an adversary who wins while the extractor finds no witness yields a solver, whose advantage appears as a term of the bound. Usual misreading: a solution must be short over the integers, not merely nonzero modulo $q$.

nodes.label: Definitions 3.4 to 3.6
nodes.name: Witness encryption, correctness, extractability
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathcal{R}$ be an NP relation: a set of pairs $(S,w)$ of an instance $S$ and a witness $w$, decidable in time $\mathsf{poly}(|S|)$, with $|w| \le \mathsf{poly}(|S|)$, where $|S|$ is the length of an encoding of $S$. For Praxis, $\mathcal{R}$ pairs Boolean quadratic systems of a fixed shape with their witnesses, the Boolean assignments that satisfy every constraint.

Witness encryption. A witness encryption scheme for an NP relation $\mathcal{R}$ and messages in $\{0,1\}^\mu$ is a pair $\mathsf{WE} = (\mathsf{Enc}, \mathsf{Dec})$ of algorithms with access to the oracles $\mathcal{O} := (\mathcal{O}_{\mathsf{GG}}, H_1, \dots, H_{n_H})$ of the generic bilinear group model and the random oracle model. The probabilistic algorithm $\mathsf{Enc}^{\mathcal{O}}(S, m)$ outputs, in time $\mathsf{poly}(|S|, \lambda)$, a ciphertext $ct$ of a message $m \in \{0,1\}^\mu$ for an instance $S$, and $\mathsf{Dec}^{\mathcal{O}}(S, ct, w)$, whose running time is not bounded, outputs a message or $\bot$.

Correctness. $\mathsf{WE}$ is correct with error $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cor}}$ if for every $(S,w) \in \mathcal{R}$ and every $m \in \{0,1\}^\mu$, $\Pr[\, \mathsf{Dec}^{\mathcal{O}}(S, ct, w) \ne m : ct \gets \mathsf{Enc}^{\mathcal{O}}(S, m) \,] \le \varepsilon_{\mathrm{cor}}$, where $S$, $w$, and $m$ are fixed before $\mathcal{O}$ is sampled, and the probability is over $\mathcal{O}$ and the coins of $\mathsf{Enc}$ and $\mathsf{Dec}$.

Extractability. $\mathsf{WE}$ is extractable with error $\delta$ and extraction time $t_{\mathcal{E}}$ if there is an extractor $\mathcal{E}$, which makes no oracle call, such that for every instance $S$, all $m_0, m_1 \in \{0,1\}^\mu$, and every adversary $\mathcal{A}$, with any advice, that runs in time $t$ and makes at most $Q$ calls to $\mathcal{O}_{\mathsf{GG}}$ and at most $Q_H$ queries to each RO, $\mathcal{E}$ runs in time at most $t_{\mathcal{E}}(|S|, Q)$ and $\Pr[\, b' = b \wedge (S, w) \notin \mathcal{R} \,] \le \frac{1}{2} + \delta(t, Q, Q_H)$ in the experiment that samples $b$ uniformly from $\{0,1\}$ and runs $ct \gets \mathsf{Enc}^{\mathcal{O}}(S, m_b)$, $b' \gets \mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{O}}(ct)$, and $w \gets \mathcal{E}(S, ct, \mathsf{tr})$, where $\mathsf{tr}$ is the transcript of $\mathcal{A}$'s answered calls to $\mathcal{O}_{\mathsf{GG}}$, in order, with their answers. The experiment fixes $S$, $m_0$, $m_1$, and $\mathcal{A}$ before it samples $\mathcal{O}$, and the probability is over $\mathcal{O}$, $b$, and the coins of $\mathsf{Enc}$, $\mathcal{A}$, and $\mathcal{E}$.

So if $\mathcal{A}$ guesses $b$ with probability $\frac12 + \varepsilon$, then $\mathcal{E}$ outputs a witness with probability at least $\varepsilon - \delta(t, Q, Q_H)$. The extractor is universal and straight-line: it is fixed before the adversary and runs once, on the transcript of the finished run.
nodes.explain: Witness encryption locks a message to a statement instead of a key: whoever knows a witness for the instance $S$ can decrypt. Correctness says that an honest witness holder recovers the message except with small probability. Extractability is the security notion: whenever an adversary can tell an encryption of $m_0$ from one of $m_1$, a fixed algorithm, shown only the adversary's group-oracle calls and their answers, outputs a witness. Tiny example: if $S$ has no witness at all, the extractor can never succeed, so the definition forces the adversary's guess to be right with probability at most $\frac12 + \delta$, which is ordinary hiding. Two points are easy to misread. $\mathsf{Dec}$ has no time bound here, because in Praxis it ends with a search that is exponential but concretely fast. And the bounded event is a correct guess together with a failed extraction, so $\delta$ bounds a joint probability, not the adversary's advantage alone.

nodes.label: Definition 4.1
nodes.name: Boolean quadratic systems, witnesses, shape
nodes.statement:
Vectors in $\mathbb{F}_q^{N+1}$ have indices $0, \dots, N$; $e_i$ is the unit vector of index $i$, and each vector $v$ defines the linear form $v(w) := \langle v, w \rangle = \sum_{i=0}^{N} v_i w_i$.

Boolean quadratic system. A Boolean quadratic system (BQS) $S$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ in $N$ unknowns is a finite list of constraints. Constraint $t$ has $F_t \ge 1$ products and vectors $a_{t,f}, b_{t,f}, c_t \in \mathbb{F}_q^{N+1}$ for $f \in [F_t]$, and reads $\sum_{f \in [F_t]} a_{t,f}(w)\, b_{t,f}(w) = w_0\, c_t(w)$. An assignment is a $w \in \mathbb{F}_q^{N+1}$ with $w_0 = 1$, and a witness of $S$ is an assignment in $\{0,1\}^{N+1}$ that satisfies every constraint. $S$ is true if it has a witness and false otherwise.

As $w_0 = 1$, entry $0$ of a vector is its form's constant term, and the factor $w_0$ makes every constraint homogeneous quadratic in $w$. With one product per constraint, $a_{t,1}(w)\, b_{t,1}(w) = c_t(w)$, a BQS is a rank-one constraint system (R1CS) with a Boolean witness. BQS express every NP relation: a witness-checking circuit gives one constraint per gate, such as $e_i(w)\, e_j(w) = w_0\, e_k(w)$ for an AND gate $w_k = w_i w_j$, plus $e_o(w)\, e_0(w) = w_0\, e_0(w)$, setting the output $w_o$ to $1$; a witness is an accepting input with the values of all gates.

Shape. A system has shape $(N, n_{\mathsf{c}}, F_{\max})$ if it has $N$ unknowns, at most $n_{\mathsf{c}}$ constraints, and at most $F_{\max}$ products per constraint. Padding with constraints $0 = 0$ (one product, zero vectors) keeps the witnesses, so we assume exactly $n_{\mathsf{c}}$ constraints. The systems of one shape and their witnesses form the NP relation of the scheme. A system has linear size if $F_{\max}\,n_{\mathsf{c}} = O(N)$ and it has $O(N)$ nonzero coefficients; the systems of Boolean circuits above have linear size, with $F_{\max} = 1$ and $n_{\mathsf{c}} \le N + 1$.
nodes.explain: This is the language of statements that Praxis encrypts to. A system is a list of equations in $N$ unknowns; each equation says that a sum of products of two linear expressions equals a linear expression, and a witness is a solution in which every unknown is 0 or 1. The extra coordinate $w_0$, always 1, lets constants be written as coefficients and makes each equation purely quadratic. Tiny example: with unknowns $w_1, w_2, w_3$, the single constraint $e_1(w)\,e_2(w) = w_0\,e_3(w)$ says $w_3 = w_1 w_2$, an AND gate. Any NP statement fits, by writing its checking circuit gate by gate. Usual misreading: an assignment may take any field values, and only a Boolean one that satisfies the constraints is a witness; being Boolean is part of the definition of a witness, not a constraint written in the list. Also, one constraint may add up many products, where an R1CS has one per constraint.

nodes.label: Definition 4.2
nodes.name: Moment matrices, linear tests, passing matrices, cheats
nodes.statement:
Rows and columns of matrices in $\mathbb{F}_q^{(N+1) \times (N+1)}$ have indices $0, \dots, N$. For an assignment $w$, every condition on a witness is linear in its moment matrix $w w^\top$: $w_j \in \{0,1\}$ exactly when $w_j^2 = w_0 w_j$, and constraint $t$ holds exactly when $\sum_f a_{t,f}^\top w w^\top b_{t,f} = e_0^\top w w^\top c_t$. The tests ask the same of any symmetric matrix $W$.

Linear tests. Let $S$ be a system in $N$ unknowns. A symmetric matrix $W \in \mathbb{F}_q^{(N+1) \times (N+1)}$ passes the Booleanity test of $j \in [N]$ if $W_{jj} = W_{0j}$, and the test of constraint $t$ if $\sum_{f \in [F_t]} a_{t,f}^\top W\, b_{t,f} = e_0^\top W c_t$. $W$ passes if it passes every test of $S$.

The passing matrices form a subspace, and $w w^\top$ passes exactly when the assignment $w$ is a witness. A cheat is a passing matrix that is not a linear combination of moment matrices of witnesses; a false system can have cheats too.
nodes.explain: The scheme starts from this observation: being a witness is a quadratic condition on $w$, but it becomes a set of linear conditions on the matrix of all pairwise products $w_i w_j$. The tests are those linear conditions, asked of an arbitrary symmetric matrix. A witness passes them with a matrix of rank one. Other matrices can pass too, and those that are not combinations of witness matrices are the cheats that the security proof has to deal with. Tiny example: with one unknown and no constraints, $W$ is 2 by 2 and passes when $W_{11} = W_{01}$; the witnesses $(1,0)$ and $(1,1)$ give the matrix with a single 1 at position $(0,0)$ and the all-ones matrix. Usual misreading: passing does not mean coming from a witness, and a system without witnesses can still have nonzero passing matrices. The rank gap lemma (Lemma 4.3) shows that none of those has rank one.

nodes.label: Definition 5.3
nodes.name: The centered sampler, the center, and the search
nodes.statement:
Fix an integer $g \ge 1$ with $g + 1 < q$, the range, and the search bound $B := (N+1)(g+1)$, with $2B + 1 < q$. Praxis hides a vector $r = (r_0, r_1, \dots, r_N)$ of small integers, the search vector, and decryption with a witness $w$ ends by searching for the integer $r(w) = \sum_i w_i r_i$. For $w \in \{0,1\}^{N+1}$ with $w_0 = 1$, $\operatorname{wt}(w)$ is the number of ones among $w_1, \dots, w_N$.

Centered sampler. For an integer $g \ge 1$ with $g + 1 < q$, the centered sampler $\mathcal{D}_g$ draws $r_1, \dots, r_N, r_\star$ independently and uniformly from $\{2, \dots, g+1\}$ and outputs the integer vector $r = (r_0, r_1, \dots, r_N)$ with $r_0 := \lceil N(g+1)/2 \rceil + r_\star - \lfloor \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i \in [N]} r_i \rfloor$, which is reduced modulo $q$ wherever it multiplies a matrix over $\mathbb{F}_q$.

Center. With $\mathcal{D}_g$, the center of the search is $c_w := \lfloor \lceil N(g+1)/2 \rceil + \frac{g+3}{2} ( 1 + \operatorname{wt}(w) - N/2 ) \rfloor$. As $r_0$ subtracts half the sum of the others, each other $r_i$ enters $r(w) - c_w$ as $\pm \frac{1}{2} ( r_i - \frac{g+3}{2} )$, symmetric about zero, so with the same law for $w_i = 0$ and $1$. Through $r_\star$, $r_0$ is uniform on $g$ consecutive integers given the others. The scheme as first stated in Section 5.1 instead draws $r_0, \dots, r_N$ independently and uniformly from $\{2, \dots, g+1\}$ and has the center $c_w := \lfloor (1 + \operatorname{wt}(w))(g+3)/2 \rfloor$; the full specification (App. A) and the theorems use $\mathcal{D}_g$.

Sign classes. The search compares elements of $\mathbb{G}_T$ up to sign. The sign class of $V \in \mathbb{G}_T$ is $\{V, -V\}$, and its name $\mathsf{name}(V)$ identifies it: $\mathsf{name}(V) = \mathsf{name}(V')$ exactly when $V' = \pm V$. The generic model gives names to every algorithm.

The search. Given elements $\Psi^\alpha$ and $\Lambda'$ of $\mathbb{G}_T$, the search returns the integer $t$ of least absolute value with $|t| \le B$ and $t \cdot \Psi^\alpha = \Lambda'$, or reports that there is no such integer. The scheme states the search by its result: any algorithm that finds this integer serves. We search outward from the center: one fixed table of the names of the baby steps $b \cdot \Psi^\alpha$ for $0 \le b < \bar b$, with $\bar b$ of order $\sqrt{g}\, N^{1/4}$, serves $b$ and $-b$ at once, and the giant steps $\Lambda' - j(2\bar b - 1) \cdot \Psi^\alpha$ for $j = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \dots$ cover the integers outward from $0$.
nodes.explain: Decryption has to find a secret integer $r(w)$, the sum of the hidden entries $r_i$ at the ones of the witness, by search, so the scheme wants that integer close to a point the decryptor can compute. The centered sampler arranges this: $r_0$ subtracts half of the other entries, so that $r(w)$ minus the center $c_w$ has, up to rounding, one law for every witness. The search then looks for a small integer $t$ with $t \cdot \Psi^\alpha = \Lambda'$, outward from $0$ by baby steps and giant steps, comparing elements up to sign so that one table entry serves $b$ and $-b$. Tiny example: for $N = 2$ and $g = 4$, entries are drawn from $\{2,3,4,5\}$ and $r_0 = 5 + r_\star - \lfloor (r_1 + r_2)/2 \rfloor$. Usual misreading: $r_0$ is not independent of the other entries, yet given them it is still uniform on $g$ consecutive integers, which the later guessing bounds use.

nodes.label: Definition 4.4
nodes.name: Stacks, rank, guessing probability, heavy and light
nodes.statement:
Praxis hides a vector $r = (r_0, r_1, \dots, r_N)$ of small integers, and decryption with a witness $w$ ends by searching for the integer $r(w) = \sum_i w_i r_i$. Fix an integer $g \ge 1$ with $g + 1 < q$, the range. The entries $r_1, \dots, r_N$ are independent and uniform on $\{2, \dots, g+1\}$, and $r_0$, given them, is uniform on $g$ consecutive integers. The vector $r$ is reduced modulo $q$ wherever it multiplies a matrix over $\mathbb{F}_q$.

A stack is a finite family $\mathbf{W} = (W_c)_{c \in C}$ of matrices with $N+1$ columns, such as one matrix for each copy of the scheme's table; it passes if every $W_c$ is a symmetric $(N+1) \times (N+1)$ matrix that passes the linear tests, and its rank $\operatorname{rank} \mathbf{W}$ is the dimension of its row space, the sum of the row spaces of the $W_c$.

Guessing probability. The guessing probability of a stack $\mathbf{W} = (W_c)_{c \in C}$ is $\operatorname{gp}(\mathbf{W}) := \max_{u} \Pr_{r}[ (W_c r)_{c \in C} = u ]$, for $r$ drawn by the sampler of the scheme at hand: independent entries, or the centered sampler $\mathcal{D}_g$, the sampler of the full specification and of the theorems. That of a matrix is that of the stack of one. For a threshold $\theta \in (0,1)$, $\mathbf{W}$ is light if $\operatorname{gp}(\mathbf{W}) \le \theta$ and heavy otherwise.
nodes.explain: The security proof reduces every way of cheating to guessing: the adversary must name the value of $W_c r$ for each matrix of a stack, for the hidden vector $r$ of small integers. The guessing probability is the chance of the best such guess, and the threshold $\theta$ splits stacks into light ones, whose guesses are charged to the error bound, and heavy ones, which the proof turns into a witness or a Module-SIS solution. Tiny example: for the single matrix with one row $e_1^\top$, guessing $W r$ means guessing $r_1$, so the probability is $1/g$. If distinct $i, j$ appear in no vector $a_{t,f}$ or $b_{t,f}$, then $e_i e_j^\top + e_j e_i^\top$ passes with guessing probability $g^{-2}$, above $\theta$ at the paper's parameters: heavy, even for a false system. Usual misreading: the rank is the dimension of the joint row space of all matrices of the stack, not the rank of one matrix, and heavy means easy to guess.

nodes.label: Definition 4.6
nodes.name: The QAP of a system; quotients and remainder of a witness
nodes.statement:
Fix a coset size $
u$ that divides $q - 1$ and exceeds $F_{\max}$; we take the least power of two above $F_{\max}$, so that $
u \le 2F_{\max}$. Write $D$ for the number $N + 2 + 
u\,n_{\mathsf{c}}$ of evaluation points. $\mathbb{F}_q^{<d}[X]$ denotes the polynomials over $\mathbb{F}_q$ of degree below $d$. A pair $(a, b)$ of vectors stands for the product $a(w)\, b(w)$; the pair's term on a matrix $W$ is $a^	op W\, b$, and each test sets a sum of terms to zero.

QAP of a system. Let $S$ be a system of shape $(N, n_{\mathsf{c}}, F_{\max})$. A choice of evaluation points for $S$ consists of points $d_0, \dots, d_N$ and $ho$ of $\mathbb{F}_q$, of cosets $\mathcal{K}_1, \dots, \mathcal{K}_{n_{\mathsf{c}}}$ of the subgroup of order $
u$ of $\mathbb{F}_q^*$, and, in each $\mathcal{K}_t$, of points $p_{t,1}, \dots, p_{t,F_t}$ and $p'_t$. It is admissible if the cosets are pairwise distinct, the points $d_0, \dots, d_N, ho$ are pairwise distinct and in no $\mathcal{K}_t$, and the $F_t + 1$ points chosen in $\mathcal{K}_t$ are pairwise distinct, for every $t$. For an admissible choice, let $\mathcal{P}_0 := \{d_0, \dots, d_N, ho\}$ and $\mathcal{P} := \mathcal{P}_0 \cup  igcup_t \mathcal{K}_t$, a set of $D$ points; let $Z_0(X) := \prod_{p \in \mathcal{P}_0} (X - p)$ and $Z(X) := \prod_{p \in \mathcal{P} \setminus \{ho\}} (X - p)$; and let $L_ho(X) \in \mathbb{F}_q^{<D}[X]$ be the polynomial with value $1$ at $ho$ and $0$ on $\mathcal{P} \setminus \{ho\}$. The QAP of $S$ for this choice consists of the polynomials $A_i(X)$ and $B_i(X)$ in $\mathbb{F}_q^{<D}[X]$, for $i \in [0,N]$, with the values on $\mathcal{P}$ listed below, where $A(X) := (A_i(X))_{i \in [0,N]}$ and $B(X) := (B_i(X))_{i \in [0,N]}$. To a matrix $W \in \mathbb{F}_q^{(N+1) 	imes (N+1)}$ the QAP assigns $P_W(X) := \sum_{i,j} W_{ij}\, A_i(X)\, B_j(X) = A(X)^	op W\, B(X)$, whose values on $\mathcal{P}$ are listed last.

At $d_j$ with $j \in [N]$: $A(d_j) = e_j - e_0$, $B(d_j) = e_j$, $P_W(d_j) = W_{jj} - W_{0j}$. At $d_0$: $A = 0$, $B = e_0$, $P_W = 0$. At $ho$: $A = e_0$, $B = e_0$, $P_W = W_{00}$. At $p_{t,f}$ with $f \in [F_t]$: $A = Z_0(p_{t,f})\, a_{t,f}$, $B = b_{t,f}$, $P_W = Z_0(p_{t,f}) \cdot a_{t,f}^	op W\, b_{t,f}$. At $p'_t$: $A = Z_0(p'_t)\, e_0$, $B = -c_t$, $P_W = -Z_0(p'_t) \cdot e_0^	op W c_t$. At the other points of $\mathcal{K}_t$: $A = 0$, $B = 0$, $P_W = 0$.

A polynomial is allowed if it lies in $\mathbb{F}_q^{<
u n_{\mathsf{c}}}[X]$ and none of its exponents is divisible by $
u$.

By the table, $P_W(d_j)$ is the term of the Booleanity test of $j$, the key point $ho$ carries the corner $W_{00}$, and $d_0$, where every $A_i$ is zero, serves the security proof. On $\mathcal{K}_t$, where $Z_0(p) 
e 0$, the values $P_W(p)/Z_0(p)$ are the terms of the test of constraint $t$. Over a coset $\delta \mathcal{G}$ of the subgroup $\mathcal{G}$ of order $
u$, the monomial $X^k$ sums to $
u\, \delta^k$ if $
u$ divides $k$ and to $0$ otherwise. So for a polynomial of degree below $
u\,n_{\mathsf{c}}$, the sums over the cosets $\mathcal{K}_t = \delta_t \mathcal{G}$ are, up to the nonzero factor $
u$, the $n_{\mathsf{c}} 	imes n_{\mathsf{c}}$ Vandermonde matrix of the values $\delta_t^
u$, distinct as the cosets are, applied to the polynomial's coefficients at the exponents divisible by $
u$; they all vanish exactly when the polynomial is allowed. $R_W$ denotes the polynomial of degree below $
u\,n_{\mathsf{c}}$ with the values $P_W(p)/Z_0(p)$ on the cosets.

Quotients and remainder of a witness. For a witness $w$, $w w^	op$ passes, with corner $1$, and $P_{w w^	op} = A_w B_w$ for $A_w := \sum_i w_i A_i$ and $B_w := \sum_i w_i B_i$. By the QAP criterion (Lemma 4.7) there are unique polynomials $h_{\mathrm{key}}$ and $h_{\mathrm{oth}}$ and a unique allowed $R_w := R_{w w^	op}$, the quotients of $w$ for the key copy and the other copies of the scheme and the remainder of $w$, with $A_w B_w - L_ho = h_{\mathrm{key}} \cdot Z \cdot (X - ho) + Z_0\, R_w$ and $A_w B_w = h_{\mathrm{oth}} \cdot Z + Z_0\, R_w$.

Placement. The theorems of the construction hold for every admissible choice of evaluation points. We place all of them in the subgroup $\mathcal{H}$ of $\mathbb{F}_q^*$ of order $2^{\lceil \log_2 D ceil}$, which must divide $q - 1$, each $\mathcal{K}_t$ a coset of its subgroup of order $
u$: the cosets first, then $d_0, \dots, d_N, ho$, in order from the powers of a generator of $\mathcal{H}$ in bit-reversed order.
nodes.explain: The QAP packs all the linear tests of a matrix $W$ into one polynomial $P_W$: each test owns some evaluation points, and the values of $P_W$ there are the terms that the test adds up. A Booleanity test has one term, so it gets a single point $d_j$, where $P_W$ must vanish. A constraint adds several terms, so it gets a whole coset, and its terms sum to zero exactly when the interpolant $R_W$ has no monomial with exponent divisible by $\nu$ (it is allowed). One more point, $\rho$, reads off the corner $W_{00}$, which will carry the key. Tiny example: for an AND gate $w_3 = w_1 w_2$, one coset point holds the pair $(e_1, e_2)$ and another $(e_0, -e_3)$, so after division by $Z_0$ the two terms are $W_{12}$ and $-W_{03}$. Usual misreading: unlike the usual QAP, division by the vanishing polynomial is not exact; a remainder is permitted, as long as it is allowed.

nodes.label: Definition 5.1
nodes.name: Forms of a matrix; the weights $U$ and $V$ from the extension field
nodes.statement:
The forms come from a uniform matrix over the ring $R_q$ of degree $d_R$, with $k$ rows and columns $0, \dots, \ell$, for $\ell := \lceil N/d_R \rceil$; its columns $1$ to $\ell$ form an MSIS instance. The number of forms $n := (k+1)\,d_R$ is even and divides $q - 1$.

Forms of a matrix. Let $M = (M_{i,j})$ be a matrix over $R_q$ with rows $i \in [k]$ and columns $j \in [0,\ell]$. For $w \in \mathbb{F}_q^{N+1}$ and $j \in [\ell]$, let $\hat w_j \in R_q$ be the polynomial $\sum_{s < d_R} w_{(j-1) d_R + s + 1}\, Y^s$, where $w_c := 0$ for $c > N$. The forms of $M$ are the linear forms $\varphi_0, \dots, \varphi_{n-1}$ on $\mathbb{F}_q^{N+1}$ with $\varphi_0(w) := w_0$, with $\varphi_e := 0$ for $0 < e < d_R$, and with $\varphi_{i d_R + s}(w)$ defined as the coefficient of $Y^s$ in $M_{i,0}\, w_0 + \sum_{j \in [\ell]} M_{i,j}\, \hat w_j$, for $i \in [k]$ and $0 \le s < d_R$. $\mathsf{Forms}(M)$ denotes the list of their coefficient vectors.

A vector $v$ with $v_0 = 0$ is in the kernel of every form exactly when the columns $1, \dots, \ell$ of $M$, a matrix in $R_q^{k \times \ell}$, map $(\hat v_1, \dots, \hat v_\ell)$ to zero.

Weights. Let $c_0 \in \mathbb{F}_q$ be such that $P(T) := T^n - c_0$ is irreducible, and write the elements of $\mathbb{F}_{q^n} := \mathbb{F}_q[T]/(P)$ as polynomials in $\mathbb{F}_q^{<n}[T]$ (polynomials of degree below $n$). Its Frobenius automorphism $\sigma$ maps $T$ to $\omega T$, where $\omega := c_0^{(q-1)/n}$ has order $n$; so $\omega^{n/2} = -1$, and $\sigma^j$ maps $a(T)$ to $a(\omega^j T)$. Together the forms are one form $z(w) := \sum_{e<n} \varphi_e(w)\, T^e$ with values in $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$ and coefficient vector $z = \sum_{e<n} \varphi_e T^e \in \mathbb{F}_{q^n}^{N+1}$. For $x \in \mathbb{F}_q$ or a formal polynomial $x$, $z[x] := \sum_{e<n} x^e \varphi_e$ is $z$ with $x$ substituted for $T$. The weights are the coefficients of two products in $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$: $U(w) := z(w) \cdot \sigma^{n/2-1}(z(w)) = \sum_{k<n} U_k(w)\, T^k$ and $V(w) := z(w) \cdot \sigma^{n/2}(z(w)) = \sum_{j<n/2} V_j(w)\, T^{2j}$.

The $n$ forms are the coefficients of the one form $z$, and $z(v) = 0$ exactly when $\varphi_e(v) = 0$ for every $e$. A conjugate $\sigma^j(z) = z[\omega^j T]$ rescales coefficient $e$ by $\omega^{je}$, so it is again a public form. The three consecutive conjugates $\sigma^{n/2-1}(z)$, $\sigma^{n/2}(z)$, and $\sigma^{n/2+1}(z)$ are $z[-T/\omega]$, $z[-T]$, and $z[-\omega T]$. The third product, $z \cdot \sigma^{n/2+1}(z)$, is the conjugate under $\sigma^{n/2+1}$ of $U$, as $\sigma^n$ is the identity, so it needs no copies of its own; and $V$ is fixed by $\sigma^{n/2}$, which maps $T$ to $-T$, so it has only even powers of $T$.
nodes.explain: Praxis uses many copies of one hidden matrix, each scaled by a weight: a quadratic function of the witness that everyone can evaluate. First, a public random matrix over $R_q$ defines $n$ linear forms in $w$; a vector with $v_0 = 0$ on which all forms vanish is exactly one that the matrix sends to zero, which is how Module-SIS enters. Second, the $n$ forms are packed as the coefficients of one element $z(w)$ of the extension field $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$, and the weights are the coefficients of $z(w)$ times a Frobenius conjugate of itself. Tiny example from the paper: for $n = 4$, $V = z \cdot \sigma^2(z)$ gives two weights and $U = z \cdot \sigma(z)$ gives four, six quadratic forms where four forms have ten products. Usual misreading: a weight is not a product of two forms but a fixed combination of such products, and $V$ has only even powers of $T$, so $n/2$ weights.

nodes.label: Sec. 5.1, Copies and shared factors
nodes.name: Copies, the grid of cells, ties, and the honest stack
nodes.statement:
Copies. Each weight has a copy of the table, whose exponent is that of the weight's power of $T$: copy $(\mathrm{U}, k)$, for $k \in [0, n-1]$, has the weight $U_k$ and the exponent $k$, and copy $(\mathrm{V}, j)$, for $j \in [0, n/2-1]$, the weight $V_j$ and the exponent $2j$. The copies of $U$ form $C_U$, those of $V$ form $C_V$, and each of the $3n/2$ copies $c \in C := C_U \cup C_V$ has weight $\xi_c$ and exponent $k_c$. Only the key copy $c_{\mathrm{key}} := (\mathrm{U}, 0)$, with weight $\xi_{\mathrm{key}} := U_0$, carries the key.

Ties. For a stack $\mathbf{W} = (W_c)_{c \in C}$, let $W_U(T) := \sum_{c \in C_U} W_c\, T^{k_c}$ and $W_V(T) := \sum_{c \in C_V} W_c\, T^{k_c}$. The stack satisfies the ties if $P(T)$ divides its tie polynomials $t_1, t_2, t_3 \in \mathbb{F}_q[T]^{N+1}$: $t_1(T) := W_U(T)\, z[-T] - W_V(T)\, z[-T/\omega]$, $t_2(T) := W_U(T)\, z[-\omega T] - W_U(-\omega T)\, z[-T/\omega]$, and $t_3(T) := W_V(T)\, z[-\omega T] - W_U(-\omega T)\, z[-T]$. Read $W_U$ and $W_V$ as matrices over $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$, and let $\sigma$ act on them entry by entry. The ties ask that $W_U\, \sigma^{n/2}(z) = W_V\, \sigma^{n/2-1}(z)$, $W_U\, \sigma^{n/2+1}(z) = \sigma^{n/2+1}(W_U)\, \sigma^{n/2-1}(z)$, and $W_V\, \sigma^{n/2+1}(z) = \sigma^{n/2+1}(W_U)\, \sigma^{n/2}(z)$, identities in $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}^{N+1}$ whose differences, before reduction modulo $P(T)$, are the tie polynomials. As $\sigma^j$ maps $a(T)$ to $a(\omega^j T)$ and $\omega^{n/2} = -1$, $P(T)$ divides the tie polynomials exactly if the stack satisfies the ties as stated in this second form.

Honest stack. The stack $\mathbf{H}(v) := (\xi_c(v)\, v v^\top)_{c \in C}$ of every vector $v$ satisfies the ties; that of a witness is its honest stack. For the stack of $v$, $W_U$, $W_V$, and $\sigma^{n/2+1}(W_U) = W_U(-\omega T)$ are $v v^\top$ times the three products at $v$, and both sides of each tie are the same product of three conjugates of $z(v)$ times $v$; for the first, $z(v)\, \sigma^{n/2-1}(z(v))\, \sigma^{n/2}(z(v))\, v$.

Cells. For positive integers $K_1$ and $K_2$ with $K_1 K_2 = n/2$, the copies are the cells of a $K_1 \times 3K_2$ grid, with one left factor for each row, a left leg $k_1 \in [0, K_1 - 1]$, and one right factor for each column, a right leg. A right leg $\mathrm{leg} = (\mathrm{X}, k_2) \in \{\mathrm{E}, \mathrm{O}, \mathrm{V}\} \times [0, K_2 - 1]$ has kind $\mathrm{X}$ and exponent $k_{\mathrm{leg}} := 2K_1 k_2$, or $2K_1 k_2 + 1$ for kind O. The cell $c = (k_1, \mathrm{leg})$ is the copy of exponent $k_c = 2k_1 + k_{\mathrm{leg}}$: $(\mathrm{U}, k_c)$ on E and O legs and $(\mathrm{V}, k_c/2)$ on V legs; every copy is exactly one cell, and the key copy is $(0, (\mathrm{E}, 0))$.
nodes.explain: Praxis has $3n/2$ copies of its hidden table, one per weight, and a stack is what a decryptor or an adversary combines along: one coefficient matrix per copy. The ties are three polynomial identities that link the matrices of different copies. The stack of a vector $v$ is the same matrix $v v^\top$ in every copy, scaled by that copy's weight, and it satisfies the ties because both sides of each tie are then the same product of three conjugates of $z(v)$. The grid is bookkeeping for sharing: a copy is addressed as a cell (row, column), so that $K_1$ left factors and $3K_2$ right factors serve all copies. Tiny example: for $n = 4$, $K_1 = 2$, $K_2 = 1$, the E leg has exponent 0 and its two cells are the copies $(\mathrm{U},0)$ and $(\mathrm{U},2)$. Usual misreading: satisfying the ties means that $P(T)$ divides the tie polynomials, not that they are zero.

nodes.label: App. A, Praxis in full: setup and encryption
nodes.name: Setup and Enc: what is sampled and what is published
nodes.statement:
Parameters. Fix a bilinear group $(\mathbb{G}_1,\mathbb{G}_2,\mathbb{G}_T,q,G_1,G_2,e)$, a shape $(N, n_{\mathsf{c}}, F_{\max})$ of systems, and a message length $\mu$. The QAP of a system has coset size $\nu$ and $D = N + 2 + \nu\,n_{\mathsf{c}} < q$ evaluation points. The key oracle $H_{\mathsf{key}}$ maps bit strings to $\{0,1\}^\mu$. The range $g$ and the search bound $B := (N+1)(g+1)$ satisfy $2B + 1 < q$. Chunks: $J, J' \ge 1$ are the numbers of chunks, with $J'$ dividing $n_{\mathsf{c}}$ ($J' = 1$ if $n_{\mathsf{c}} = 0$), and the chunk lengths are an integer $\Delta$ with $J \Delta \ge D$ and $\Delta' := \nu\,n_{\mathsf{c}} / J'$.

$\mathsf{Setup}(S)$, for a system $S$ of the shape: choose admissible evaluation points for $S$; compute $A_i(X)$ and $B_i(X)$, for $i \in [0,N]$, and $Z_0(X)$, $Z(X)$, and $L_\rho(X)$; return $\mathsf{pp} := ( S, \text{the evaluation points}, (A_i, B_i)_{i}, Z_0, Z, L_\rho )$. $\mathsf{Setup}$ is deterministic and has no secret, so $\mathsf{Enc}(\mathsf{pp}, m)$ and $\mathsf{Dec}(\mathsf{pp}, ct, w)$ stand for $\mathsf{Enc}(S, m)$ and $\mathsf{Dec}(S, ct, w)$.

$\mathsf{Enc}(\mathsf{pp}, m)$, for a message $m \in \{0,1\}^\mu$. A line with free indices holds for all left legs $k_1$, right legs $\mathrm{leg}$, cells $c = (k_1, \mathrm{leg}) \in C$, and $i, j \in [0, N]$, with $\mathrm{X}$ the kind of $\mathrm{leg}$.

(1) Sample $\mathsf{seed}$ uniformly from $\{0,1\}^{\ell_{\mathsf{seed}}}$; set $M := ( H_{\mathsf{seed}}(\mathsf{seed}, i, j) )_{i \in [k],\, j \in [0, \ell]}$ and $(\varphi_e)_{e<n} := \mathsf{Forms}(M)$.

(2) Draw $r \gets \mathcal{D}_g$, and sample uniformly $y$ from $\mathbb{F}_q^{N+1}$, $\tau$ from $\mathbb{F}_q \setminus \mathcal{P}$, and $\Omega_{12}$ from $\mathbb{F}_q$.

(3) Sample uniformly from $\mathbb{F}_q^*$: $\Omega_{22}, \alpha, \pi, s_{\mathrm{E}}, s_{\mathrm{O}}, s_{\mathrm{V}}, \upsilon, \zeta, \zeta', \zeta'', \eta_1, \eta_2, \eta_3$.

(4) Sample $\varepsilon$ uniformly from $\mathbb{F}_q^* \setminus \{ -\omega^{-2k_1} : k_1 \in [0, K_1 - 1] \}$; let $\Omega$ be the $2 \times 2$ matrix with rows $(1, \Omega_{12})$ and $(0, \Omega_{22})$.

(5) $\pi_{k_1} := \pi\, \upsilon^{2k_1} (1 + \varepsilon\, \omega^{2k_1})$; $s_{\mathrm{leg}} := s_{\mathrm{X}}\, \upsilon^{k_{\mathrm{leg}}}$; $\gamma_c := \pi_{k_1} s_{\mathrm{leg}}$; $\kappa := \gamma_{c_{\mathrm{key}}}\, L_\rho(\tau)$.

(6) $z_{-} := z[-\upsilon/\omega]$; $z_{\circ} := z[-\upsilon]$; $z_{+} := z[-\omega\upsilon]$.

(7) The tie mask of each right leg: $\vartheta_{\mathrm{leg}} := \upsilon^{k_{\mathrm{leg}}} ( \eta_1 z_{\circ} + \eta_2 z_{+} ) - \varepsilon^{-1} (-\omega\upsilon)^{k_{\mathrm{leg}}} ( \eta_2 z_{-} + \eta_3 z_{\circ} )$ if $\mathrm{X} \in \{\mathrm{E}, \mathrm{O}\}$, and $\vartheta_{\mathrm{leg}} := \upsilon^{k_{\mathrm{leg}}} ( \eta_3 z_{+} - \eta_1 z_{-} )$ if $\mathrm{X} = \mathrm{V}$.

(8) The factors: $F^{k_1}_i := \pi_{k_1} ( y_i,\ A_i(\tau) )$, a row of length two, and $H^{\mathrm{leg}}_j := ( s_{\mathrm{leg}} (r_j + A_j(\tau)) + \vartheta_{\mathrm{leg},j},\ s_{\mathrm{leg}} (B_j(\tau) - y_j) )^{\top}$, a column of length two.

(9) $ct_1$ and $ct_2$ are the elements of $\mathbb{G}_1$ and of $\mathbb{G}_2$ listed below; $ct_2^\alpha := \alpha \cdot ct_2$, entry by entry, and a superscript $\alpha$ on an element of $ct_2$ denotes its $\alpha$-copy in $ct_2^\alpha$.

(10) $\mathsf{K}^\alpha := [\alpha\kappa]_T$; $\tilde{m} := m \oplus H_{\mathsf{key}}( [\kappa]_T )$.

(11) Return $ct := ( \mathsf{seed}, ct_1, ct_2, ct_2^\alpha, \mathsf{K}^\alpha, \tilde{m} )$.

Published in $ct_1$: the left factors $\mathsf{F}^{k_1}_i := [F^{k_1}_i\, \Omega]_1 \in \mathbb{G}_1^2$ for all $k_1$ and $i$; the quotient powers $\mathsf{P}^{\mathrm{quo}}_k := [\zeta \tau^k]_1$ for $k \in [0, \Delta - 1]$; the remainder powers $\mathsf{P}^{\mathrm{rem}}_k := [\zeta' \tau^k]_1$ for $k \in [0, \Delta' - 1]$ with $\nu \nmid k$; the cancellation column $\mathsf{Y}_i := [\zeta'' y_i]_1$ for all $i$.

Published in $ct_2$: the right factors $\mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{leg}}_j := [\Omega^{-1} H^{\mathrm{leg}}_j]_2 \in \mathbb{G}_2^2$ for all right legs and $j$; the search bases $\mathsf{S}^{\mathrm{leg}} := [s_{\mathrm{leg}}]_2$; the quotient bases $\mathsf{B}^{\mathrm{quo}}_{c,j} := [\gamma_c\, Z_c(\tau)\, \tau^{j\Delta}/\zeta]_2$ for all $c$ and $j \in [0, J - 1]$; the remainder bases $\mathsf{B}^{\mathrm{rem}}_{c,j} := [\gamma_c\, Z_0(\tau)\, \tau^{j\Delta'}/\zeta']_2$ for all $c$ and $j \in [0, J' - 1]$; the tie bases $\mathsf{B}^{0}_{a,e} := [\pi\, \eta_a\, P(\upsilon)\, \upsilon^e/\zeta'']_2$ for $a \in [3]$ and $e \in [0, n-2]$; the cross bases $\mathsf{B}^{\iota}_{a,e} := [\pi\, \eta_a\, \varepsilon^{\iota} \upsilon^e/\zeta'']_2$ for $(a, \iota) \in \mathcal{I}$ with $\iota \ne 0$ and $e \in [0, 2n-2]$, where $\mathcal{I} := ([3] \times \{-1, 0, 1\}) \setminus \{(1,-1)\}$. Here $Z_c(X)$ is $Z(X)(X - \rho)$ for the key copy and $Z(X)$ for every other copy. With the tie bases, the cross bases are the cancellation bases.

What the factors encode. $F^{k_1}_i H^{\mathrm{leg}}_j = \gamma_c ( y_i\, r_j + y_i\, A_j(\tau) - A_i(\tau)\, y_j + A_i(\tau)\, B_j(\tau) ) + \pi_{k_1}\, y_i\, \vartheta_{\mathrm{leg},j}$, entry $(i,j)$ of the table of cell $c$ plus the term of the tie mask $\vartheta_{\mathrm{leg}} \in \mathbb{F}_q^{N+1}$ of its right leg. The table's parts are the search term $y\, r^\top$, the symmetry term $y\, A(\tau)^\top - A(\tau)\, y^\top$, and the QAP term $A(\tau)\, B(\tau)^\top$. The factors are published under the hidden basis $\Omega$. The key scalar is $\kappa = \gamma_{c_{\mathrm{key}}} L_\rho(\tau)$; the key element $[\kappa]_T$ is not published, only $\mathsf{K}^\alpha$ and the masked message $\tilde{m}$. The pairing of $\mathsf{P}^{\mathrm{quo}}_k$ with $\mathsf{B}^{\mathrm{quo}}_{c,j}$ encodes $\gamma_c\, Z_c(\tau)\, \tau^{k + j\Delta}$, and $k + j\Delta$ takes each value below $J\Delta$ once, so the combinations encode $\gamma_c\, Z_c(\tau)\, h(\tau)$ for $h \in \mathbb{F}_q^{<J\Delta}[X]$, as one chunk of $J\Delta$ powers would; likewise for the allowed remainders, as $\nu$ divides $\Delta'$.
nodes.explain: This is the ciphertext. For each cell, encryption hides a table of rank at most two whose entries combine the secret small integers $r_j$ (the search term), a term that is zero along symmetric matrices, and the values of the QAP at a secret point $\tau$. It publishes not the table but two thin factors, in $\mathbb{G}_1$ and $\mathbb{G}_2$, under a hidden 2 by 2 basis $\Omega$ that cancels when a left factor is paired with a right factor. The other elements serve whoever combines along a passing stack: powers of $\tau$ with bases that remove the quotient and remainder parts of the QAP term, and cancellation bases that remove the tie masks' terms. The message is masked by a hash of the key element $[\kappa]_T$, never published; only $\alpha$ times it is, with an $\alpha$-copy of $ct_2$ for the search. Usual misreading: $ct_2^\alpha$ is not a second independent ciphertext, it is $ct_2$ scaled by one secret $\alpha$.

nodes.label: App. B.1, Cancellation polynomials and masks
nodes.name: Cancellation polynomials and the mask identity
nodes.statement:
For a stack $\mathbf{W}$, the sums $W_U$ and $W_V$ and the tie polynomials $t_1$, $t_2$, and $t_3$ are those of the copies and ties.

Cancellation polynomials. For a witness $w$, let $U_w$ and $V_w$ be the sums $W_U$ and $W_V$ with $\xi_c(w)$ for $W_c$, $U'_w$ and $V'_w$ these sums with the term of cell $c = (k_1, \mathrm{leg})$ times $\omega^{2k_1}$, and $U''_w$ the sum $U_w$ with that term times $(-\omega)^{k_{\mathrm{leg}}}$, and let $z^-_w$, $z^\circ_w$, $z^+_w$ be $w^\top z[-T/\omega]$, $w^\top z[-T]$, $w^\top z[-\omega T]$. Its cancellation polynomials are $x^0_1 := ( U_w\, z^\circ_w - V_w\, z^-_w ) / P$ and $x^+_1 := U'_w\, z^\circ_w - V'_w\, z^-_w$; $x^0_2 := ( U_w\, z^+_w - U_w(-\omega T)\, z^-_w ) / P$, $x^+_2 := U'_w\, z^+_w$, and $x^-_2 := -U''_w\, z^-_w$; $x^0_3 := ( V_w\, z^+_w - U_w(-\omega T)\, z^\circ_w ) / P$, $x^+_3 := V'_w\, z^+_w$, and $x^-_3 := -U''_w\, z^\circ_w$. A superscript $\pm$ abbreviates $\pm 1$, so these are the eight polynomials $x^\iota_a$ for $(a, \iota) \in \mathcal{I} = ([3] \times \{-1, 0, 1\}) \setminus \{(1,-1)\}$: $x^{\pm}_a \in \mathbb{F}_q^{<2n-1}[T]$ for the cross terms and $x^0_a \in \mathbb{F}_q^{<n-1}[T]$ for the others. Also let $x^-_1 := 0$.

Masks. By the lines of $\mathsf{Enc}$ that set the scalars, the conjugates $z_-, z_\circ, z_+$, and the tie masks, as $k_c = 2k_1 + k_{\mathrm{leg}}$, the part without $\varepsilon$ of $\pi_{k_1} \vartheta_{\mathrm{leg}}$ is $\pi ( \upsilon^{k_c} (\eta_1 z_\circ + \eta_2 z_+) - (-\omega\upsilon)^{k_c} (\eta_2 z_- + \eta_3 z_\circ) )$ for the kinds E and O and $\pi\, \upsilon^{k_c} (\eta_3 z_+ - \eta_1 z_-)$ for V; the terms with $\varepsilon$ or $\varepsilon^{-1}$ are the cross terms. Summed with the $W_c$ of a stack $\mathbf{W}$, the part without $\varepsilon$ gives $\pi \sum_a \eta_a\, t_a(\upsilon)$; summed with the $\xi_c(w)\, w^\top$ for a witness $w$, all parts give the second identity below. This is the mask identity, identically in the coins, with $\Theta^{\pm}$ free of $\varepsilon$:

$\sum_{c = (k_1, \mathrm{leg}) \in C} \pi_{k_1} W_c\, \vartheta_{\mathrm{leg}} = \pi \sum_{a \in [3]} \eta_a\, t_a(\upsilon) + \varepsilon\, \Theta^{+} + \varepsilon^{-1} \Theta^{-}$, and

$\sum_{c = (k_1, \mathrm{leg}) \in C} \pi_{k_1} \xi_c(w)\, w^\top \vartheta_{\mathrm{leg}} = \pi \sum_{a \in [3]} \eta_a ( P\, x^0_a + \varepsilon\, x^+_a + \varepsilon^{-1} x^-_a )(\upsilon)$.
nodes.explain: The tie masks that encryption adds to the right factors must disappear for an honest decryptor and must stay for a stack that breaks the ties. The mask identity says what the masks contribute when summed along a stack: the tie polynomials evaluated at the secret point $\upsilon$, plus cross terms marked by the secret coin $\varepsilon$ or its inverse. For a witness, the same sum is written through eight explicit polynomials, the cancellation polynomials; their coefficients tell the decryptor how to combine the published cancellation bases so that one pairing with the cancellation column removes the masks' terms. Three of them involve a division by $P$; that these divisions are exact for a witness is part of the honest combination lemma (Lemma 5.4), not of this definition. Usual misreading: the identity holds identically in the coins, as an identity of polynomials, not just with high probability, and $x^-_1$ is zero because no cross term carries $\eta_1 \varepsilon^{-1}$.

nodes.label: App. A, Praxis in full: decryption
nodes.name: Dec and Comb: what decryption computes
nodes.statement:
$\mathsf{Dec}(\mathsf{pp}, ct, w)$, for a witness $w$ of $S$ and $ct = (\mathsf{seed}, ct_1, ct_2, ct_2^\alpha, \mathsf{K}^\alpha, \tilde{m})$. Indices are as in $\mathsf{Enc}$.

(1) $M := ( H_{\mathsf{seed}}(\mathsf{seed}, i, j) )_{i,j}$; $(\varphi_e)_{e<n} := \mathsf{Forms}(M)$; evaluate $\xi_c(w)$ for $c \in C$.

(2) If $\xi_{\mathrm{key}}(w) = 0$, return $\bot$.

(3) Compute $h_{\mathrm{key}}$, $h_{\mathrm{oth}}$, and $R_w$, the quotients and the remainder of $w$.

(4) Compute $x^\iota_a$, the cancellation polynomials of $w$, for $(a, \iota) \in \mathcal{I}$.

(5) $\mathsf{F}^{k_1}_w := \sum_i w_i\, \mathsf{F}^{k_1}_i$; $\mathsf{F}^{\mathrm{leg}}_w := \sum_{k_1} \xi_{(k_1, \mathrm{leg})}(w)\, \mathsf{F}^{k_1}_w$; $\mathsf{Y}_w := \sum_i w_i\, \mathsf{Y}_i$.

(6) $\mathsf{P}^{\mathrm{key},j}_w := \sum_k h^{(j)}_{\mathrm{key},k}\, \mathsf{P}^{\mathrm{quo}}_k$; $\mathsf{P}^{\mathrm{oth},j}_w := \sum_k h^{(j)}_{\mathrm{oth},k}\, \mathsf{P}^{\mathrm{quo}}_k$; $\mathsf{P}^{\mathrm{rem},j}_w := \sum_k R^{(j)}_{w,k}\, \mathsf{P}^{\mathrm{rem}}_k$.

(7) $(\Lambda, \Psi) := \mathsf{Comb}(ct_2)$; $(\Lambda^\alpha, \Psi^\alpha) := \mathsf{Comb}(ct_2^\alpha)$.

(8) $\Lambda' := \Lambda^\alpha - \xi_{\mathrm{key}}(w) \cdot \mathsf{K}^\alpha - c_w \cdot \Psi^\alpha$.

(9) The search: $t$ is the integer of least absolute value with $|t| \le B$ and $t \cdot \Psi^\alpha = \Lambda'$.

(10) If there is no such integer, return $\bot$.

(11) $K := \xi_{\mathrm{key}}(w)^{-1} \cdot ( \Lambda - (c_w + t) \cdot \Psi )$.

(12) Return $\tilde{m} \oplus H_{\mathsf{key}}(K)$.

$\mathsf{Comb}(ct_2)$, which uses the sums of lines (5) and (6); on $ct_2^\alpha$, every element of $ct_2$ is replaced by its $\alpha$-copy.

(a) $\mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{leg}}_w := \sum_i w_i\, \mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{leg}}_i$; $\mathsf{B}_w := \sum_{(a,\iota) \in \mathcal{I}} \sum_e x^\iota_{a,e}\, \mathsf{B}^\iota_{a,e}$.

(b) $\Lambda := \sum_{\mathrm{leg}} e( \mathsf{F}^{\mathrm{leg}}_w, \mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{leg}}_w ) - \sum_{j<J} e( \mathsf{P}^{\mathrm{key},j}_w,\ \xi_{\mathrm{key}}(w)\, \mathsf{B}^{\mathrm{quo}}_{c_{\mathrm{key}},j} ) - \sum_{j<J} e( \mathsf{P}^{\mathrm{oth},j}_w,\ \sum_{c \ne c_{\mathrm{key}}} \xi_c(w)\, \mathsf{B}^{\mathrm{quo}}_{c,j} ) - \sum_{j<J'} e( \mathsf{P}^{\mathrm{rem},j}_w,\ \sum_{c} \xi_c(w)\, \mathsf{B}^{\mathrm{rem}}_{c,j} ) - e( \mathsf{Y}_w, \mathsf{B}_w )$.

(c) $\Psi := \sum_{\mathrm{leg}} e( \mathsf{F}^{\mathrm{leg}}_{w,1}, \mathsf{S}^{\mathrm{leg}} )$.

(d) Return $(\Lambda, \Psi)$.

The pairing of a pair in $\mathbb{G}_1^2$ with a pair in $\mathbb{G}_2^2$ is the sum of the pairings of their coordinates, $\mathsf{F}^{\mathrm{leg}}_{w,1}$ is the first coordinate of $\mathsf{F}^{\mathrm{leg}}_w$, and $x^\iota_{a,e}$ is the coefficient of $T^e$ in $x^\iota_a$. In line (6), $h^{(j)}_{\mathrm{key}}, h^{(j)}_{\mathrm{oth}} \in \mathbb{F}_q^{<\Delta}[X]$ for $j < J$ and $R^{(j)}_w \in \mathbb{F}_q^{<\Delta'}[X]$ for $j < J'$ are the chunks of $h_{\mathrm{key}}$, $h_{\mathrm{oth}}$, and $R_w$, as in $h_{\mathrm{key}}(X) = \sum_{j<J} X^{j\Delta}\, h^{(j)}_{\mathrm{key}}(X)$, with coefficients $h^{(j)}_{\mathrm{key},k}$, $h^{(j)}_{\mathrm{oth},k}$, and $R^{(j)}_{w,k}$ of $X^k$; $c_w$ is the center for the centered sampler $\mathcal{D}_g$. Line (9) states the search by its result: any algorithm that finds this integer serves.
nodes.explain: Decryption with a witness $w$ combines the published elements along the honest stack of $w$. It sums the factors with the bits of $w$ and the public weights, and pairs once per right leg and coordinate. Along the honest stack these pairings encode three things: the search term $r(w)\,\psi$, the QAP term, and the terms of the tie masks. Pairings of the quotient and remainder powers with their bases reduce the QAP term to $\xi_{\mathrm{key}}(w)\,\kappa$, and one pairing with the cancellation bases removes the masks' terms, which leaves $\Lambda = [\xi_{\mathrm{key}}(w)\,\kappa + r(w)\,\psi]_T$ and $\Psi = [\psi]_T$ (this is Lemma 5.4). The decryptor does not know $r(w)$, so it searches on the $\alpha$-copies for $t = r(w) - c_w$, then removes the search term from $\Lambda$ and is left with the key element. Usual misreading: the search runs on the $\alpha$-copies, where $\mathsf{K}^\alpha$ is published, and its result is then used on the plain elements.

nodes.label: App. B.3, Stacks and kernel vectors
nodes.name: Honest and usable stacks, kernel vectors, short multiples
nodes.statement: The stack of a vector $v \in \mathbb{F}_q^{N+1}$ is $\mathbf{H}(v) := (\xi_c(v)\, v v^\top)_{c \in C}$, the honest stack of a witness; $v$ is a kernel vector if it is nonzero and $z(v) = 0$; a short multiple of $v$ is an $x \in \mathbb{Z}^{N+1}$ with $\|x\|_\infty \le \beta$ whose reduction modulo $q$ is a nonzero multiple of $v$; and the search vector is the $r$ of $\mathsf{Enc}$. Here $\beta$ is the MSIS norm bound. A stack is usable if it passes and satisfies the ties.
nodes.explain: When the adversary succeeds with a heavy stack, the proof looks at the stack's row space. Either it contains a kernel vector, a nonzero vector on which every public form vanishes, or it does not. A kernel vector is only given modulo $q$, while a Module-SIS solution is a short integer vector, so the proof asks for a short multiple: an integer vector with entries at most $\beta$ in absolute value that reduces to a nonzero multiple of the kernel vector. Without a kernel vector, the classification lemma (Lemma B.6) shows that a usable stack of rank at most three is a combination of honest stacks of witnesses. Tiny example: modulo $q = 101$, the vector $(0, 34, 1)$ has the multiple $(0, 1, 3)$, since $3 \cdot 34 = 102$. Usual misreading: a kernel vector need not be short or Boolean, and it has $v_0 = 0$, because the first form is $w_0$.

nodes.label: Lemma B.7, conditions (I1) to (I6)
nodes.name: Constants and conditions of the inverse theorem
nodes.statement:
The inverse theorem (Lemma B.7) and the lemmas of its proof are stated for a prime $q$, the number $N$ of unknowns, the range $g$, the threshold $\theta$, an integer $\beta$, an integer $b$, and positive reals $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$, $R_{\mathrm{tr}}$, $\Lambda_1, \Lambda_2, \Lambda_3$, $\Gamma_1, \Gamma_2, \Gamma_3$, $A_{\mathrm{inv}}$, $P_1$, and $P_2$ that satisfy the following conditions, in which $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}} := \theta - 100\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$, $\xi_{\mathrm{tr}} := (1 + 2/g)^{254}$, $H_3 := \xi_{\mathrm{tr}} / (g^3\mu_{\mathrm{tr}} - \xi_{\mathrm{tr}}/g)$, $H_1 := \Gamma_1/(g\mu_{\mathrm{tr}})$, $H_2 := \Gamma_2/(g^2\mu_{\mathrm{tr}})$, and $T_{\mathrm{tr}} := R_{\mathrm{tr}}\, g \sqrt{N/3}$.

(I1) $b \ge 7$ and $2^b \le g < 2^{254}$.

(I2) $R_{\mathrm{tr}} \ge 20$, $1000\, e^{-99 R_{\mathrm{tr}}^2/200} \le \varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}} < \mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$, and $g^3 \mu_{\mathrm{tr}} > \xi_{\mathrm{tr}}/g$.

(I3) $\Lambda_1 \ge 2\sqrt{3}\, R_{\mathrm{tr}} \sqrt{N}$, $\Lambda_2 \ge 27\sqrt{2}\, \pi R_{\mathrm{tr}}^2 N$, and $\Lambda_3 \ge 144\sqrt{2}\, \pi R_{\mathrm{tr}}^3 N^{3/2}$.

(I4) $\Gamma_3 \ge \xi_{\mathrm{tr}} (1 + H_3/g)$; $A_{\mathrm{inv}} \ge \mu_{\mathrm{tr}}/(\mu_{\mathrm{tr}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}})$; $P_2^{b-1} \ge (g^{-3} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}})/\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$ and $P_1^{b-1} \ge (g^{-2} + 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}})/\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$; $\Gamma_2^{b-1} \ge g^{-2}/\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$ and $\Gamma_1^{b-1} \ge g^{-1}/\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$; $\Gamma_2 \ge A_{\mathrm{inv}} \Lambda_1 \Gamma_3 P_2$ and $\Gamma_1 \ge A_{\mathrm{inv}} \max\{\Lambda_1 \Gamma_2, \Lambda_2 \Gamma_3\}\, P_1$.

(I5) $\Lambda_d \Gamma_d < \mu_{\mathrm{tr}} q$ for $d \in \{1,2,3\}$; $g^{-4} < \mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$; and $H_1 T_{\mathrm{tr}} < q$, $4 H_2 T_{\mathrm{tr}}^2 < q$, and $54 H_3 T_{\mathrm{tr}}^3 < q$.

(I6) $2\beta < q$, $H_1 \le \beta$, $2 H_2\, q \le \beta^2$, and $6 \lfloor H_3 \rfloor q^2 \le \beta^3$.
nodes.explain: The inverse theorem is proved with explicit constants, and its helper lemmas (prefix lattices, trimming, sparsity, regularization) are stated in terms of the same constants. This blob collects them so that each lemma can be read alone. Here $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$ is the density that one trimming may lose and $R_{\mathrm{tr}}$ the radius of the trimming ellipsoid; $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$, slightly below $\theta$, is the density that survives the losses; the $\Lambda_d$ are the geometric factors from counting lattice points in an ellipsoid; the $\Gamma_d$ bound the product of fiber density and height that makes a lattice of rank $d$ regular; the $H_d$ bound heights; and $\beta$ is the norm bound of the short multiple. The conditions (I1) to (I6) are the inequalities that the steps of the proof need, and admissibility condition (P3) asks for them. Usual misreading: nothing here is asymptotic. These are concrete inequalities to check at given parameters, and $b$ is only an auxiliary integer with $2^b \le g$.

nodes.label: Definition B.1
nodes.name: The events $\mathsf{Tgt}$ and $\mathsf{Fail}$ and the bound $E$
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathsf{Tgt}$ be the event that $\mathcal{A}$ queries $H_{\mathsf{key}}$ at $[\kappa]_T$, $\mathsf{Fail}$ the event that $\mathcal{E}$ outputs no witness of $S$, and $f_i := \Pr[\mathsf{Tgt} \wedge \mathsf{Fail}]$ in the experiment of extractability with $b = i$. Of the adversary's $L$ labels (the generators' and the ciphertext's), $L_1$, $L_2$, and $L_T = 2$ are in $\mathbb{G}_1$, $\mathbb{G}_2$, and $\mathbb{G}_T$; $\varepsilon_f := (3D + 2n + 2K_1 + 67)/(q - D)$ bounds the probability of a coincidence in $\mathbb{F}_q$; and $\mathcal{A}$ makes at most $Q < 2^\lambda$ calls to $\mathcal{O}_{\mathsf{GG}}$ and at most $Q_H \le 2^\lambda$ queries to $H_{\mathsf{key}}$.

Bound $E$. Let $N_{\mathrm{cmp}}(u) := uL + u(u+1)/2$ and $N_{\mathsf{free}} := 2^{\ell_{\mathsf{lab}}} - L - 3 \cdot 2^{\lambda+1} - 1$, which is positive under admissibility condition (P2), $3(L + 3 \cdot 2^{\lambda+1} + 1) \le q$. For an integer $u \ge 0$,

$E(u) := ( \binom{L_1}{2} + \binom{L_2}{2} + \binom{L_T}{2} + L ) \varepsilon_f + N_{\mathrm{cmp}}(u) (\theta + \varepsilon_f) + ( \binom{L + 3u}{2} + L + 3u ) \varepsilon_f + (8u + 8)\, \varepsilon_f + (2L + 4u + 2^{\lambda+2}) / N_{\mathsf{free}} + 4u \cdot 2^{-126} + 2^{-128}$.

The security proof uses $E$ at $u := 2Q + 2$. It pays for what the generic model leaves to chance in $Q$ calls: guessed labels, coincidences in $\mathbb{F}_q$, comparisons that succeed with a light stack, and unlucky coins of the extractor and the reductions.
nodes.explain: $E$ is the ledger of everything in the security proof that is left to chance in the generic model. The proof shows that an adversary reaches the hidden key element only in a few ways, and each unlikely way is paid by terms of $E$: two elements given to the adversary that happen to coincide, a comparison that succeeds by a lucky guess about the hidden small integers (the term with $\theta$) or by a coincidence among the random coins (terms with $\varepsilon_f$), a made-up string that happens to be the label of the key element (the term with $N_{\mathsf{free}}$), and bad luck in the random choices of the reductions and the extractor. The argument $u$ counts steps; the proof takes $u = 2Q + 2$ for an adversary with $Q$ group-oracle calls. Usual misreading: $E$ does not contain the Module-SIS advantage, which is a separate term $s_b$ of the extraction theorem.

nodes.label: Sec. 5.4, Admissibility (P1) to (P5)
nodes.name: Admissible parameters
nodes.statement:
Admissible parameters meet the conditions of the construction and of its optimizations (those stated with the parameters of the scheme) and the five below; $\theta$ is the threshold above which a stack is heavy, and $\beta$ the MSIS norm bound.

(P1) $D \le J\Delta \le D + n$ and $n \le D$, which bounds the degrees of the published exponents in the coins of $\mathsf{Enc}$.

(P2) $3(L + 3 \cdot 2^{\lambda+1} + 1) \le q$, so that a run touches a small part of each group. Here $L$ counts the labels given to the adversary (the generators' and the ciphertext's).

(P3) The conditions (I1) to (I6) of the inverse theorem (Lemma B.7) on $(q, N, g, \theta, \beta)$, which include $g^{-4} < \theta$ and $2\beta < q$. Under them, a nonzero vector in the row space of a heavy stack on which all forms vanish has a short multiple, which solves MSIS.

(P4) $24\beta^4 < q^3$, so that the lifting step finds a short multiple if one exists, in polynomial time (Lemma B.9).

(P5) $E(2) \le 2^{-\lambda}$ and $E(2^{\lambda+1}) - E(2) \le 1 - 2^{-\lambda}$ for the quadratic polynomial $E$ of Definition B.1, an explicit bound on what is left to chance, so that the proof's generic term $E(2Q+2)$ is at most $(Q+1)/2^\lambda$ (Lemma B.2); this requires $\theta < 2^{-(2\lambda+1)}$.
nodes.explain: The extraction theorem is stated for admissible parameters, and each of the five conditions feeds one step of its proof. (P1) keeps the published exponents of bounded degree, so that a comparison that is not an identity holds only by a rare coincidence. (P2) makes each group large compared with what one run touches, so that guessing a label is unlikely. (P3) and (P4) concern the lattice branch: a kernel vector in the row space of a heavy stack must have a short multiple (P3), and a reduction must be able to find it in polynomial time (P4). (P5) says that the chance terms collected in $E$ add up to at most $(Q+1)/2^\lambda$. Tiny check: (P3) asks $g^{-4} < \theta$ and (P5) forces $\theta < 2^{-(2\lambda+1)}$, so $g$ must exceed $2^{(2\lambda+1)/4}$, about $2^{\lambda/2}$. Usual misreading: the conditions do not assume that Module-SIS is hard. They are inequalities on the parameters that can be checked, and the paper's instantiation meets them.

nodes.label: App. B.3, Coins, exponents, expressions
nodes.name: Coins, exponents, sectors, expressions and their stacks
nodes.statement:
From here on, the parameters, $S$, its evaluation points, and the scheme are those of the extraction theorem (Theorem 5.9). The matrix $M$ is fixed: the bounds on expressions, runs, and marks hold for each $M$, and the reductions, like the proof of the extraction bound, take $M$ uniform. The fourth term of $E(2)$ is $24\,\varepsilon_f$ and no term is negative; so $24\,\varepsilon_f \le E(2) \le 2^{-\lambda}$ by (P5), and $\varepsilon_f < 1$. A linear operation, a call of $\mathsf{add}$ or $\mathsf{smul}$, returns $\mathsf{lab}_s( c_1\, \mathsf{lab}_s^{-1}(\mathsf{u}_1) + c_2\, \mathsf{lab}_s^{-1}(\mathsf{u}_2) )$, where $c_1 = c_2 = 1$ for $\mathsf{add}(s, \mathsf{u}_1, \mathsf{u}_2)$, and $(c_1, c_2, \mathsf{u}_2) := (c, 0, \mathsf{u}_1)$ for $\mathsf{smul}(s, c, \mathsf{u}_1)$.

Coins and exponents. Let $\mathbf{c}$ be the tuple of the values that $\mathsf{Enc}$ samples after the seed and $r$, from $y$ to $\varepsilon$; it is valid if each entry lies in the set from which $\mathsf{Enc}$ samples it, which has at least $q - D$ elements, as $K_1 < n \le D$. The coins of $\mathsf{Enc}$ are a uniform valid $\mathbf{c}$ and an independent $r \gets \mathcal{D}_g$. For valid $\mathbf{c}$ and every $r \in \mathbb{F}_q^{N+1}$, $\mathsf{Enc}$ defines the exponent $\mathsf{X}(\mathbf{c},r)$ of each published element $\mathsf{X}$. The generators have exponent $1$, the coordinates $\mathsf{F}^{k_1}_{i,1}$ and $\mathsf{F}^{k_1}_{i,2}$ of $\mathsf{F}^{k_1}_i$ have $\pi_{k_1} y_i$ and $\pi_{k_1} ( \Omega_{12}\, y_i + \Omega_{22}\, A_i(\tau) )$, and $\mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{leg}}_{j,1}$ and $\mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{leg}}_{j,2}$ of $\mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{leg}}_j$ have $h^1_{\mathrm{leg},j} - (\Omega_{12} / \Omega_{22})\, h^2_{\mathrm{leg},j}$ and $h^2_{\mathrm{leg},j} / \Omega_{22}$, for the entries $h^1_{\mathrm{leg},j}$ and $h^2_{\mathrm{leg},j}$ of $H^{\mathrm{leg}}_j$; so $r$ enters only through the term $s_{\mathrm{leg}}\, r_j$ of the $\mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{leg}}_{j,1}$ and their $\alpha$-copies. Each exponent is homogeneous in each of $\pi$, $\zeta$, $\zeta'$, $\zeta''$ and, jointly, in $(\Omega_{12}, \Omega_{22})$, written $\Omega$; its class is the monomial of these degrees. For a sector $\mathsf{s} \in \{\mathrm{plain}, \alpha\}$ and $\mathsf{X}$ in $ct_2$, $\mathsf{X}^{\mathsf{s}}$ is $\mathsf{X}$ or its $\alpha$-copy, of exponent $\alpha_{\mathsf{s}}\, \mathsf{X}(\mathbf{c}, r)$, for $\alpha_{\mathsf{s}} := 1$ or $\alpha$.

Expressions. Let $\mathcal{X}_1$ consist of $G_1$ and the elements of $ct_1$, and $\mathcal{X}_2$ of $G_2$ and those of $ct_2$ and $ct_2^\alpha$. An expression $\mathsf{E}$ of $\mathbb{G}_1$ or $\mathbb{G}_2$ is a vector in $\mathbb{F}_q^{\mathcal{X}_1}$ or $\mathbb{F}_q^{\mathcal{X}_2}$, read as $\sum_a \mathsf{E}_a\, a$; its value is $\operatorname{val}(\mathsf{E}; \mathbf{c}, r) := \sum_a \mathsf{E}_a\, a(\mathbf{c},r)$. One of $\mathbb{G}_T$ is a pair $\mathsf{D} = ( (\mathsf{D}_{ab})_{a \in \mathcal{X}_1, b \in \mathcal{X}_2}, \mathsf{D}_K )$, read as $\sum_{a,b} \mathsf{D}_{ab}\, e(a,b) + \mathsf{D}_K\, \mathsf{K}^\alpha$, of value $\operatorname{val}(\mathsf{D}; \mathbf{c}, r) := \sum_{a,b} \mathsf{D}_{ab}\; a(\mathbf{c},r)\, b(\mathbf{c},r) + \mathsf{D}_K\, \alpha\, \kappa$; $G_T$ is the pair $(G_1, G_2)$, and the pairing of $\mathsf{E}_1$ and $\mathsf{E}_2$ is $(\mathsf{E}_{1,a} \mathsf{E}_{2,b})_{a,b}$. The terms without $\alpha$ form the plain sector, and those with $\alpha$ the alpha sector.

Stacks and identities. Let $\mathsf{D}$ be an expression of $\mathbb{G}_T$ and $\mathsf{s}$ a sector. For a cell $c = (k_1, \mathrm{leg})$, let $W^{\mathsf{s}}_c(\mathsf{D})$ be the matrix with entries $\mathsf{D}_{ab}$ for $a = \mathsf{F}^{k_1}_{i,1}$ and $b = (\mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{leg}}_{j,1})^{\mathsf{s}}$, in row $i$ and column $j$, and let $u^{\mathsf{s}}_c(\mathsf{D})$ be the vector with entries $-\mathsf{D}_{ab}$ for $a = \mathsf{F}^{k_1}_{i,1}$ and $b = (\mathsf{S}^{\mathrm{leg}})^{\mathsf{s}}$. The stack of $\mathsf{D}$ in sector $\mathsf{s}$ is $\mathbf{W}^{\mathsf{s}}(\mathsf{D}) := (W^{\mathsf{s}}_c(\mathsf{D}))_{c \in C}$. For $\chi \in \mathbb{F}_q$ and $r \in \mathbb{F}_q^{N+1}$, $\mathsf{D}$ is $\chi\kappa$ identically at $r$ if $\operatorname{val}(\mathsf{D}; \mathbf{c}, r) = \chi\, \kappa(\mathbf{c})$ for every valid $\mathbf{c}$, and formally if this holds at every $r$. Two expressions of one group are formally equal if their values agree at every valid $\mathbf{c}$ and every $r$.
nodes.explain: In the generic model the adversary can only add, scale and pair what it was given, so every element it forms is described by an expression: its coefficients on the published elements, or on pairs of them in the target group. The value of an expression is the corresponding formula in the coins of encryption. For example, $G_T$ is the expression with coefficient 1 on the pair $(G_1, G_2)$, of value 1. The proof asks whether a comparison holds as an identity in the coins or only for special values. The stack of a target-group expression collects, cell by cell, its coefficients on pairs of first coordinates of a left and a right factor: the matrices along which the adversary combined the hidden tables. Sectors separate pairs with $ct_2$ from pairs with its $\alpha$-copy. Usual misreading: identically at $r$ fixes the search vector and varies only the other coins; formally also varies $r$.

nodes.label: App. B.4, Runs, the monitor, good and charged marks
nodes.name: Runs, the monitor, and first marks (good, charged)
nodes.statement:
Runs. The run $\mathsf{R}_m$ is the experiment of extractability until $\mathcal{A}$ outputs, with $\mathsf{Enc}$ encrypting $m$ and no bit $b$; the $L$ labels given to $\mathcal{A}$ are received. On every run with $m_0$ or $m_1$, $\mathcal{A}$ makes at most $Q < 2^\lambda$ calls to $\mathcal{O}_{\mathsf{GG}}$, rejected ones included, and at most $Q_H \le 2^\lambda$ queries to $H_{\mathsf{key}}$; we may assume it on every sequence of answers, as stopping $\mathcal{A}$ before a call or query beyond these changes no such run. The label of $[\kappa]_T$ is the target label.

The monitor. A label that $\mathcal{A}$ guesses gets a new guess variable (M2); so a generic expression is an expression over $\mathcal{X}_1$ and $\mathcal{X}_2$ enlarged by guess variables of $\mathbb{G}_1$ and $\mathbb{G}_2$, plus, in $\mathbb{G}_T$, a linear combination of guess variables of $\mathbb{G}_T$. Let $\mathsf{X}^\circ$ be $\mathsf{X}$ with every guess variable set to zero. Generic expressions are formally equal if the coefficients of each product of guess variables in them are, the empty product included, and $\mathsf{X}$ has a guess variable if it is not formally equal to $\mathsf{X}^\circ$.
