The monitor, a function of a finished run for the analysis only, reads the calls of $\mathcal{A}$ to $\mathcal{O}_{\mathsf{GG}}$ and its queries to $H_{\mathsf{key}}$, in order, and keeps for each group a table of entries, labels with generic expressions. It stops when it sets a mark, the run's first mark; a run in $\mathsf{Tgt}$ has one (M4).

(M1) Start. The received labels are entered with the expressions of their elements. The mark is $\mathsf{init}$ if two received elements of a group have one label and expressions that are not formally equal.

(M2) Operand. An operand string of a linear operation or pairing, answered or rejected, that is a label of its group and has no entry, a guessed label, is entered with a new guess variable.

(M3) Result. A result is that of an answered linear operation or pairing, computed from the entries of its operands, or, at the first answered name request on a label $\mathsf{u}$, the negative of the entry of $\mathsf{u}$, at the other label of its name. A result $\mathsf{F}$ at a label without an entry is entered; at a label with an entry $\mathsf{X}$ not formally equal to $\mathsf{F}$, the mark is $\mathsf{coll}$, or $\mathsf{diff}(\mathsf{F}^\circ - \mathsf{X}^\circ)$ if the group is $\mathbb{G}_T$ and $\mathsf{F} - \mathsf{X}$ has no guess variable.

(M4) Target. The first query of $H_{\mathsf{key}}$ at the target label sets $\mathsf{key}(\mathsf{X}^\circ)$ if the label has an entry $\mathsf{X}$, but $\mathsf{coll}$ if $\mathsf{X}$ has a guess variable, and $\mathsf{guess}$ if it has no entry.

Good and charged marks. A mark $\mathsf{diff}(\mathsf{D})$ or $\mathsf{key}(\mathsf{D})$ has the expression $\mathsf{D}$ and the multiple $\chi = 0$ or $1$. Its mark stack is $\mathbf{W}^{\mathrm{plain}}(\mathsf{D})$ if this stack is nonzero and $\mathbf{W}^{\alpha}(\mathsf{D})$ otherwise, and its mark sector is this stack's sector. The mark is good if $\mathsf{D}$ is $\chi\kappa$ identically at the run's search vector $r$ and its mark stack is nonzero and heavy; this stack is then usable (by the view lemma, Lemma B.4(a)), of rank at most three (by the heavy stacks lemma, Lemma B.8(a)). A first mark is charged if it is $\mathsf{coll}$, or has an expression and is not good; so a first mark is $\mathsf{init}$, $\mathsf{guess}$, charged, or good.
nodes.explain: The monitor is a device of the proof only. It replays a finished run of the adversary and writes, next to every label the adversary touched, the expression that the adversary computed there. It stops at the first event that expressions alone do not explain: two expressions that are not formally equal land on one label, or the adversary queries the key oracle at the label of the key element. That event is the first mark. A mark is good when the adversary's success is an identity in all coins except the search vector and its stack is nonzero and heavy; from this case a witness or a Module-SIS solution is obtained. A collision mark, or a mark with an expression that is not good, is charged to $E$. Usual misreading: good does not mean harmless. A good mark is the adversary's real success, the one that the extractor and the reductions exploit.

nodes.label: App. B.4, The coupling and the symbolic game
nodes.name: The coupling and the symbolic game
nodes.statement:
The coupling. Let $\mathsf{R}_\$$ be $\mathsf{R}_m$ with a uniform string $h$ in place of the masked message $m \oplus H_{\mathsf{key}}([\kappa]_T)$, so $\mathsf{Enc}$ does not query $H_{\mathsf{key}}$. In $\mathsf{R}_m$ the value of $H_{\mathsf{key}}$ at the target label is uniform and enters only the masked message and answers to queries there. So $\mathsf{R}_m$ has the law of $\mathsf{R}_\$$ with $H_{\mathsf{key}}$ answering $h \oplus m$ at the target label, and on the same coins they agree up to and including the first query of $\mathcal{A}$ there, without its answer. This part, with the label injections and the coins of $\mathsf{Enc}$, determines $\mathsf{Tgt}$ and the first mark; so their probabilities may be computed in $\mathsf{R}_\$$, where $h$ and $H_{\mathsf{key}}$ are independent of the label injections and the coins of $\mathsf{Enc}$.

The symbolic game. In the symbolic game, $\mathcal{A}$ runs as in $\mathsf{R}_\$$, but $\mathcal{O}_{\mathsf{GG}}$ knows only the images of the label injections, the sets of labels: it keeps the monitor's table by (M1) to (M3), giving each received element and each result the label of the entry formally equal to it or else a uniformly random label of its group without an entry, which exists by (P2). It rejects calls as in the generic bilinear group model, so a name request unless it is on a received label of $\mathbb{G}_T$ or the answer to a linear operation in $\mathbb{G}_T$ or a pairing, and answers one with the name of its label and its result's. So the game uses no coin of $\mathsf{Enc}$, which allows a union bound; the evaluation, made afterwards, samples $(\mathbf{c}, r)$ as $\mathsf{Enc}$ does and an independent uniform value in $\mathbb{F}_q$ for every guess variable, giving every entry a value. A collision is a pair of entries $\mathsf{X}$, $\mathsf{X}'$ of one group, not formally equal, with equal values; it occurs when the later of the two is made, and has $\mathsf{D} := \mathsf{X} - \mathsf{X}'$ and $\chi := 0$. A key value is an entry $\mathsf{X}$ of $\mathbb{G}_T$ of value $\kappa$; it has $\mathsf{D} := \mathsf{X}$ and $\chi := 1$. Either event is good if $\mathsf{D}$ lies in $\mathbb{G}_T$, has no guess variable, and meets the conditions of a good mark at the evaluation's $r$, and bad otherwise.
nodes.explain: Two devices let the proof compute probabilities without the adversary's choices depending on the secret coins. The coupling replaces the masked message by a random string: until the adversary queries the key oracle at the key element it sees no difference, so that query and the first mark can be studied without the message. The symbolic game goes further: the oracle answers by comparing expressions formally and uses no coin of encryption; the coins are sampled afterwards. The paper notes that this game agrees with a run until values collide, that is, until two entries that are not formally equal get equal values. Since the game is fixed before the coins, each possible collision or key value can be bounded separately and the bounds added. Usual misreading: the symbolic game is not the adversary's real view; it matches the real run only up to the first collision.

nodes.label: App. B.4, Records
nodes.name: Records kept by the reductions and the extractor
nodes.statement: The reductions and the extractor follow the answered calls and keep for a label of each group a computable record of an expression: a reduction its value at a point and its formula in the calls, the extractor its sketch data. They start from the received labels, give an operand without a record that of $0$, which it keeps, compute the record of a result from those of its operands, and keep it if its label has none. Until the monitor sets a mark, a label with a record has an entry $\mathsf{X}$, and the record is that of an expression formally equal to $\mathsf{X}^\circ$; an entry whose label has no record is a guess variable that no answered call had as an operand, so it occurs in no result. By induction: $\mathsf{X} \mapsto \mathsf{X}^\circ$ commutes with linear combinations and pairings, and a result that sets no mark meets no entry or one formally equal to it. So at a first mark $\mathsf{diff}(\mathsf{D})$, set by a result $\mathsf{F}$ at a label with the entry $\mathsf{X}$, the label has a record, at the latest from this call if it is one of its operands, as $\mathsf{F} - \mathsf{X}$ has no guess variable, and the result's record minus the label's is that of $\mathsf{D}$, up to formal equality. Formally equal expressions of $\mathbb{G}_T$ have equal stacks, by the view lemma (Lemma B.4(a)) for their difference at every $r$, so equal sketches.
nodes.explain: The extractor and the reductions do not store a full expression for every label, which has one coefficient per pair of published elements. Each keeps a small summary, a record, and updates it along the adversary's calls: the record of a result is computed from the records of its operands. A reduction records the value of the expression at a point of its own; the extractor records sketch data. The invariant stated here makes the summaries trustworthy: until the first mark, a label with a record carries the summary of the expression that the monitor wrote there, with guess variables set to zero. So at a first mark that compares two expressions, the difference of the two records is the record of the mark's expression. Usual misreading: records are computed by real algorithms, while the monitor is an analysis device; the invariant links the two.

nodes.label: App. B.5, The reductions (R1) to (R5)
nodes.name: The reductions $\mathcal{B}_0$ and $\mathcal{B}_1$
nodes.statement:
Each reduction $\mathcal{B}_b$ of the extraction theorem tries up to two expressions from a private monitor and, if one is a good first mark's, recovers the row space of its mark stack from three random combinations of the rows, gradients in $r$, which cost $O(1)$ operations for each call of $\mathcal{A}$, while an expression has $|\mathcal{X}_1| |\mathcal{X}_2| + 1$ coefficients:

(R1) Run. On a challenge $A \in R_q^{k \times \ell}$, sample a uniform seed $\mathsf{seed}$ and set $H_{\mathsf{seed}}(\mathsf{seed}, i, j)$ to $A_{i,j}$ for $i \in [k]$ and $j \in [\ell]$; encrypt $m_b$ with this seed, and run $\mathcal{A}$ on the ciphertext, ignoring its output and sampling the label injections lazily; $\mathcal{A}$ queries the ROs directly; sampling them lazily instead gives the same law and an algorithm without oracle access.

(R2) Coins. Sample independently, also of the run, a private test point $\mathsf{a}_{\mathrm{p}}$ and, for $l \in [3]$ and each sector $\mathsf{s}$, a recovery point $\mathsf{a}^{(l,\mathsf{s})}$: uniformly random valid tuples, each with a uniform vector of $\mathbb{F}_q^{N+1}$ in place of $r$.

(R3) Private monitor. Keep records with the values at $\mathsf{a}_{\mathrm{p}}$ to the end of the run. Then run (R4) and (R5) in turn with $\mathsf{D} := \mathsf{F} - \mathsf{X}$ for the first result $\mathsf{F}$ in $\mathbb{G}_T$ whose label has a record $\mathsf{X}$ of another value, and with $\mathsf{D}$ the record of the target label, each if it exists; then output $\bot$.

(R4) Gradients. For each $l$ and $\mathsf{s}$, compute $\nabla^{(l,\mathsf{s})}(\mathsf{D}) \in \mathbb{F}_q^{N+1}$, the gradient in $r$ at $\mathsf{a}^{(l,\mathsf{s})}$ of the value of the part of $\mathsf{D}$ in sector $\mathsf{s}$: with the exponents taken there, its entry $j$ is $\alpha_{\mathsf{s}} \sum_{\mathrm{leg}} s_{\mathrm{leg}} \sum_{a \in \mathcal{X}_1} a\, \mathsf{D}_{a b}$ for $b = (\mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{leg}}_{j,1})^{\mathsf{s}}$.

(R5) Output. Find a kernel vector $v$ in the span of the $\nabla^{(l,\mathsf{s})}(\mathsf{D})$ of the plain sector or, if there is none, of the alpha sector. If $v$ exists and $\mathsf{LIFT}(v)$ returns $x$, output $\hat x$ and stop. Here $\mathsf{LIFT}$ is the algorithm of the lifting step (Lemma B.9), which returns a short multiple of $v$, or $\bot$ if there is none, and $\hat x \in R^\ell$ has the entries $\hat x_j$ of the definition of forms, taken over $\mathbb{Z}$.

Running times count operations: arithmetic operations and equality tests in $\mathbb{F}_q$; additions, subtractions, halvings, and comparisons of integers of absolute value below $2^{\ell_{\mathsf{lab}}}$; XORs and writes of strings of at most $\ell_{\mathsf{lab}}$ bits or elements of $\mathbb{F}_q$; uniform samples from an explicitly given finite set, or from the elements of $\mathbb{F}_q$ or strings of length $\ell_{\mathsf{lab}}$ that are not keys of a table; oracle calls; and insertions into and lookups in tables keyed by labels, names, oracle inputs, or elements of $\mathbb{F}_q$, where an insertion at a key that is present keeps and returns the stored value. They also count the length of the algorithm's description, advice included, one for each element of $\mathbb{F}_q$ or string of length $\ell_{\mathsf{lab}}$, with code packed into such strings. The oracle calls of $\mathcal{A}$ count in its running time $t$, the lifting step counts bit operations on its integers, and the constants in $O()$ are absolute.
nodes.explain: A reduction turns the adversary into a Module-SIS solver, for the case where the row space of the adversary's heavy stack contains a kernel vector. It plants its challenge in the public matrix by programming the seed oracle, runs the adversary once, and follows its group-oracle calls. It keeps cheap records: the value of each expression at a private random point, which detects the first label where two different expressions meet. For that expression it computes three gradients in the search vector at random points; these are random combinations of the rows of the stack, which span its row space except with small probability (Lemma B.14). It then finds a kernel vector in that span and lifts it to a short integer vector. Usual misreading: the reduction ignores the adversary's output and does not observe its random-oracle queries, and there is one reduction for each message, $\mathcal{B}_0$ and $\mathcal{B}_1$.

nodes.label: App. B.6, Sketches and tests
nodes.name: The extractor $\mathcal{E}$: sketches and tests
nodes.statement:
Sketches. $\mathcal{E}$ samples, for every cell $c$, $l \in [3]$, and sector $\mathsf{s}$, an independent uniform probe vector $v^{(l,\mathsf{s})}_c \in \mathbb{F}_q^{N+1}$. The sketches of an expression $\mathsf{D}$ of $\mathbb{G}_T$ in sector $\mathsf{s}$ are the vectors $\sum_c W^{\mathsf{s}}_c(\mathsf{D})\, v^{(l,\mathsf{s})}_c$, linear in $\mathsf{D}$. The record of a label, its sketch data, are in $\mathbb{G}_T$ the sketches of its expression, not its $|\mathcal{X}_1| |\mathcal{X}_2| + 1$ coefficients; in $\mathbb{G}_1$ the $K_1$ vectors $a_{k_1}$ of its coefficients on the $\mathsf{F}^{k_1}_{i,1}$; and in $\mathbb{G}_2$, with $b_{\mathrm{leg},\mathsf{s}}$ the vector of its coefficients on the $(\mathsf{H}^{\mathrm{leg}}_{j,1})^{\mathsf{s}}$, the $9n$ numbers $\langle b_{\mathrm{leg},\mathsf{s}}, v^{(l,\mathsf{s})}_c \rangle$ for $c = (k_1, \mathrm{leg})$. A pairing has $W^{\mathsf{s}}_c = a_{k_1} b_{\mathrm{leg},\mathsf{s}}^\top$ and the sketches $\sum_c \langle b_{\mathrm{leg},\mathsf{s}}, v^{(l,\mathsf{s})}_c \rangle\, a_{k_1}$.

Tests. A test of three vectors computes the reduced row echelon form of their span $\mathcal{V}'$, with coordinates in the order $0, \dots, N$. Its candidates are the vectors of $\mathcal{V}'$ with entry $1$ at coordinate $0$ and entries in $\{0,1\}$ at the other pivots: at most four, as the pivot entries determine a vector of $\mathcal{V}'$, and none unless $0$ is a pivot. It finds the first candidate that is a witness of $S$, or nothing. For every result in $\mathbb{G}_T$, after its operands have records and before its own is kept, $\mathcal{E}$ tests the sketches of the result's record and, if its label already has one, those of their difference, in the plain sector and then in the alpha sector. It outputs the first witness found, or $\bot$.
nodes.explain: The extractor reads a witness off the adversary's group-oracle calls. For every target-group element the adversary forms, it keeps three sketches per sector: the stack of the element's expression applied to random probe vectors. For symmetric matrices these are random vectors of the stack's row space, and three of them span a row space of dimension at most three except with small probability (Lemma B.16). If that row space contains a witness, the test finds it: it lists the vectors of the span that have 1 at coordinate 0 and are Boolean at the other pivots, at most four, and checks each against the system. Tiny example: if the span is the line through a witness $w$, the only candidate is $w$. Usual misreading: the extractor does not know when the first mark happens. It tests every result as it comes, and it checks candidates, so its output is always $\bot$ or a witness.

nodes.label: App. B.7, Boxes, prefixes, lattices
nodes.name: Boxes, prefixes, and lattice vocabulary (saturated, height, fibers, regular)
nodes.statement:
In the proof of the inverse theorem, $v$ is the vector of that theorem: nonzero, in $\mathbb{F}_q^{N+1}$, with $v_0 = 0$ and $\operatorname{gp}(v^\top) > \theta$. Symbols other than the theorem's are local to its proof.

Boxes and prefixes. For a finite set $I$, the box on $I$ is $[2, g+1]^I$, and $r_I$ is uniform on it, as $r_1, \dots, r_N$ are independent and uniform on $[2, g+1]$ for both samplers. The density of a set $F$ of box points is $\Pr[F] := |F|/g^{|I|}$; a condition on the entries at $I' \subseteq I$ has the same density in the boxes on $I'$ and $I$. For $u \in \mathbb{F}_q^I$, $\operatorname{gp}(u^\top)$ is the largest density of a modular fiber $\{ r : u^\top r = t \bmod q \}$, and $\operatorname{gp}(v^\top)$ is the guessing probability of the matrix $v^\top$, as $v_0 = 0$. Renumbering $1, \dots, N$, let $v_1, \dots, v_{N_0}$ be the nonzero ones among $v_1, \dots, v_N$, and $v_{[i]} := (v_1, \dots, v_i)$; a short multiple of $v_{[N_0]}$ (defined as for $v$), extended by zeros, is one of $v$ with $x_0 = 0$. Conditioning on $r_{i+1}$ shows that $\operatorname{gp}(v_{[i]}^\top)$ does not increase with $i$, and $g + 1 < q$ makes $x \mapsto v_1 x \bmod q$ injective on $[2, g+1]$; so $\theta < \operatorname{gp}(v^\top) = \operatorname{gp}(v_{[N_0]}^\top) \le \operatorname{gp}(v_{[i]}^\top) \le 1/g$ for $i \in [N_0]$.

Lattices. A lattice $\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^I$ of rank $d$ has basis matrices $B \in \mathbb{Z}^{I \times d}$, unique up to $B \mapsto BU$ for a unimodular $U$; $B_J$ denotes the rows $J \subseteq I$ of $B$. It is saturated if $\Theta = \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{R}}(\Theta) \cap \mathbb{Z}^I$, as are the integer points of any subspace; two saturated lattices of equal rank, one inside the other, are equal. For $d \ge 1$, its height $h(\Theta)$ is the largest $|\det B_J|$ over the sets $J$ of $d$ indices, and it has a largest minor at $J$ if $|\det B_J| = h(\Theta)$. Its fibers are the sets $\{ r : B^\top r = t \}$ of box points, for $t \in \mathbb{Z}^d$; its largest fiber density $m(\Theta)$ is the largest density of one, at most $g^{-d}$, as fixing the entries outside a set $J$ with $\det B_J \ne 0$ leaves at most one value of $r_J$, as in Odlyzko's lemma; and it is regular if $d \in [3]$ and $m(\Theta)\, h(\Theta) \le \Gamma_d/g^d$. As $(BU)^\top = U^\top B^\top$, none of these depends on $B$. The reduction of $\Theta$ modulo $q$ is $\bar\Theta := \{ x \bmod q : x \in \Theta \} = B\, \mathbb{F}_q^d$. A nonempty $F \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^I$ has affine dimension $\dim F$, that of the span of its differences, and normal lattice $F^\perp$ of the integer vectors whose inner product with the points of $F$ is constant, saturated of rank $|I| - \dim F$, as the orthogonal complement of a span of integer vectors has a basis of integer vectors. A set $F$ of box points lies in a fiber of $F^\perp$, so $\Pr[F] \le m(F^\perp)$, and if it lies in a fiber of $\Theta$, then $\Theta \subseteq F^\perp$.
nodes.explain: Vocabulary for the proof of the inverse theorem. The random integers $r_i$ range over a box; the density of a set of box points is its probability. A lattice is a set of integer vectors, each read as a linear function of $r$; its fibers are the sets of box points on which these functions take fixed values. The height is the largest minor of a basis matrix; the largest fiber density says how much of the box one fiber can hold. Regular means that the product of the two is small; saturated means that the lattice contains every integer vector of its real span. Tiny example: for $B=(1,1)^\top$ the fibers are the sets $r_1+r_2=t$, the height is 1, and the densest fiber, $t=g+3$, has density $1/g$. Usual misreading: a fiber is a set of box points, not a coset of the lattice; a modular fiber fixes a value modulo $q$, not over the integers.

nodes.label: App. B.7, Trimming
nodes.name: Trimming ellipsoids and trimmed sets
nodes.statement: For a lattice $\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^I$ of rank $d \in [3]$, with $|I| \le N$ and a basis matrix $B$, let $\mathcal{T}_\Theta$ be the trimming ellipsoid of the $y \in \mathbb{R}^d$ with $(y - y_\Theta)^\top \Sigma_\Theta^{-1} (y - y_\Theta) \le R_{\mathrm{tr}}^2$, where $y_\Theta := \frac{g+3}{2} B^\top \mathbf{1}$, for the all-ones vector $\mathbf{1}$, is the mean of $B^\top r_I$ and $\Sigma_\Theta := \frac{g^2}{12} B^\top B$. A set $F$ of points of a box on indices containing $I$ is trimmed by $\Theta$ if $B^\top r_I \in \mathcal{T}_\Theta$ for all $r \in F$, and $F$ trimmed by $\Theta$ is the set of these $r \in F$. Neither depends on $B$: replacing $B$ by $BU$ replaces $B^\top r_I - y_\Theta$ by $U^\top (B^\top r_I - y_\Theta)$ and $\Sigma_\Theta$ by $U^\top \Sigma_\Theta U$.
nodes.explain: Trimming removes the atypical points of a set of box points, so that what remains can be counted. Each $r_i$ is uniform on $g$ consecutive integers with mean $(g+3)/2$, so $B^\top r_I$ has mean $y_\Theta$; the trimming ellipsoid is the region whose distance from that mean, measured by $\Sigma_\Theta$, is at most $R_{\mathrm{tr}}$. A set is trimmed when all its points map into this region. The proof of the inverse theorem trims a dense set and then counts lattice points in the ellipsoid, while trimming lowers the density by at most $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$ (Lemma B.19).
